Physarum Polycephalum (Slime Mold): Chemical Properties   Olivia Cozariuc, Tamir Kegeles, Ethan Levene, Audrey Pepin Abstract The protist true slime mold  Physarum polycephalum  is a model organism, an organism sufficiently abundant and easily grown to the degree that a large body of scientific literature surrounds it. Possessing multiple phenotypic stages in its life cycle (spore, amoeboid, plasmodial, sclerotium), the plasmodial stage of the slime mold is its most recognizable. This iconic stage consists of a slimy network of veins which actively seek out sources of nutrition. It is in this stage that the slime mold is observed to solve pathfinding problems and inspire computational algorithms. Biological design solutions found in its locomotion and various taxis mechanisms point to the importance of chemical reactions in the organism. Nutrition affects slime mold behavior and pathfinding abilities with identifiable differences between starvation and satiation. Growth is directed both by chemical reactions in chemotaxis and by network organization via shuttle streaming, which interacts reciprocally with the actomyosin cortex. Finally, a resemblance is noted between the rhythmic self-organization of the slime mold and the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction, both in wave-like behavior and reaction specifics.   Introduction This paper follows our previous investigations of the slime mold’s properties in general and with a focus on its ability to solve mazes using basal intelligence. Firstly, the relationship between slime mold survival and the composition of its nutritional environment is described, specifically in reference to the optimal ratio of  proteins  to carbohydrates in its growth medium.  Physarum polycephalum  is sensitive to the protein-carbohydrate ratio of its nutritional intake. As such, the slime mold has been observed to directionally navigate towards optimal food sources via chemically enabled food-sense. Furthermore, migratory behavior is analyzed in the context of starvation and satiation. Migratory behavior and dynamic growth in the true slime mold are connected to shuttle streaming and tubular contractility, which are dependent on actomyosin interactions with calcium  ions  (Ca 2+ ). These interactions are enabled by chemical signaling from food sources, enabling a comprehensive solution for motility and food selectivity using the same signaling methods.   The next section focuses on the slime mold’s actomyosin network and its relation to dynamic growth. The interplay between myosin function, actin-myosin structures spanning Physarum Polycephalum and oscillation of Ca 2+  ions is explored in detail to explain the shuttle streaming and peristaltic wave organization discussed in our previous paper. We finish by introducing biolipids excreted by P. Polycephalum and their derivatives, both of which have clinical applications in cancer treatment.   Finally, we characterize Ca 2+  fluctuations and slime mold growth in reference to Belousov-Zhabotinsky reactions by highlighting commonalities in their wave-like propagation. Modeling the slime mold as a Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction elucidates how such a basal organism can manage transport and behavior as consequences of a chemical reaction rather than a thinking process.  In bio-computation, this comparison is used to enable biological computation using the slime mold’s behavior as outputs and its environment as inputs by modelling the slime mold as a wave-propagating reaction. Additionally, logic gates using the slime mold’s vein network are described.  Finally, we consider future applications of this comparison in cognition and scientific research.   Nutrition   Physarum polycephalum  consumes different substances to grow the necessary network and structure to thrive or to survive. One such category is carbohydrates and proteins, both playing a significant part in understanding the system’s nutritive intake. Carbohydrates are biomolecules made up of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms. Their structure can further be classified into saccharides, identifying the extent of the molecule. Proteins are polymers made of chains of amino acids connected with peptide linkages. If the slime mold consumes too much sugar or carbohydrates, osmotic pressure effects cause this higher concentration to increase the risk of mortality. Similarly, high protein concentration also changes the organism by fragmenting the plasmodium into multiple independent organisms (Dussutour et al., 2010). Therefore, different concentrations of each one lead to different structural adaptations and behaviors. There are favorable ratios of proteins to carbohydrates that allow an optimal growth, general health and survival, but this varies based on the context and environment. The effect of the consumption of various concentrations of carbohydrates and protein is shown in Fig. 1 introducing experimental results on survival rate, density, and growth rate.   
 Fig. 1: Demonstration of the differences after 60 hours in the behavior of 350 plasmodial fragments when placed in contact with carbohydrates and proteins. (Dussutour et al., 2010)  Slime mold’s growth is influenced by the difference in the quality of nutrients; it uses its veinous network to adapt and respond to nutritional cues through nutrient sensing, allowing growth responses and, consequently, movement. On nutrient-poor substrates, it grows sparsely and extensively, whereas on nutrient-rich substrates it grows in a compact format, even without veins sometimes. This compact growth shows a reduction in migration if resources are abundant in the surrounding environment of the organism. (Achenbach et al., 1979) Furthermore, macronutrient concentration is also significant regarding the overall behavior of  Physarum polycephalum . This is because the plasmodium can respond and sense the macronutrient content and accordingly adjust growth and movement, with the objective of optimizing carbohydrate and protein intake (Achenbach et al., 1979). The near-optimal protein-to-carbohydrate ratio allows minimal migration, and as you get further and further from this ratio, migration increases significantly. This migration, as shown in Fig. 2, shows the impact of the balance of macronutrients on the resulting movements of the slime mold.   
 Fig. 2 : Behavior of slime mold with regards to distinct ratios of protein to carbohydrate, for example, nine proteins to one carbohydrate. (A) represents an unrestricted general interaction between slime mold and food, (B) shows the preference of the organism regarding higher proteins concentrations rather than higher concentration of carbohydrates, and (C) illustrates the ideal ratios of nutrition the slime mold consumes. (Dussutour et al., 2010)  Starvation  The age of a microplasmodia, a plasmodium of  Physarum  created by shear forces and grown in a shaking liquid culture creating quasi-spherical vital fragments (Lee et al., 2018), is determined by external factors such as temperature and nutrient content. In the case of starvation, slime mold assures its survival by a structural adaptation called mesoplasmodial growth. The glucose depletion, low nutrients, and low vitality cause this growth to be an adaptative response to nutrient scarcity, and it might also be associated with a carbohydrate metabolism pathway. Alternatively, a  foraging  strategy might form during prolonged starvation and as a response to stimuli like temperature and light. This foraging strategy consists mostly of fragmentation growth and a reduction in invaginations, making the organism smaller and harder to detect. This form of morphogenesis representing an increase in the number of independent organisms can occur because of chemical exposure to  UV  irradiation, low temperatures, or in response to abundant nitrogenous resources. (Dussutour et al., 2010). Overall, starvation induces a foraging strategy, constituting a fragmentation process. This opens a larger area for food searches, helping the slime mold survive poor nutritional conditions.    Plasmodial Veins  The slime mold has a dynamic invagination system allowing adaptations to physiological needs. The invagination system is controlled by the vein’s nutritional content instead of physical properties, which explains why it is so dynamic, since the nutritional content is continuously changing depending on the environment. Two types of veins exist: the transporting and the nutrition-absorbing/excretory type (Wohlfarth-Bottermann, 1974). The nutritional veins have a plasmalemma invagination occupying about 80% of the total surface area of the species, while the transporting veins have only about 40% of the plasmalemma invagination. The increase in invagination allows the ectoplasmic tubes of plasmodial veins to absorb nutrients in a non-particular form more easily. This results in a migrating plasmodium front that primarily appears undifferentiated but, in truth, has endoplasmic channels and a system of plasmalemma invaginations or, in other words,  ectoplasmic tubes (Achenbach et al., 1979).  The chemistry behind plasmodial veins in  Physarum polycephalum  can be summarized with the complex plasmalemma invaginations happening in the ectoplasmic wall. This growth increases the surface area, and it also improves the absorption of nutrients and its consequent waste excretion. To stabilize the dynamic structure, OsO 4  is present highlighting that the invaginations are mostly present in the ectoplasmic regions instead of the endoplasmic region, where they can bind to actomyosin fibrils. These fibrils are made of actin and myosin, which facilitate the ectoplasmic contraction and relaxation, generating a hydrostatic pressure gradient inducing shuttle streaming within the endoplasmic core. This rhythmic expansion and contraction  patterns  are chemically controlled by ionic and osmotic shifts, overall improving nutrient and ion transport through plasmodial veins (Wohlfarth-Bottermann, 1974).  Nutrient Selectivity  The  Physarum polycephalum  has a flexible food search strategy that is comparable to the collective behaviors in social insects, fungi and other decentralized systems, where the search for food and exploitation strategies are controlled by the contact with resources. This behavior is shown in Fig. 3, where we can distinguish the search front as a collection of pseudopods searching for nutrients.  
 Fig. 3: General representation of the slime mold’s contact with a food source at the food disk, its search for nutrition by the search front and its pseudopods, during or after consumption of the food disk. (Latty & Beekman, 2009).  The amoeboid nature of plasmodia enables simultaneous searching and exploration for food, allowing biomass to form even on non-nutritive surfaces during this behavior (Latty & Beekman, 2009). Additionally, the difference in quality of nutrients is once again of significance during the food search. Indeed, the acellular slime mold has a certain knowledge of the different varieties of quality available, since it shows a significant preference between food options that vary in quality. In this decisional context, it will prefer the nutrient-rich option. This happens because there is a transfer of information between contractile regions of the tubule, which differs depending on the quality of the nutrient. When the food is of the same quality, information transfer is balanced. In contrast, in food of different quality, the regions close to the rejected food act as information sources, transferring the information around the chosen food (Ray et al., 2019). This is shown in Fig. 4, as the direction of information transfer between two of the same food sources is not precise, while the direction of information transfer between different food sources is precisely towards the higher quality one.  
 Fig. 4: Representation of information transfer direction depending on the same quality of 10% oat-agar, and different quality of oat-agar, 2% and 10%. (Ray et al., 2019)  Fractal dimension is an important index to characterize fractal patterns by quantifying their complexity, by using a ratio of the change in detail to the change in scale. (Zhang et al., 2018). The calculation of fractal dimension may be quantified as the following statistical relationship:          Where  D f  is the fractal dimension,  N(l)  is the number of spheres needed to cover an object, and  l  is the size of the spheres used as a measure (Klapetek, 2013).  As the food quality improves, the fractal dimension of the plasmodia increases, resulting in a more compact growth, contrary to the extensive growth seen with lower-quality food. More specifically, high-quality food triggers the plasmodia to search for nutrients locally in an area-restricted search tactic. Contrarily, lower-quality food leads to a broader and outward search, similar to the previously explained behavior associated with starvation. A summary of the search behavior and its connection to nutrient quality is shown in the graphs cumulated in Fig. 5.  
 Fig. 5: The importance of food quality is shown in three different graphs: a) Food quality versus fractal dimension, b) Food quality versus local fractal dimension, and c) Food quality versus proportion of local search. (Latty & Beekman, 2009)  Not only is the area of search influenced by food quality, but the timing of research behaviors also is influenced by this. The exploitation behavior of the slime mold causes the organism to abandon low-quality food sources rapidly, letting it initiate the search for better-quality food. Even before the disk of lower-quality nutrients is fully absorbed by the organism, the search behaviors are already triggered. For higher-quality food, the search will resume later as the organism is already satisfied. A similarity between low-quality food and high-quality food is the speed of consuming a food disk, which does not change between one or the other. This helps the plasmodium to exploit resources, and this behavior outcompetes bacteria and fungi. To optimize the overall intake of nutrients, the slime mold favors this search strategy in patchy, correlated landscapes. These are areas where it is easier for the organism to consume higher quality foods and leave the poorer quality food earlier (Latty & Beekman, 2009).  Finally,  Physarum polycephalum  holds a particular search strategy that prioritizes higher quality food due to the two types of veinous network associated with nutrition consumption: the transporting type and the nutrition absorbing type of vein. These components allow the species to optimize its energy usage while also favoring its most effective structure to be capable of movement.   Information Transfer  Since slime mold navigates through a maze because of its ability to sense, respond to, and adapt to external stimuli, the organism can go through a maze by following nutritional cues. This is possible because food stimuli generate intracellular signaling processes that include ATP and Ca 2+ . This is significant for protoplasmic flow as well as contraction-relaxation  cycles , which shows that the information transfer in the organism is connected to signaling that is nutrient-driven. Information transfer is, therefore, important for understanding how the slime mold can navigate through a maze. Studies have shown that attractive food sources cause local regions of a cell to act as information sources, and the more distant regions are the destinations where this information is received. This information generated by nutrient stimuli can change its direction of flow depending on the problem encountered by the organism. The plasmodium enters a decision-making phase that opens the possibility of adapting to internal communications depending on their nature, which results in problem-solving capabilities (Ray et al., 2019).   In summary, the information transfer between contractile regions is what helps the slime mold to make decisions regarding food sources and their quality. The maze mimics environmental mechanisms, where different paths transmit distinct food cues. As the organism senses its surroundings, nutrient signals along the path or at the exit guide its movement. To find an optimal path to the nutrient cues at the maze exit, for example, the transfer of information is made in a denser fashion with regard to higher-quality food than with lower-quality food. The contractile behavior in the tubules reflects the decision-making across the path choices. Just like the preference towards higher quality nutrients for general food searches, in a maze context, the same process applies, since it has the same aptitude to sense these variances and select the pathway that leads to the more suitable food source.   To summarize the role of nutrition in the maze-solving process,  Physarum polycephalum  can navigate through a maze because of the general and comprehensive information transfer throughout its entire system generated by nutrition cues. This is illustrated in Fig. 6, where slime mold solves a maze based solely on the nutritional cue at the end of the maze. This allows the organism to continuously balance its explorative and exploitative behaviors in order to find the most efficient path toward the exit or the food stimuli. This attitude is fed by the tubule’s contractile behavior that changes dynamically. The tubes contractile behavior is driven by the actin and myosin filaments, oscillation patterns of Ca 2+ concentrations and chemotaxis (Terry et al., 2009). Dead ends transfer less information, resulting in a loss of biomass in those areas, and nutrient-rich areas receive more information or a greater contractile behavior, resulting in a gain in biomass.  
 Fig. 6: Maze solving process of the slime mold with a nutritional stimuli at the end, showing its ability to find the shortest path possible. (Awad et al., 2021)  Dynamic Growth   Protoplasmic Streaming  Physarum polycephalum  present complex network of tubes spreading over surfaces. The plasmodium’s ramifications are anything but random. With information collected from the environment, the plasmodium can strategically orient its growth towards favorable conditions. The plasmodium’s size varies between 100μm to 10 cm (Kuroda et al., 2015). To ensure a growth at a rate of 1 mm to 1 cm per hour (Kay et al., 2022), the tubular network must work in harmony (Alim, 2018). An experiment by Adamatzky showed that, in a Petri dish, two plasmodia can even merge. Their tubes blend to form a new combined cell (Adamatzky, 2010). No matter the plasmodium’s size, the cell is able to function.  
 A remarkable coordination of all the parts of its intricate system is necessary to ensure a shift towards a specific direction. By the means of the various tubes, the plasmodium can even pursue different food tracks (Adamatzky, 2010). The process allowing the plasmodium to move and to grow in a structured way is known as protoplasmic streaming. The term protoplasm considers the cytoplasm with the nucleus (Uza & Kunita, 2024). Protoplasmic streaming relies on the control of the tubes’ diameter. Protoplasmic tubes are dynamic since they can vary in thickness and can be redirected depending on the location and the quantity of food present in the environment. The protoplasmic flow is bidirectional because the direction of propagation alternates periodically comparable to muscle contraction (Uza & Kunita, 2024).  A contraction results in a shrinkage of the tube’s diameter which could indicate that the tube was growing towards a poor environment with unfavorable conditions (Uza & Kunita, 2024). That local shrinkage will redirect the expansion towards another front where the tube will appear larger (Fig. 7).  
 Fig. 7:  Physarum plasmodium  migrating towards a hotter environment (Durham & Ridgway, 1976).  The fluctuation in thickness is a result of various biochemical and physicochemical processes (Uza & Kunita, 2024).  To understand the functioning of peristaltic streaming, it is important to be familiar with the chemical composition of the tubular network.  Inside the protoplasmic tubes also known as cytoplasmic tubes (Fig. 8), the cytoplasm travels passively (Nakamura & Kohama, 1999). The cytoplasm stream is paced by the contractions. Some investigators even compare  Physarum polycephalum  to a beating heart since the protoplasmic flow resembles a heart’s pulsation (Kishimoto, 1958). The slime mold’s cytoplasm is hemmed in a gel-like structure which acts as a protective barrier (Alim, 2018).   
 Fig. 8: Protoplasmic tubes of  Physarum polycephalum . Note that the cytoplasm travels through the tubular network. The main tubes appear darker (Adamatzky, 2015).  Actomyosin  Actin is a protein crucial for cell structure. It is present in most cells and especially abundant in muscle cells and in eukaryotic cells like  P. polycephalum . Specific proteins like fimbrin, fascin and alpha-actinin guide the assembly of actin bundles creating polar actin filaments found in the cytoskeleton (Laskey et al., 2024). The cytoskeleton in eukaryotic cells such as slime mold is formed of a system of filaments found in the cytoplasm. Comparable to a framework, the cytoskeleton maintains the cell’s shape and allows it to it be in motion (Laskey et al., 2024).   Actin has a strong predisposition to interact with other proteins such as cofilin, profilin and tromodulin (Dominguez & Holmes, 2011). This behavior enables actin-myosin interactions which then allows muscle contraction, cell division and cell travel (Cooper, 2000).   Myosin is another protein that can be found in the cytoskeleton. Myosin’s function is to convert chemical energy into mechanical energy (Cooper, 2000).  In other words, this protein acts as a motor fuelled with ATP. Subsequently, the myosin filaments slide onto the actin filaments causing, for example, the plasmodium to move (Laskey et al., 2024). However, the efficiency of actin-myosin interactions is at the mercy of calcium ions (Ca 2+ ) since they can interfere with the process and inhibit myosin and actin (Murakami-Murofushi et al., 2002). Calcium binds to protein like calmodulin which undergo conformational changes allowing it to interact with myosin light chain kinase (MLCK). Once activated, MLCK increases myosin-actin interactions in muscle cells but not in  P. polycephalum  (Nakamura & Kohama, 1999).  Physarum polycephalum’s  cytoplasm is surrounded by actin and myosin forming a mesh-like structure (Fig. 9). The tubes’ thickness is in fact controlled by the actomyosin contraction (Uza & Kunita, 2024). The term actomyosin refers to the combination of actin and myosin forming a structure present in the cytoskeleton of the cell. Actomyosin is contractile, a key element allowing protoplasmic streaming. Therefore, actomyosin can contract and relax leading to variation in the diameter of the protoplasmic tubes (Uza & Kunita, 2024). Intracellular and extracellular phenomena can alter actomyosin’s action. A decisive factor is the concentration of Ca 2+  (Nakamura & Kohama, 1999).   
 Fig. 9: Actin filaments formation. Note the mesh-like structure (Quezada et al., 2022).   Calcium Inhibition  Intracellular levels of Ca 2+  are rigorously regulated by cells. If the concentration exceeds 0.2 micromoles per liter, the endoplasmic reticulum will trap the ion excess, and the plasma membrane will block the entry of Ca 2+  (Nakamura & Kohama, 1999).  When excited—such as by an electrical signal—cells increase intracellular Ca²⁺ concentration [Ca²⁺] by releasing stored ions and permitting an influx of Ca²⁺. In  Physarum polycephalum , an elevated [Ca 2+ ] was found to inhibit actomyosin and, as a result, the plasmodium’s motion. Therefore, low [Ca 2+ ] allows protoplasmic streaming. The concentration of Ca 2+  is then inversely proportional to the protoplasmic flow. The same effect was observed with different plants (Nakamura & Kohama, 1999).  An in-vitro experiment with  P. polycephalum  demonstrated why [Ca 2+ ] controls actin-myosin interactions (Nakamura & Kohama, 1999). A note needs to be made about Ca 2+ action: Ca 2+  inhibits myosin specifically and not actin. Myosin is an adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase), an enzyme that breaks down ATP into ADP with a free phosphate (Dominguez & Holmes, 2011). Ca 2+  inhibits the ATPase activity of actomyosin (Fig. 10). When myosin is bound with Ca 2+ , the protein turns inactive. Myosin returns to being active when it loses the ion (Nakamura & Kohama, 1999).  
 Fig. 10: Impact of calcium ion on myosin. Note that myosin filaments unfold when exposed to calcium ions and high temperatures (Hu et al., 2022).  Of note, calcium ions do not induce the same response in all phyla. In human muscle cells, they generate the opposite effect. Ca 2+  inhibit protoplasmic streaming whereas they activate muscle contraction (Nakamura & Kohama, 1999). In muscles, the increase in [Ca 2+ ] leads to interactions between myosin and actin which causes muscles contraction. Muscles relax as the Ca 2+  levels lower (Nakamura & Kohama, 1999).  Cyclic phosphatidic acid (cPA)  Physarum polycephalum  secretes different macromolecules that can be found on the outer shell of the plasmodium (Huynh et al., 2017). They are called exopolysaccharides (EPS) which are far from inert.  P. polycephalum ‘s EPS are composed of two galactants bound to different phosphorous and sulfur atoms. In fact, they act as a reserve nutrient source, as a protective layer shielding the plasmodium and as a designated area for bacteria cell aggregation (Huynh et al., 2017).  Physarum polycephalum ‘s EPS were studied and a bioactive lipid, more specifically a cyclic phosphatidic acid was found.  The first cPA was isolated from  Physarum polycephalum  in 1992 (Fujiwara, 2008). That specific cPA was then named Physarum lysophosphatidic acid (PHYLPA). There exist several derivatives of cyclic phosphatidic acid which present different radical R groups (Fig. 11).   
 Fig. 11: Structure of cyclic phosphatidic acid (cPA) and of Physarum lysophosphatidic acid (PHYLPA) (Murakami-Murofushi et al., 2002).  Derivatives of cPA can be found in various species and even in mammals (Murakami-Murofushi et al., 2002). Cyclic phosphatidic acids can control cells growth and therefore minimize cancer cells proliferation and propagation. cPA also increase the intracellular [Ca 2+ ] and provoke the formation of actin stress fiber, a type of actin filaments. Past a certain threshold, cPA were found to be effective in inhibiting metastasis in various tumor cell lines (Murakami-Murofushi et al., 2002). To improve their efficiency, cPA have been derived to form carba cyclic phosphatidic acids (CCDA) (Fig. 12).  
 Fig. 12: Structures of carba-cPAs. Note that these two compounds showed very high anti-invasive activities (Murakami-Murofushi et al., 2002).  CCPA seem to be better suited for clinical use since they have significantly lower side effects than the current methods of cancer treatment (Murakami-Murofushi et al., 2002). CCPA present a design solution that can be engineered to create alternative low invasive treatments for cancer patients.   Understanding, Applying, and Comparing Slime Mold and Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) Reactions   This section aims to further elucidate certain characteristics of calcium driven reactions of slime mold and compare these to the fascinating Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reactions. BZ reactions are an accessible way to understand complex chemical wave propagation (Hill and Morgan, 2003). The result of the reaction can be seen in Fig. 13. Further, there is much to understand about how their intricate commonalities can be applied to future experiments and scientific advancements.   
 Fig. 13: Various images of the chemical wave oscillation from BZ reactions, forming intricate patterns (Zhabotinsky, 2007).  Calcium Driven Slime Mold Reactions   Slime mold functionality is driven by chemical reactions. This discussion focuses on aspects of these processes that influence nutrition and growth, highlighting their relevance to the comparison between slime mold morphology and BZ reactions. Slime mold can sense chemical gradients, and further attract or repel by adapting its oscillations. It is covered with hundreds to thousands of biochemical oscillators that help to enable these changes. Specifically, activity, ‘cognition’ and growth are identifiably controlled by the interference of actin polymerization waves and calcium waves from the surroundings (Vallverdú et al., 2018). The slime mold model of cognition or lack thereof (whilst completing traditionally cognitive tasks) can be harnessed in other scientific settings and will be expanded upon. To test the hypothesis that the oscillatory contractions of slime mold were due to Ca 2+ reactions, actin and myosin were extracted. The calcium-specific photoprotein, aequorin was injected into actin and myosin that were specific to slime mold. Aequorin helps detect changes in [Ca 2+ ] . Cycle to cycle calcium levels adapted heavily in this experiment, indicating that contraction of the slime mold happens in times of elevated Ca +  concentration. Further as seen in Fig. 14, the varying measured calcium levels correlated to an electrical current with an oscillatory sinusoidal wave (Ridgway et al., 1976).  
 Fig. 14: In A, B and C, three separate experiments, measurements were taken of calcium changes and electrical current after aequorin injection, with the top lines demonstrating the varying calcium concentrations, and the bottom lines sinusoidal electrical currents (Ridgway et al., 1976).  The electric potential of slime mold oscillates at an amplitude of 1-10 mV and period of 50-200 s. The preservation of this potential is accomplished with calcium ion exchange that ensures a consistent membrane potential. It has also been found that the streaming, another way to describe the wave propagation, reverses direction every 54 s. There is a strong belief that this is because the wave originates from a ‘root’ and extends to the growth areas of the organism (“tree branches” or lattice) before returning (Adamatzky, 2015).   The aforementioned reaction, and wave propagation, can be demonstrated using what is called a Voronoi diagram (Voronoi, 1908). P is a non-empty finite set of planar points. In a Voronoi diagram, a region including a single point q contains all the points closer to q than any other region of P. For a reaction-diffusion oriented reaction like with slime mold, a Voronoi diagram can be used to demonstrate wave propagation. Using two drops of a specified reagent for the organism like slime mold, the two drops (following the laid-out principles regarding plane P and drops q) should result in the waves going the same distance before meeting. In a beautiful display, slime mold waves propagate in intricate circles (Fig. 15) outwards before meeting another wave (a splitting point on the actual slime mold) (Adamatzky, 2015).   
 Fig. 15: Voronoi diagram computation using  Physarum  (slime mold) over time. In A, you can see the initial drops of reagent, and as the slime mold grows its “waves” collide. B and D, the splitting points from the actual slime mold approximate a Voronoi diagram (Adamatzky, 2015). Further the wave propagation, as seen, is quite intricate, beautiful, and complex.    BZ Reactions  BZ (also spelled Zhabotinskii) reactions, discovered in 1951 by Soviet biophysicist Boris Belousov are the most accessible and studied tools to understand chemical reactions that result in wave propagation (oscillations) and further, pattern formation (Hill and Morgan, 2003). In these reactions, transition-metal ions catalyze the oxidation of many different (organic) reductants. The reaction always includes bromate (BrO – ) in an acidic water solution. The reaction is usually homogeneous meaning that it distributes evenly across the medium. Amazingly, the BZ reaction forms oscillatory waves like that of slime mold, that when modeled, create ornate, stunning patterns. Further, this enables the study of chemical waves without many reactants, magnification or long amounts of time. This is an incredibly accessible reaction. Fig. 16   and Fig. 17 demonstrate the incredible art form that the wave propagation takes in BZ reactions (Zhabotinsky, 2007).   
 Fig. 16: More images of the spiral waves within the concentric circles found in BZ reactions (Zhabotinsky, 2007).   
 Fig. 17: Another demonstrative image of the ornate complexity of a BZ reaction (Ball, 2015).   Commonalities   BZ reactions and calcium driven reactions in slime mold are important reactions to compare, as they both have similar beneficial observations. At their core, they are both reactions that enable macroscopic visualization of chemical wave propagation. These are examples of reaction-diffusion processes. Furthermore, with each increment of this reaction, wave excitation occurs. Wave propagation in slime mold helps illustrate how its chemical reactions contribute to self-organization and cognitive-like tasks, despite the absence of a central  nervous system .  Applications   There are various interesting subsets and applications associated with chemical wave propagation, the common theme of slime mold with BZ reactions.   Computational Modeling   Wave propagation of slime mold is excited by reaction diffusion, and because of this power it can be harnessed for incredible computing applications. The functional aspects of slime mold can be modeled as outputs in processing. Two examples of logic gates, fundamental decision-making aspects in digital circuits, that can be modeled from reactions like that of slime mold (or BZ reactions) are ballistic gates and microfluidic gates. Ballistic gates aim to differentiate and utilize the functionality that comes from slime mold having active and non-active zones. Further, microfluidic gates aim to model the reversal in cytoplasmic flow during wave propagation to act as a logic gate with reversal functionality or on off capabilities. In Fig. 18, there is an example of how slime mold can be modeled in this way (Adamatzky, 2015).   
 Fig. 18: + and – show the polarity on ends of slime mold structures. Further, this shows the way in which wave propagation changes directions at these points. This could be used to model a similar reversal or on/off functionality with a logic gate (Adamatzky, 2015).   Similarly, different sensors can be modeled from slime mold, sensing things like colors, chemicals and more, all based on chemical wave propagation (Adamatzky, 2015).   Patterns and Wave Structure   Additionally, the geometric patterns of these reactions in both slime mold and BZ reactions offer more than beauty. The self-organization characteristics in biological systems, including geometrical shapes, are fascinating. Pattern formation is due to the wave propagation effects. The travelling waves vary in shape, speed and concentration features (based on the reactions) and end upon collision (i.e. splitting point of slime mold). This is what enables pattern formation in chemical systems (Cassani et al., 2018). This can help the scientific community further explore ideas of self-organization, and how to harness this power for technological efficiency. Additionally, in biological systems, pattern formation is present in many organisms. The reasoning for this organization often stems from efficiency and functionality. Examples include  fish  scaling, coral reefs, and spider webs. These intricate structures can similarly be used to improve biomimetic experimentation and technology (Serna and Barragán, 2017).  The spiral waves, found in both slime mold and BZ reactions (Fig. 14 and Fig. 16), have their own unique properties and applications to be understood. Spiral waves have unique energetic properties that necessitate more research. For example, they are associated with cardiac events. They have unique spatiotemporal patterns, that directly affect things like their frequency (Sandstede and Scheel, 2023). Future study of spiral waves can center from their accessibility in these reactions.  Cognition The idea of cognition is a heavily studied ideal, especially for simple organisms that appear to do complex tasks, without centralized cognitive centers. To understand the cognition of something like slime mold, scientists coined Cognitive Biology as a field to understand how an organism’s biological processes directly impact their cognitive abilities, rather than the naive assumption that there is a need for a brain, like that of humans (Vallverdú et al., 2018).   In slime mold, cognition is engrained in its networks, and most deeply in its reaction diffusion responses. If data is provided as attractants and repellants, to stimulate reaction diffusion reactions, slime mold can complete an impressive array of tasks. These include computational  geometry , logic, arithmetic and image processing (Vallverdú et al., 2018). While the idea of knowledge is different for an organism like slime mold, it still exists. For example, slime mold is known to avoid areas with a certain chemical at a certain threshold (Vallverdú et al., 2018).   The central idea of cognition in slime mold is driven by chemistry. Furthermore, BZ reactions and the reactions in slime mold are accessible ways to study and explore these varied applications. More centrally though, the other parts of this paper discussed Slime Mold’s growth and nutrition, or in other words its survival. Chemical reactions are a large part of what enables these, yet they also unlock the potential to understand so much more about this fascinating organism at other levels, and science at large.   Conclusion Physarum polycephalum ‘s similarity to BZ reactions, dynamic growth, and nutrition, are the chemical aspects of the slime mold’s biology that help explain how such a basic organism manages complex logic problems such as maze-solving.  Physarum ‘s complex behaviors are then explained via the chemical reactions leading to intracellular signaling of calcium ions throughout its tubular network.  Physarum  uses the concentration of these calcium ions to control tubular contractility in its actomyosin network. Chemical reactions with food allow it to develop a food sense that triggers reactions and transfers information about food sources’ quality and location. These reactions are directly related to the calcium-actomyosin interactions that enable slime mold’s motility. Thus, the slime mold has developed a simple solution for motility and for food sensing, inherently connecting the two aspects of its biology to enable the survival and complex decision-making in an organism without a nervous system. This is further elucidated by comparing the oscillations of  Physarum olycephalum  with the wave-propagation observed in BZ reactions. The consideration of the slime mold as a living diffusion reaction opens biocomputational avenues such as logic gates within its vein network and using the slime mold to compute Voronoi diagrams. This comparison also shows how wave-propagation leads to pattern formation in biological systems and has further applications in the study of basal cognition at large.

title: A Chemical Composition to Make Them Cower: A Dive Into the Structure and Protective Adaptations of Sea Sponges
authors: Olivia Ghiaur, Camille Heaney, Chris Hu, Vadim Zamaruyev
abstract: Sponges have several feeding modes and use a variety of food sources, which underlies their key role in the cycling of several elements and importance in the foodweb. Sponges also produce a variety of toxins that they use in allelopathy against competitors, and in camouflage and defense against predators. The biomineralization of sponge skeletons has an interesting evolutionary history, is a multi-step process, and confers sponges a remarkable morphological plasticity. As a result, these animals can change their shape to adapt to their environment as they grow. Apart from adaptations of biological importance, the porous structure of spongin is a source of inspiration for new filtering and catalytic biomimetic devices.
content:
A Chemical Composition to Make Them Cower: A Dive Into the Structure and Protective Adaptations of Sea Sponges  Olivia Ghiaur, Camille Heaney, Chris Hu, Vadim Zamaruyev Abstract Sponges have several feeding modes and use a variety of food sources, which underlies their key role in the cycling of several elements and importance in the foodweb. Sponges also produce a variety of  toxins  that they use in allelopathy against competitors, and in camouflage and defense against predators. The biomineralization of sponge skeletons has an interesting evolutionary history, is a multi-step process, and confers sponges a remarkable morphological plasticity. As a result, these animals can change their shape to adapt to their environment as they grow. Apart from adaptations of biological importance, the porous structure of spongin is a source of inspiration for new filtering and catalytic biomimetic devices.  Introduction With so many evolutionary niches to fill, Porifera utilized the power of  chemistry , allowing them to not only change their environment but change themselves (Valery et al., 2003). Each new interaction opened the door for a new adaptation. The abundance of silicon and oxygen led to the  evolution  of silicatein (Fig. 19) and collagen (Fig. 23). The latter two, along with spongin, drove the emergence of different spicules incorporated in bodies of increasing size and complexity through the cooperation of various specialized cells. The resulting phenotypic plasticity opened new avenues of interaction between sponges and other species. Sponges became prey and predators. These interspecific interactions triggered further chemical diversification. Sponges developed molecules for camouflage and defense and became important middlemen in the flow of chemical elements. In other words, chemistry sparked diversity (Valery et al., 2003).  Consumption Sea sponges have adapted to living in environments ranging from nutrient poor to rich, light to dark, and with or without symbionts. As such, sponges have developed many pathways by which to take in nutrients from their surroundings (Valery et al., 2003).  Diffusion Like all cells, the external, lining cells of sea sponges are capable of  diffusion  from the water directly into the cell. Diffusion occurs when there is a high concentration of a dissolved material in one medium (either gas or liquid) and this medium is separated from another by a boundary (in the case of sea sponges, a cell membrane). The dissolved material filters through the boundary until the external and internal mediums have the same concentration of material (Bailey, 2019).  Pinocytosis Pinocytosis (Fig. 1) refers to the formation of a pocket to engulf extracellular fluid. As opposed to diffusion, this process is more controlled, occurring with larger or less polar molecules which cannot enter channels in the phospholipid bilayer. Instead, the cell bilayer folds in on itself, holding the polar medium and its content with the polar head of the bilayer. This pocket pinches off inside the cell creating a vesicle. From here lysosomes are deployed within the vesicle to break apart the nutrients into sea-sponge friendly packages. The remainder is handled by exosomes and released from the cell (Britannica, 2014).  
 Fig. 1.  Pinocytosis [Adapted from Karpińska et al., 2022]  Phagocytosis Phagocytosis enables unicellular  organisms  to consume particles larger than 0.5 µm in diameter (Fig. 2). Particles are sent through the ostia of sea sponges into choanocyte chambers. Choanocytes have flagella which allow them to “hold” microorganisms in one place (Steinmetz, 2019). Upon sensing the particle, choanocytes signal the remodel of the cytoskeleton and phospholipid bilayer to extend to cover the particle. Once these membranes close, a phagosome is formed. During maturation, this distinct vesicle binds with lysosomes and other hydrolytic enzymes to produce reactive oxygen species (like superoxide), and becomes very acidic (pH around 4.5). These work together to degrade the ingested material (Uribe-Querol & Rosales, 2020).    
 Fig. 2.  Stages of the mechanism of phagocytosis. Blue arrows indicate the direction of the steps. (Ojas A. Deshpanda, 2023)  Carnivory In the class Demospongiae, the family of Cladorhizidae adapted to fit environments with far less nutritional content. Appearing as a sea sponge “skeleton”, this class lacks the classic poriferan aquiferous system but maintains the siliceous spicule structure. The spicules have evolved hook-like qualities, used to entangle the legs of small crustaceans.  Digestion is done by migrating elongate cells, which specialize from stem cells at the base of the sponge structure. A few hours after the prey have been captured, a layer of pinacocytes form around the prey. Then archeocytes and bacteriocytes concentrate around the prey creating a cyst-like structure on the sponge. Within a week, identifiable nutrients from the prey are phagocytosed and the undigested elements (like carapaces or gills) are released (Vacelet & Duport, 2004).  Symbiosis Porifera do not function isolated from other organisms, they have symbionts that are paired with them through a plethora of systems, including but not limited to the dissolution of carbon and nitrogen, vitamin biosynthesis and toxin formation (Carrier et al., 2022).  In clear shallow waters, sea sponges work with photosynthetic symbionts, like zooxanthellae and cyanobacteria. These use the energy of photons to excite electrons forcing them to create glucose and ATP from water and carbon dioxide (AKA photosynthesis). This is a vital pairing because it directly contributes to the ability of sea sponges to fixate dissolved carbon, by receiving it in the form of glucose from the microbial symbionts.  Deep-sea sponges pair with chemoautotrophic bacteria to help fix Carbon dioxide (CO 2 ). Specific ammonia-oxidizing archaea, like  Nitrosopumilaceae , fixate carbon in the form of the 3-hydroxypropionate/4-hydroxybutyrate cycle (Garritano et al., 2023). The 3-hydroxypropionate/4-hydroxybutyrate carbon fixation cycle (Fig. 3) takes dissolved CO 2  from the water and synthesizes it into acetyl CoA. This process is more efficient than sponge diffusion which is critical in nutrient deficient waters (Loder et al., 2016).  
 Fig. 3.  3-hydroxypropionate/4-hydroxybutyrate carbon fixation cycle (Loder et al., 2016)  There are two overarching groups of sponges in relation to symbionts: low microbial abundance (LMA) and high microbial abundance (HMA). These are important distinctions because sea sponges are a collection of cells rather than tissue-based, meaning that the symbiont microbes are incorporated within the cellular structure of the host. This relationship is so integral that about 50% of sponge biomass is made of their bacterial symbionts (Kiran et al., 2018).  Nutrition In the carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorous, cycles sea sponges function as sources, sinks, and cyclers (Valery et al., 2003).  Oxygen While H 2 O is polar and O 2  is nonpolar, dissolved oxygen (DO) is critical to almost all aquatic life. Oxygen is able to dissolve in water due to the hydrophobic effect, but in the oceans, oxygen mainly comes from the release of photosynthetic organisms (Mader et al., 2017).  Sea sponges use oxygen for respiration to create ATP, which powers cellular activity.   Carbon  There are two overarching types of carbon which sea sponges ingest, dissolved organic matter (DOM) and particulate organic matter (POM).   DOM is largely inaccessible to microorganisms, but exists in bodies of water in the form of glucose, amino acids, etc. Sponges are uniquely capable of taking up this matter directly via pinocytosis (Rix et al., 2020) and receive the synthesized form of DOM from their carbon fixing symbionts.  Sponge ingested POM can be alive, in the form of pico- or nano-planktonic cells, or non-living, in the form of detritus. For sponges this digestion process occurs via phagocytosis.  The use of carbon in sea sponges can be summarized as (I)ngestion, biomass (P)roduction, (R)espiration, and (E)xcrement, which relate as follows:  Equation 1.    I = P + R + E Depending on temperature, pumping activity, and physiological processes, such as growth and  reproduction , the respiration rate of sponges can be between 0.21 to 24.6µmol O 2 cm -3 h -1  (Maldonado et al., 2012). These varied respiration rates are related to the metabolic efficiency of the sea sponge by the ratio between ingestion and respiration. Thus, at times when there is high carbon availability and they are internally active, sponges are at their most successful.  The extra carbon is released from the sponge system in the form of detritus. This is crucial for the benthic ecosystem (Fig. 4) as it allows other macro-organisms to use the fixated carbon, which they cannot access in the open water, and further contribute to the cycle.  
 Fig. 4.  Carbon cycling surrounding sea sponges. POC det  represents detrital POC (Maldonado et al., 2012).  Nitrogen and Phosphorous  Two other nutrients that are vital in metabolic processes are nitrogen and phosphorus.   Marine sponges are capable of taking in dissolved inorganic nitrogen and phosphorus, like NH 4 +  , NO 3 – , and PO 4 3-  , through diffusion and pinocytosis, and organic forms of nitrogen, like amino acids, primarily through phagocytosis. However, this process is quite inefficient, and symbionts are much more competent in this task. Symbiotic bacteria, archaea, and fungi have all been regularly found associated with sponges as ammonia-oxidizers, nitrite-oxidizers, and denitrifiers (Fig. 5.) (Karpińska et al., 2022). 
 Fig. 5.  Nitrogen fixation in marine sponges (Kiran et al., 2018).  This association is integral for sea sponges as nitrogen and phosphorus are necessary for protein and nucleic acid production, but it is also necessary for the surrounding flora and fauna. The importance of porifera in the nitrogen cycle has been found in sea habitats from temperate to tropical. This is because they act as a source of dissolved organic nitrogen (Fig. 6) for pelagic environments and are players in the remineralization of organic nitrogen (Bell, 2008).  
 Fig. 6.  Nitrogen and phosphorous cycle at the poriferan level (Maldonado et al., 2012)  Effect on ecosystem  The role of sea sponges as keystone species in their habitats is common because they do not just physically reshape an environment, they nutritionally reshape it as well.  Benthic (those on the base of the sea) and pelagic (open ocean) environments are connected. Their coupling contributes to various biogeochemical cycles, as benthic fauna are important in organic matter retention and remineralization, while pelagic organisms produce fresh organic matter (Ehrnsten et al., 2019). Sea sponges participate in this relationship as their pumping system sends material upwards, facilitating benthic-pelagic exchange and bioturbation on the sea floor (Bell, 2008). They also function as an intermediate between dissolved and microbial nutrition, and higher levels of the food chain.  Chemical defenses of sponges  Sponges are sessile, which means they are rooted in the same location their entire lives. Sponges cannot escape predators. As a result, they have evolved to have chemical defense mechanisms. Sponges contain an abundance of secondary metabolites that protect them from predators, prevent fouling of other organisms, and compete for space in crowded environments. As sponges filter water, they can digest microorganisms or retain them within their porous bodies. Some of these microorganisms are involved in the biosynthesis of the natural products of sponges which enables chemical defenses. Sponges prevent fouling by having clear pathways for water filtration, they can conquer densely populated areas with their metabolites, and they have mechanisms to produce potent toxins without destroying themselves (Varijakzhan et al., 2021).   Additionally, the environment of the sponge has an influence on the accumulation of toxic constituents within the sponge. Sponges that live in tropical environments have more chemical compounds made for defense than sponges that live in colder environments. Tropical environments have more intense competition and feeding pressures which has resulted in tropical sponges containing more toxins (Proksch, 1994).  Allelopathic ability  Allelopathy is when toxins are secreted to prevent the growth of other organisms around the sponge, also allowing sponges to secure space for their larvae (Singh & Thakur, 2016). Sponges grow in environments that are crowded with other sessile organisms. They have developed the chemical defense mechanism of allelopathy to secure their spots in the limited benthic habitat. The allelochemical properties of sponges and other organisms are not well understood. The interactions can be through direct contact or the release of chemicals into the environment around the sponge (Ternon et al., 2016).  One example of an allelopathic sponge with a direct toxic effect is Cliona tenuis (Fig. 7). This sponge produces clionapyrrolidine A [(−)-(5S)-2-imino-1-methylpyrrolidine-5-carboxylic acid], a compound that, upon contact, kills coral tissue and reduces the photosynthetic efficiency of certain corals. The toxin only works through forced contact, this implies that the contact that would result in coral death can only happen during a storm. (Chaves-Fonnegra et al., 2008).   
 Fig. 7  Image of Cliona tenuis from Grand Cayman (Charpin, 2023).  Another example of an allelopathic sponge is the  Crambe crambe  which releases chemicals into the seawater.  C. crambe  synthesizes the bioactive polycyclic guanidine alkaloids (PGA). There are two families of PGAs: the first family, crambescins, contains two cyclic rings, and the second family, crambescidins, contains five cyclic rings (Fig. 8). The sponge contains high concentrations of these compounds, which may be involved in the chemical mediation of other marine micro and macro-organisms. Additionally, the water surrounding the sponge contained PGAs, which means that the sponge has a continuous transfer of metabolites into the seawater.  The sponges can release chemicals into the environment by creating spherulous cells that contain spherules filled with metabolites. The spherulous cells exit the sponge through the oscula and burst creating a shield of metabolites around the sponge (Fig. 9). It is demonstrated that PGA compounds cause defects in the embryos of sea squirts. Sea squirts are other sessile creatures competing for space, and C. Crambe prevents their development, proving its allelopathic abilities (Ternon et al., 2016).  
 Fig. 8.  The Chemical structures of two ring Crambescins A, Crambescins B, and Crambescins C. The chemical structure of five ring Crambescidins (Ternon et al., 2016).  
 Fig. 9.  Schematic of how the chemical shield is formed by C. crambe. Left green circle shows crambescins and right red circle shows crambescidins (Ternon et al., 2016).  Antifouling ability  Sponges settled on the sea floor do not want other organisms such as algae, barnacles, ascidians, and bryozoans to settle on top of them and evolved anti-fouling abilities. Biofouling is a multistep process that allows larger organisms to stick to underwater surfaces (Fig. 10). The process begins with a conditioning film where an organic particulate layer is formed by proteins, carbohydrates, and glycoproteins. The surface is then conditioned for microorganisms to stick through electrostatic and Van der Waals forces.  Then, microorganisms will stick to the surface as they naturally pass by the surface via the movement of water. Next, the microorganisms will secrete an extracellular polymeric substance anchoring them to the surface. This creates a gel matrix that allows for enzymatic interactions, nutrient exchange, and environmental stressor protection. The initial soft macro-fouling allows for the growth of hard macro-fouling of organisms; starting with small eukaryotes and followed by large eukaryotes. (Müller et al., 2013). One metabolite used in sponges to prevent the settlement of the barnacle  Balanus improvisus  is agelasine D (Fig. 11) (Sjögren et al., 2008). An additional compound is ageloxime D. Agelasine D has antimicrobial properties and Ageloxime D inhibits the biofilm of the barnacle.  (Hertiani et al., 2010).

Some sponges have symbiotic relationships with the bacteria that enter their bodies. In particular, the sponges of the order Dysideidae have a cyanobacteria living within them that produces polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs). The natural PBDEs are remarkably like the toxic human-made brominated flame retardants (Fig. 12a & b)(Agarwal et al., 2017). The PBDEs of the sponges are used as a chemical defense against predators. The mechanism by which they are toxic against other organisms is unknown. However, they provide the sponge with some microbial resistance. The PBDEs created by the cyanobacteria tend to accumulate and crystallize at high concentrations in the ectosome tissues of the sponge. This could be how sponges avoid the toxic effects of the compounds(Poston & Saha, 2019).

The Sponge has a symbiotic relationship with the bacteria  Candidatus Entotheonella.  The bacterium within the sponge produces a toxin called Calyculin A. The structure of the toxin contains tetraene, oxazole, phosphate and dimethylamino groups. The toxin is synthesized via a hybrid pathway of polyketide synthase (PKS) and non-ribosomal peptide synthase (NRPS). Then, there are modifications such as nitrile formation to finish the structure. This toxin works by inhibiting the protein phosphatase 1 and 2A (Wakimoto et al., 2014). These proteins are important in the regulation of cell functions such as cell signaling, metabolism, cell cycle transitions, embryonic development and stress response (Courtney & Deiters, 2019). The disruption in these functions from the toxin can lead to cellular death. When the sponges work together with the bacteria, they can have a chemical defense from Calyculin A (Wakimoto et al., 2014).

However, the toxin works by targeting enzymes that are important to all eukaryotic cells. To combat this, the relationship with the bacteria has evolved to have a mechanism to prevent self-toxicity. The mechanism used by the sponge and the symbiotic bacteria is to store the toxin as a derivative, phosphocalyculin A. Phosphocalyculin A has an additional phosphate group this diminishes the toxicity since the single phosphate group on Calyculin A is responsible for the inhibitions of protein phosphatases 1 and 2A. When the sponge tissue is disturbed, the bacteria will release phasphatase CalL which will activate the toxin by converting phosphocalyculin A into Calyculin A (Fig. 14). This mechanism allows the sponge to contain the toxin within itself without being harmed and rapidly activate the toxin when needed (Jomori et al., 2021).  
 Fig. 14.  Phosphate-activated chemical defense mechanism of conversion of Phosphocalyculin A to Calyculin A (Jomori et al., 2021).  Silica Biomineralization in Sponges  The earliest fossil evidence of sponges dates to the Ediacaran (542–580 Ma) the latest period of the Proterozoic era preceding the Cambrian (McMenamin, 2005). In early Cambrian ecosystems, sponges were one of the most diversified groups. They were the second most diverse group in the Chengjiang biota (520-530 Ma) where both demosponge and hexactinellids were identified (Fig 15). A key innovation underpinned the ecological success of these animals: their skeleton. A skeleton provides a species with the opportunity to scale up and develop a complex organization. The skeleton of sponges relied on two key molecules: collagen which formed the extracellular matrix and silicatein which produced spicules. Collagen needed oxygen, which was abundant since the great oxidation event that happened 2.4 billion years ago (Olejarz et al., 2021). Silicatein needed silicon (Muller et al., 2011).

(Muller et al., 2011).  Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth’s crust, and its concentration was significantly higher in the Ediacaran oceans than today (Tyler, 2013). These concentrations were attributable to two processes. The first process was the chemical weathering of feldspar minerals containing silicon, such as NaAlSi 3 O 8 -CaAl 2 Si 2 O 8 . Reacting with CO 2 , these minerals produced acids that were washed into the ocean. Notably, calcium (Ca 2+ ) and sodium (Na + ) were washed away along with silicon. The second process was sulfate reduction. Unfortunately, this reaction did not produce any silicon. Instead, it produced bicarbonate (HCO 3 – ). The abundance of bicarbonate, calcium, and sodium ions contributed to the alkalization of the ocean. The resulting “soda ocean” favored the dissolution of silicon (Muller et al., 2011). Its concentration increased up to 1000-2200 micromolars and remained higher than 650 micromolars up to the Jurassic period (145-201.2 Ma) (Maldonado et al., 2011) (Iqbal, 2021).   Having successfully occupied their niche for 400-500 million years, sponges were disturbed at the end of the late Cretaceous (65-96 Ma) (Sims et al., 2006). The diversification of diatoms, a type of green algae, endangered their peaceful existence. Needing silicon to grow their siliceous shells called frustules, diatoms developed an active pumping mechanism to siphon silicon out of their environment. As a result, silicon levels in the oceans decreased to an average of 10μM (Maldonado et al., 2011). Sponges were in danger as their essential resource was becoming scarcer and scarcer. Some evolved spongin and calcareous skeletons (Maldonado et al., 2020). However, 75% of extant sponges still have siliceous skeleton and consume 8.6 X 10 10  and 7.3 x 10 12  moles of silicon yearly (Maldonado et al., 2011).   Capturing Silicon To begin building its skeleton, a sponge needs silicon. It needs to capture this element from the environment and concentrate it inside of its body. To this end, sponges developed a two-step transport system (Fig. 16). First, aquaglyceroporins 3 and 9 let silicon enter the epithelium cells of the sponge. Second, transporters resembling the arsenite-antimonite (arsB) and low-silicon (Lsi2) transporters actively transport silicon outside of the epithelial cell using the energy of a proton gradient (Schuldiner, 2014). The arsB and Lsi2 transporters underpin the proper function of the aquaglycoroporins because their active silicon efflux creates the gradient necessary for the passive silicon influx through the latter. From these findings, Maldonado et al. concluded that the active transporters must be responsible for the saturation of the sponge silicon capturing system in the range of 150-200μM. They also proposed that the promiscuity of these proteins barred the improvement of their silicon transport speeds (Maldonado et al., 2020).

In this environment, it triggers the differentiation of progenitor cells into sclerocytes (the cells that produce spicules) and promotes the synthesis of collagen to hold the newly made spicules (Muller et al., 2011).   Making Spicules Once the raw material is inside of the sponge, the synthesis of the spicule begins. Sclerocytes absorb silicon containing molecules from the mesohyl and express silicatein, the enzyme that catalyses the formation of silica (Muller et al., 2011).   Silicatein reacts with orthosilicic acid, tetraethoxysilane, and organic oxysilanes leading to their polycondensation into silica. (Schroder et al., 2011).  At its active site, silicatein has three amino acids that form its catalytic triad: asparagine, histidine, and serine (Fig. 19) (Muller et al., 2011). During catalysis, the oxygen atom of a hydroxyl group of serine attacks the silicon of the orthosilicic acid following an SN2 mechanism. At the same time, the hydrogen of the same hydroxyl group (which had formed a hydrogen bridge with histidine) attacks one of the hydroxyl groups of the substrate. This step results in the release of the hydroxyl group as a water molecule and the bonding of the substrate with the serine. In the next step, histidine and asparagine form hydrogen bridges with the substrate attached to the serine. The new position of the substrate-serine complex favors attacks by other orthosilicic acid molecules.  Thus, leading to polycondensation (Schroder et al., 2011).

It begins by the formation of the axial filament rich in silicatein within the sclerocyte. The filament serves as a scaffold for the subsequent deposition of multiple layers of silica. Significantly, silicatein is present both within the layers of silica and on the surface of the spicule contributing to its growth. When the first layer of silica is deposited, the spicule is ejected and grows in the mesohyl. Their silicatein binds to galectin molecules and arranges into strings parallel to the surface of the spicule. In later stages, the strings bind to collagen fibres, form a net and envelop the spicule (Muller et al., 2011).   While this mechanism of growth accounts for the diversity of spicule morphology, Mohri et al. identified an additional factor that contributes to it. Their transcriptomics analysis of the expression of silicatein in the different sclerocytes of freshwater demosponge  Ephydatia fluviatilis  showed surprising results. Six isoforms of silicatein, similar enzymes whose sequence is modified during production, exhibit different temporal activity in different sclerocytes. As a result, the cells produce different types of spicules (Fig. 20) (Mohri et al., 2008).

 Arranging the Skeleton  When all the spicules are made, the skeleton needs to be assembled like a puzzle. Unlike all other animals, sponges synthesize their skeletal elements away from their final position. Because of this unique trait, sponge cells need to cooperate to arrange the skeleton like a colony of termites would arrange their nest. The process is even more significant as it is the only known instance of cells cooperating to work with an inorganic material.   Nakayama et al. discovered the steps of this process in  E. fluviatilis . Its cells divide the labour and iterate a sequence of “transport-pierce-raise up-cementation” steps (Fig. 21). At the beginning, a group of transport cells transports the spicule along the internal epithelium of the mesohyl. In a favorable location, the cells pierce the epithelium and embed half of the spicule in it. They also raise the spicule up. Basopinacocytes cement the dangling spicule at the base of the sponge with collagen fibers. Similarly, spicules can be added to already fixed ones by travelling along the upper surface of the epithelium. The iteration of these steps results in a pole-and-beam structure molded in accordance with the shape of the external environment (Nakayama et al., 2015).

(Nakayama et al., 2015).  Conclusion on Silica Biomineralization  In sum, high silicon levels characterized the environment in which sponges evolved 542-580 million years ago, and silicon became a key resource for these animals. As they developed silicon-fixing and silica-producing systems, sponges became able to build skeletons. Silicatein and collagen produced by multiple cooperating cells participated in the formation of larger and more complex skeletal structures. Despite being outcompeted by diatoms after 400-500 million years of thriving, sponges are still important players in oceanic silicon cycling.  Spongin: A Structural Protein with Superpowers  Another vital structural component of sea sponges is spongin.  Role and Composition of Spongin  Spongin provides the three-dimensional scaffold that supports sponge tissues in many species of Porifera, mainly in Demospongiae, the largest class of sponges, encompassing over 90% of the species in the phylum. Its 3D fibrous network (Fig.22) allows sponges to withstand dynamic marine currents and stresses while providing pores as entrances for feeding channels (Pozzolini et al., 2021).

(Domingues et al., 2021)  Produced by spongioblasts, spongin remains an enigmatic material for which the exact chemical structure has yet to be defined. While its classification as a collagen has been debated in literature, it would be indisputable to define it as a collagen-like biopolymer (Ehrlich et al., 2018). Indeed, like collagen, spongin consists of long chains of amino acids woven together in a triple-helical structure (Fig. 23) that provides both tensile strength and flexibility, and is predominately constituted of glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline amino acids (table 1) (Pozzolini et al., 2021).

 Engineering applications of Spongin  Spongin has been harvested, sold, and used for millennia for its  absorption  properties in applications related to cleaning, to the point where the application has been intertwined with the namesake of the sponge, even after cleaning tools transitioned to being made of synthetic materials. While the term  spongin  was only coined by Georg Städeler in 1859, the material was already valued in the medical world for its softness, high compressive strength, ability to retain shape, and high sorption rates, as well as in the pharmaceutical world for its iodine content as early as in the 18 th  century (Ehrlich et al., 2018) (Sipkema et al., 2005).    Nowadays, spongin is an intriguing material to use in water purification processes.  To Remove Mercury in Water Remediation   The presence of heavy metals in water is a threat to all forms of life but can be an especially concerning problem for apex predators, as these contaminants bio-accumulate in the food chain. Mercury (Hg) is classified as the third most dangerous substance in the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR)’s substance priority list, and can cause harm to the human  immune system , kidneys, and lungs if present in the body. Therefore, remediating industrial and domestic wastewater containing Hg is a priority.  Spongin is a promising material that can serve as a sustainable, economical, and eco-friendly option for mercury remediation. Indeed, in their natural environments, sponges serve as biomonitors for several contaminants, as they sorb a multitude of contaminants in their environment by virtue of  filter feeding . Consequently, it is possible to harness the chemical properties and lattice structure of spongin to create a natural water treatment system that can be easily separated from the treated water without requiring time-consuming processes such as filtration or centrifugation (Domingues et al., 2021). Moreover, marine sponges can easily be cheaply obtained in large quantities, as sponge farms are already a well-established industry.  To extend the use of spongin materials to harsh conditions such as stirred media, it is possible to increase its stiffness by heat-treating it at 180˚C, as it is the highest temperature at which the adsorbed water is lost, but also not hot enough for the degradation of the organic phase of the protein can occur at 200˚C (Fig. 24). This treatment results in a significant volume shrinkage, with the volume of open pore space going down from 85.2% to 51.6% (Domingues et al., 2021).

Thus, with adequate additions to the surface chemistry of the biopolymer, it is possible to increase the efficiency of the treatment to a level where it can be commercially implemented.   As a Scaffold for Catalysis   Spongin can be thermally stable at high temperatures. Indeed, there are hydroxyproline residues capable of forming hydrogen bonds between the strands of this biopolymer as well as a high content of hydroxylysine (Fig. 22), which is known to be involved in crosslinking reactions, and the more crosslinks there are, the more stable it can be at high temperatures (Pozzolini et al., 2021). This stability also allows it to be carbonized while retaining its structural integrity and porous nature, conferring it various industrial applications (Żółtowska et al., 2021).  Carbonized spongin-based scaffolds have demonstrated significant efficacy in supporting nickel-based catalysts, especially in the context of environmental remediation. Research conducted by Żółtowska et al. (Żółtowska et al., 2021) involved the modification of spongin-based scaffolds with nickel compounds through a sorption-reduction technique, resulting in the formation of three distinct NiO/Ni(OH)₂/Ni composites. These composites, originating from the carbonized spongin scaffolds, exhibited exceptional catalytic performance in both oxidation and reduction reactions.   The fibrous three-dimensional structure of the spongin-derived scaffolds is pivotal to the catalytic processes. The distinctive architecture of these biocarbons allows for effective dispersion of the nickel phase and promotes interactions with reactants. This structural benefit, in conjunction with the catalytic characteristics of the nickel phase, establishes a highly efficient platform for catalytic applications. Consequently, these composites are adept at catalyzing oxidation reactions of phenolic compounds, such as methylchlorophenoxypropionic acid (MCPP) and 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid (4-CPA), achieving oxidation efficiencies of up to 99%, as well as facilitating the reduction of 4-nitrophenol (Żółtowska et al., 2021).   The incorporation of heteroatoms such as bromine, iron, and nitrogen within the spongin-based scaffolds enhances the functionalization of the resultant biocarbons. These heteroatoms generate a variety of surface functional groups, which improve the adsorption and catalytic capabilities of the composite materials (Norman et al., 2018). Furthermore, the carbonized spongin-based supports exhibit remarkable chemical and thermal stability, rendering them suitable for catalytic applications across diverse environmental conditions.  Conclusions Sponges have developed numerous chemical design solutions to thrive in their aquatic environment. This includes multiple feeding techniques and partnerships between other organisms. Chemical defense mechanisms allow the sponges to survive in crowded environments or areas with mobile predators. Sponges can produce chemicals to prevent the settlement of other organisms, they can create chemical shields around their bodies, and they have developed mechanisms to avoid self-toxicity. Additionally, even without the silicon density they once had, sponges are designed to collect silicon from the environment to form their spicules and make their skeleton. Sponges are also supported by spongin which is a material that provides support to sponges against the environmental forces. All in all, sponges are chemically diverse creatures that have developed brilliant methods to survive in their environment, which humans can learn from utilize in the form of pharmaceuticals and biomimetic structures.

title: Small Bodies, Big Potential: Chemically Bonding Salps and their Environment
authors: Steven Lin, Stephanie Roy, Daniel Tang, Canyu Wu, Mollee Ye
abstract: Salps are gelatinous invertebrate marine organisms belonging to the phylum Chordata. The chemical and cellular processes that occur within their fragile bodies contain fascinating and novel information in various subjects varying from organic chemistry to immunology to environmental science. Salps are encased in a transparent tunic that does not absorb visible light, making them nearly invisible to sighted predators. This tunic is mainly composed of a network of crystalline cellulose molecules, leading to a durable, yet lightweight exoskeleton. The high tensile strength of cellulose fibers is due to the hydrogen bonding and crystalline structure that protects them from environmental debris. The preference of possessing the cellulose Iβ allomorph provides better flexibility for the salp’s movement compared to cellulose Iα or cellulose II. The innate immune system of salps functions with a combination of reactive enzymes such as hydrolytic enzymes and phenoloxidase, proteins such as specialized anti-microbial proteins, signal factors such as tumor necrosis factor-α and carbohydrate-binding lectins. Communication between salps occurs within chains and relies on synaptic activity between epithelial cells and specialized sensory and button cells. Finally, salps function as an efficient cleaner condensing particulate organic matter and moving carbon along the biogeochemical cycle in marine ecosystems. These studies reveal the important information behind the salps that can be utilized in bioengineering fields.
