The Chemistry of Longevity: How the Naked Mole Rat Defies Aging  Clayton Dame, David Bensemana, Lana Habhab, Min Seo Song Abstract Bioengineers and synthetic biologists strive to understand the biochemical pathways that promote longevity. The naked mole rat has become a model organism for the study of such pathways. To thrive in their hypoxic  environment , the naked mole rats reduced levels of T4  hormones  decrease their metabolic rate; it sustains high levels of glycolysis to ensure continuous ATP generation in hypoxic environments by avoiding the use of phosphofructokinase, its increased rate of autophagy reduces oxidative damage while eliminating unnecessary cellular components; it displays resistance to acidosis by using anaerobic respiration in only critical organs when the environment becomes extremely hypoxic; it has minimal sensitivity to acid-induced pain by having smaller voltage-gated Na +  channels in their nerves.  To acquire  water  and nutrients, they generate water through metabolic processes and reduce water loss by increased concentration of vasopressin; they store calcium in their teeth and bones; and they absorb calcium and excrete pyrophosphate more efficiently due to their increased concentrations of the klotho hormone.  To resist DNA degradation and proper formation of  proteins , the naked mole rat manages protein stress effectively through delayed activation and precise regulation of the unfolded protein response; it enhances telomerase activity and maintenance with the presence of SOX17 binding site; and even maintains age-independent metabolic pathways through unchanged gene expression.  To avoid age-associated structural damage, it exhibits longer hyaluronan polymers, which creates remarkably strong cartilage that is highly resistant to trauma.  These biochemical traits enable the naked mole rat to maintain cellular integrity and minimize age-associated damage, which significantly extends their lifespan. This paper seeks to explore the biochemical foundations of mammalian longevity through the lens of the naked mole rat to understand the chemical pathways that extend lifespan.  Introduction Longevity can be defined as the length of the life of an organism.  As an organism ages, many mechanisms occur which contribute to the process of aging. One of these mechanisms is the process of cellular senescence.  Cellular senescence is the permanent proliferation arrest of cells.  It is caused by endogenous and exogenous stresses on the cells.  Examples of these stresses are damage to DNA from telomere dysfunction and replication under suboptimal environments, and structural damage to the cell.  Different organisms undergo cellular senescence at varying rates, which contributes to their diverse lifespans.  By understanding the chemical pathways which causes cellular senescence among species, we can better understand longevity (Micco, 2021).   If we want to truly understand longevity, we must look outwards to species which defy the process of aging.  One species we can turn to is the naked mole rat ( Heterocephalus glaber ).  The naked mole rat can live up to 30 years long, which is much longer than expected for its size. The predicted longevity of a mammal can be described by the Prothero and Jurgens equation found below.          The longevity quotient describes the ratio between the observed maximum lifespan of a species and the lifespan predicted based on its mass.  A higher longevity quotient shows a species’ ability to withstand age-related destructive processes (Shilovsky et al., 2022). In 2022, Buffenstein and Craft calculated the longevity quotient of the naked mole rat to be approximately 5 (Figure 1) (Buffenstein & Craft, 2021).    
 Fig. 1.  A graph showing the longevity quotient plot for 6 species. The dotted line represents the predicted longevity quotient, and the bar represents the species’ actual longevity quotient. This graph highlights that the naked mole rat longevity quotient is five times greater than the expected value (Buffenstein & Craft, 2021).  The naked mole rat is an excellent candidate for studying and understanding longevity. Before we dive into the chemistry of the naked mole rat, it is important to recognize their living conditions. The naked mole rat is a subterranean rodent that lives in the East African desert. This mammal lives in a subterranean tunnel system, which is both hypoxic (low levels of O 2 ) and hypercapnic (high levels of CO 2 ) (Park et al., 2017). These conditions have driven the evolution of unique biochemical pathways that have ultimately contributed to the naked mole rat’s remarkable longevity as a byproduct.  Metabolic Pathways  To understand the factors that contribute to the extended longevity of a mammal, it is important to examine the key biochemical mechanisms that regulate aging. The metabolic pathways of the naked mole rat offer a unique perspective on the processes of aging and longevity, as well as their implications for other mammalian species. These pathways include a low basal metabolic rate, unique fructose metabolism, high tissue water content, regulated mineral flux, sustained metabolic efficiency with age, and an elevated rate of autophagy.  Basal Metabolic Rate  The basal metabolic rate (BMR) measures the energy that an animal expends at rest to sustain the chemical processes that maintain its essential bodily functions. It excludes energy used for physical activity or thermoregulation. The BMR can often be predicted through various methods. These prediction models have led researchers to believe that the naked mole rat would have a higher BMR. However, Buffenstein and Craft synthesized experimental data from multiple studies, each with distinct experimental protocols, to present a comprehensive view of the naked mole rat’s BMR. This amalgamation of findings reveals that the naked mole rat’s actual BMR is approximately 60% of the predicted value. Researchers attribute this decreased BMR in naked mole rats to low levels of thyroid hormones. As seen in Figure 2, T4 thyroid hormones are pivotal in the regulation of metabolic rate, as their concentration in the blood directly influences key  signaling  pathways that drive energy expenditure. These pathways include heart rate, BMR, glucose and amino acid uptake, respiration rate, oxygen delivery to tissues, and heat production, all of which contribute to heightened energy use (Buffenstein & Craft, 2021).  
 Fig. 2.  This diagram shows the ways in which T4 hormones signal metabolic pathways. The most important pathways that this hormone affects (highlighted in pink) are heart rate, basal metabolic rate, glucose and amino acid uptake, respiration rate, oxygen delivery to tissues, heat production and several synthesis pathways (cholesterol synthesis, lipolysis, glycogenlolysis, gluconenogenesis). Thus, the secretion of this hormone is proportional to the basal metabolic rate of an animal, as it increases the pathways linked to heightened energy use (Adapted from Buffenstein & Craft, 2021).  Consequently, the naked mole rat conserves energy by maintaining low levels of T4 hormones, which allows it to avoid the spikes in energy expenditure typically associated with higher T4 concentrations. This adaptation promotes a steady metabolic rate, which supports its efficient energy use and plays a crucial role in the naked mole rat’s longevity and resilience.  Fructose metabolism   The production of energy intermediates, such as ATP, through oxidative phosphorylation often damages the tissue components over long-term periods. ATP production is a central aspect of metabolism, as it is responsible for most of the active processes that occur in the body.   ATP production is often broken down into four steps: glycolysis, pyruvate processing, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Glycolysis is a series of 10 reactions that follow a linear pathway. In this process, glucose is broken down into smaller molecules to facilitate further processing while allowing some energy extraction, as seen in Figure 3 below (Reece et al., 2021).  
 Fig. 3.  The series of 10 reactions that break down glucose to pyruvate during glycolysis (Aryal et al., 2022).  The naked mole rat does not always have the ability to metabolize glucose in their hypoxic environments, as these processes rely on oxygen-dependent pathways, such as oxidative phosphorylation. Instead, in these low-oxygen environments, the stress hormone, cortisol, will trigger the release of both aldose reductase and sorbitol dehydrogenase: these enzymes will catalyze the reaction that transforms glucose into fructose, as seen in Figure 4 below (Buffenstein & Craft, 2021).  
 Fig. 4.  The series of chemical reactions that occur when a naked mole rat detects a low-oxygen environment. It shows the sequence of events: the release of cortisol, which triggers the release of aldose reductase and sorbitol dehydrogenase to form fructose (Adapted from Buffenstein & Craft, 2021).  The shift to a fructose-dependent glycolysis allows this metabolic pathway to bypass the phosphofructokinase checkpoint in glycolysis. This enzyme is normally allosterically inhibited by a high concentration of ATP, which means that it will lower the rate of glycolysis if ATP is abundant in the cell. By avoiding this rate-limiting step, the naked mole rat sustains high levels of glycolysis and ensures continuous ATP generation in hypoxic environments (Reznick et al., 2021).  While this alternative metabolic pathway adapted to sustain energy production in low-oxygen environments, it also mitigates the production of harmful by-products that contribute to aging and cellular senescence. The bypass of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation reduces the generation of reactive oxygen species; less electrons leak from the electron transport chain to partially reduce oxygen molecules into superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radicals (Reece et al., 2021). These reactive oxygen species damage cells by oxidizing molecules and disrupting cellular structures and functions, which ultimately accelerates aging and disease processes. Thus, the naked mole rat’s tissues undergo less cumulative oxidative damage by avoiding extensive reactive oxygen species production.  Water Balance and Mineral Flux  The naked mole rat struggles to obtain water because its subterranean environment lacks direct water sources and has limited access to fresh plant material. To combat this water shortage, the naked mole rat gets most of its water from its diet and metabolism, as shown in Figure 5.  
 Fig. 5.  The naked mole rat’s sources of water intake and the sources of water loss (Buffenstein & Craft, 2021).  Its fructose metabolism generates metabolic water as a byproduct of cellular respiration. This alternative pathway also plays a key role in water retention, as it triggers the secretion of the antidiuretic hormone, vasopressin, to limit pulmocutaneous and urinary water loss (Buffenstein & Craft, 2021).  The naked mole rat also exhibits unique adaptations in their mineral metabolism. Their subterranean environment is void of sunlight, which is required to synthesize vitamin D. This vitamin is essential for the absorption of calcium and pyrophosphate by activating the transport proteins in the intestines. While these mammals are naturally vitamin D deficient, they have developed different mechanisms to aid in their mineral absorption. They have increased their production of the klotho hormone, which optimizes their absorption of Ca 2+  in the gut and renal system by activating the ion channels that absorb this ion in these systems. Furthermore, they have made mineral reservoirs using their bones and teeth to store excess minerals for future use. They increase the mineral density in these structures as they grow and then modulate their gradual release when dietary mineral availability is lower. Their mechanism for pyrophosphate regulation is also unique, as the klotho hormone also regulates and increases renal pyrophosphate excretion through similar ion channels. Their vitamin D deficiency also minimizes the absorption of pyrophosphate. Thus, their blood plasma shows a decreased concentration of pyrophosphate compared to other  animals  their size. This low concentration of pyrophosphate helps reduce mitochondrial stress and the production of reactive oxygen species, whose effects are discussed in section 1.2. This low level of inorganic phosphate has even been linked to increased lifespan, as seen in Figure 6 below (Buffenstein & Craft, 2021).  
 Fig. 6.  This figure plots the lifespan of an animal as a function of its inorganic phosphate concentration (Buffenstein & Craft, 2021).  Ultimately, the naked mole rat minimizes its dependence on external resources and avoids dehydration or electrolyte imbalances. Thus, their highly efficient mineral utilization contributes to a stable and minimally fluctuating metabolism, which, combined with their low metabolic rate, reduces energy demands (Buffenstein & Craft, 2021).  Autophagy  Autophagy, the degradation of damaged or unnecessary cellular components, is crucial for cellular maintenance (National Cancer Institute, n.d.). Autophagy is activated under unfavorable conditions such as hypoxia, starvation, and microbial infection. Autophagy is activated to produce amino acids when the species is nutrient deficient, so it can continue to synthesize proteins. It has been previously studied that long-lived birds and mammals maintain high levels of autophagy. A study conducted by Zhao et al. compared autophagic activity in naked mole rats and mice, which suggests that a high autophagic rate could contribute to its longevity (Zhao et al., 2014).   To quantify the level of autophagy in the naked mole rat and mice, LC3-I, LC3-II, and beclin 1, which are proteins involved in the formation of autophagosomes, were measured. Greater levels of these proteins indicate greater amounts of autophagosomes, which indicates a greater autophagic rate. From a western blot  analysis  in Figure 7, the naked mole rat shows thicker bands in LC3-I and LC3-II in the brain, lungs, liver, and kidneys. However, beclin 1 showed higher expression in the mouse over the naked mole rat. Despite the lower beclin 1 level in the naked mole rat, the increase in LC3-I and LC3-II caused a greater amount of autophagosome in the naked mole rat than in the mouse (Figure 8) (Zhao et al., 2014).   
 Fig. 7.  Western blot analysis on Beclin 1, LC3-I, LC3-II in one-day-old mouse and one-day-old naked mole rat tissues of brain, lung, liver, and kidney (Zhao et al., 2014).  
 Fig. 8.  Electron microscope of autophagosomes in liver, kidney, skin, and lung tissues from one-day-old naked mole rats and one-day-old mice. Parts in boxes are autophagosomes (Zhao et al., 2014).  It can be hypothesized that naked mole rat’s hypoxic and hypercapnic environment imposes oxidative stress, which has caused them to adapt and perform greater levels of autophagy (Zhao et al., 2014). In addition, the naked mole rat’s environment with scarce resources could have encouraged greater autophagy to eliminate and recycle unnecessary cellular components. Thus, the naked mole rat has evolved to increase autophagy to overcome oxidative stress and nutrient deficiency from their environment. The naked mole rat shows high autophagy and longevity similar to other long-lived mammals (Shepard & Kissil, 2020).    Acidosis resistance  Acid-induced damage and pain can cause cellular damage and chronic stress which can negatively impact longevity. As a result of poor ventilation and dense populations, the naked mole rat’s burrows have been found to have high concentrations of CO 2 . When measured, the burrows were found to have CO 2  concentrations of 0.17 ± 0.09% with a maximum recorded concentration of 0.4 % CO 2 .  Outside of the tunnels, it was found to be 0.03 ± 0.00% (Holtze, 2018). In mammals, high concentrations of inhaled CO 2  cause hypercapnia, which leads to the conversion of bicarbonic acid to bicarbonate + H +  (Figure 9) inside the species.  The presence of additional protons leads to the acidification of the bodily fluids and tissue causing a state of acidosis. The naked mole rat showed resistance to this state by not exhibiting physical symptoms of acidosis even at levels as high as 10% CO 2  compared to the mouse which does at 1% CO 2  (Park et al., 2017).    The increased level of acidification led the naked mole rat to evolve insensitivity to the damage and pain typically induced by acidic environments (Pamenter, 2022).    
 Fig. 9.  The chemical process of CO 2  converting bicarbonic acid to bicarbonate + H +  (Editors of Teaching Medicine, 2024).  Resistance to damage in acidic environments  A study by Husson and Smith compared the number of dead neurons after incubation of both mouse and naked mole rat neuronal cultures in a solution for 2 hours at 37 C° at pH 7.4 and then at pH 5. After incubation at pH 7.4, the death of mouse and naked mole rat neurons were comparable, with the percentage of dead mouse neurons being 20.31 ± 3.50% and that of the naked mole rat being 13.31 ± 1.53%.  However, after incubation at  pH 5, the percentage of dead mouse neurons was 60.55 ± 4.87% and that of the naked mole rat was 22.29 ± 2.30% (Figure 10) (Husson & Smith, 2018). Therefore, the neurons of the naked mole rat showed resistance to an acidic environment.    
 Fig. 10.  Image of the epifluorescence microscopy showing stained necrotic neurons before and after two hours of incubation in different pH solutions of the naked mole rat (b) and mouse (a) (Husson & Smith, 2018).    The neurons of the naked mole can withstand the more acidic environment by having more hyperpolarized cellular membranes. The naked mole rat’s neurons have been shown to have an action potential of up to -80 mV, whereas the mouse has been shown to have a resting potential of -48 ± 8 mV (Penz et al., 2015) (Tompkins et al., 2024). The more negative resting potential leads to more resistance to cellular death because it allows for a higher concentration of H +   ions  outside of the cell. This allows for the interior of the cell to maintain its ideal pH of 7.4.  The more negative resting potential is the result of smaller voltage-gated Na +  channels, which are also only activated at more depolarized potentials. When the inward peak current density of cortical neurons was measured in the naked mole rat, it was found to be 28.79 ± 3.83 pA/pF (picoamperes/picofarades). Whereas in the mouse, it was found to be 202.50 ± 21.35 pA/pF.  Also, the voltage-gated Na +  channels of the cortical neurons of the naked mole rat were found to be fully open at a potential of -12.43 ± 3.02 mV versus the mouses -31.27 ± 2.61 mV (Husson & Smith, 2018). The hyperpolarized membranes keep the inside of the neurons from becoming acidic and consequently leading to their death, even when placed in acidic solutions.  Even in extreme hypercapnic and hypoxic environments, the naked mole rat can maintain its systemic pH. As a result of the lack of O 2 , the naked mole rat must upregulate its anaerobic respiration to maintain its production of ATP, as discussed in the fructose metabolism section. While most mammals downregulate their entire metabolism in response to a lack of O 2 , the naked mole rat upregulates its rate of anerobic respiration. However, the by-products of anaerobic respiration are typically acidic and can cause tissue damage. Although there have been no studies on adults, studies by Farhat and colleagues showed that  in vivo , the naked mole rat can use only anaerobic respiration in the brain and heart while simultaneously downregulating the process in the rest of the body. The study showed that after 4-6 weeks in a hypoxic environment, key enzymes of glycolysis such as pyruvate kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, and many others decreased significantly in the body while remaining constant in the heart and brain (Farhat, 2020).    Insensitivity to acid-induced pain   Although the naked mole is capable of feeling pain and demonstrates the same thermal and acute mechanical pain stimuli responses as the mouse, it is completely insensitive to acid-induced pain (Vice and Browe, 2021). When the mouse was injected with an acidic saline at pH 5 in its hind paw, it immediately showed a reaction and started licking the site of injection. In contrast, when the naked mole rat was injected in the analogous site, it showed no reaction (Figure 11). The same behavior was observed when the naked mole rat was placed in an acidic bath solution at pH 5. The lack of pain response originates from the same mutation that allows neurons of the naked mole rat to survive acidic environments. The voltage-gated Na +  channels ability to minimize the flow of protons stops the acid-sensing ion channels from being continually activated by the protons in acidic conditions (Amoroso et al., 2023). If the naked mole rat was in continuous acid-induced pain, it would be under chronic stress. Studies have shown that chronic stress can activate a plethora of mechanisms, which are designed to be used only temporarily in life-or-death situations, to be constantly activated. By avoiding this state, the naked mole rat can increase its longevity (Harvanek et al., 2021).    
 Fig. 11.  A graph by Amosroso and colleagues from an experiment showing that the naked mole rat is insensitive to acid-induced pain. The behavioral test (A) involved the injection of an acidic solution into the hind paw and measured how long the naked mole rat (NMR) and the mouse licked the sight of injection. The physiological test (B) examined potential spikes in acid pain-sensing C-Fibers of the naked mole rat (Amoroso et al., 2023).  DNA Repair Pathway  There have been studies that confirm the strong relationship between somatic mutation and aging. As animals age, DNA damage increases, which leads to somatic mutation. DNA damage occurs when exposed to factors such as UV light and oxidation. The naked mole rat, which lives in a hypoxic environment with low UV light exposure, has developed a distinct DNA repair pathway compared to mice. Their limited exposure to UV light resulted in an underdevelopment of the nucleotide excision repair pathway, which removes UV-induced damaged or distorted bulky-helix regions of DNA (Evans, 2013). Instead, they developed greater efficiency in Base Excision Repair pathway, which eliminates or repairs oxidation-induced inappropriate base pairs. This adaptation is associated with their hypoxic environment that increases oxidative stress and accumulations of reactive oxygen species, which can damage DNA. As shown in Figure 12, the naked mole rat has greater efficiency of uracil excision after exposure to irradiation compared to mouse (Evdokimov et al., 2018). Greater base excision repair capacity allows the naked mole rats to efficiently eliminate or repair incorrect base pairs, preventing abnormal protein synthesis. Thus, their greater efficiency in the base excision repair pathway could contribute to less somatic mutation, and therefore slower aging.   
 Fig. 12.  Efficiency of Base Excision Repair rate for the naked mole rat (NMR), and mouse after exposure to irradiation (Evdokimov et al., 2018).   In addition, studies show that certain DNA repair genes are greatly upregulated in naked mole rats compared to mice. The study gathered 130 genes involved in DNA repair and found that 34 of those genes had more than two times the expression in the naked mole rat than in the mouse (Evdokimov et al., 2018). These include genes such as p53, MSH3, NHEJ1, CEBPG, and RPA4, which are essential in mismatch repair, base excision repair, and tumor suppression (Shepard & Kissil, 2020) (Evdokimov et al., 2018).   Even though the naked mole rats possess an underdeveloped nucleotide excision repair pathway, they have an alternative base excision repair pathway that is more suitable for their hypoxic environment. Also, the upregulation in DNA repair genes decreases somatic mutation, which contributes to their longevity (Shepard & Kissil, 2020).  Damage Resistant Cartilage  Chondrocytes are the cells which make up the structure of cartilage.  The health of these cells is crucial to maintain cartilage homeostasis. Damage to chondrocytes can be directly scaled to the deformation of the cartilage (Chen et al., 2003).  Taguchi and colleagues set out to determine if there is a relationship between longer hyaluronan polymers and stiffer cartilage: the bonding of these polymers can be seen in Figure 13. To find the relationship, they quantified the Young’s modulus and hyaluronan polymer molecular weight of the naked mole rats, and the mouses cartilage. They used pulse-field electrophoresis to find that the molecular weight of the hyaluronan polymer in the naked mole rat cartilage is two-fold compared to the mouse.  They determined that the increase in molecular weight means that its polymer length must be much greater than that of the mouse.  They then estimated the Young’s modulus of both the mouse and the naked mole rat by applying 0.5 N to cartilage tissue samples from both species.  They imaged the samples under a laser scanning confocal microscope before and after 5 min of the force being applied.  Using these images, they created tissue stretch maps and were able to calculate their Young’s modulus being 22.18MPa for the naked mole rat and 6.95 MPa for the mouse.  The study concluded that the resistance that the naked mole rat’s cartilage displays to damage may be related to its longer cartilage hyaluronan polymers (Taketo Taguchi, 2020). Even in older age, the naked mole rat is capable of creating higher polymer length hyaluronan. The naked mole rat has demonstrated a high-level of anabolism and a low-level catabolism of hyaluronan. The increase and decrease are the result of two amino acid changes in the hyaluronan synthase HAS2 gene.  Even in later life, this mutation causes the naked mole rat to possess the highest molecular weight hyaluronan present in any other mammal examined, which contributes to their longevity (Tian et al., 2013).    
 Fig. 13.  The polymer bonding of hyaluronan which may be responsible for increasing the naked mole rats cartilages resistance to damage (Lu et al., 2017).  The Specialized Unfolded Protein Response of The Naked Mole Rat  One of the aspects that contribute to the longevity and resistance to diseases of the naked mole rat is the unfolded protein response, which is a critical cellular mechanism activated by the accumulation of misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum. This response maintains protein balance by enhancing the cell’s ability to properly fold proteins and degrading damaged proteins. In this process, the protein, inositol-requiring enzyme 1, senses unfolded proteins through a specialized domain on its structure that detects the accumulation of misfolded proteins and initiates their repair. Additionally, protein kinase R, such as the endoplasmic reticulum kinase, reduces overall protein synthesis to decrease the number of misfolded proteins. Furthermore, the activating transcription factor 6 moves to the nucleus during stress to activate genes that help the cell manage unfolded proteins (Du et al., 2020).  In the naked mole rat, the unfolded protein response is crucial for managing cellular stress due to misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum, which maintains protein homeostasis. This process involves key molecular interactions, including  hydrogen bonds  that stabilize secondary and tertiary structures—such as alpha-helices and beta-sheets—which are essential for proper protein folding (LibreTexts, 2021). Thermodynamic stability is increased by hydrophobic interactions that help isolate nonpolar amino acids within the protein’s core (Fiveable.me, 2024). Moreover, the structure and function of the protein are secured by disulfide bonds, which provide powerful covalent interactions between cysteine residues (JoVE, 2024). These processes are essential for the protein’s correct folding, which supports the naked mole rat’s longevity and cellular stability.  To study the role of the unfolded protein response of the naked mole rat, an experiment was conducted by Du and colleagues which aimed to examine the cellular mechanisms that contribute to the longevity and stress resilience of the naked mole rat (Du et al., 2020).   Fibroblast cells from naked mole rats and C57BL/6J mice were cultured in nutrient-rich media and exposed to stress experiments. RNA extraction and the X-box binding protein 1 (XBP1) splicing assay were used to evaluate the unfolded protein response, which indicates how cells manage protein folding under stress. Techniques such as quantitative polymerase chain reaction analyzed gene expressions associated with this response to provide insights into the naked mole rat’s resilience to stress. The cells were subjected to stressors like tunicamycin or thapsigargin, and their viability was assessed through a luminescent assay measuring ATP levels. Statistical analysis, including paired t-tests and two-way analysis of variance, was used to compare the stress resilience between the naked mole rat and mice (Du et al., 2020).  The study found that naked mole rat fibroblasts need more stress to activate the inositol-requiring enzyme type 1 pathway compared to the mouse. This pathway is key for the unfolded protein response, which identifies and repairs misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum. It involves the splicing of XBP1 messenger ribonucleic acid into XBP1 protein 1 spliced, a transcription factor that enhances the cell’s ability to fold proteins correctly and manage cellular stress. This transcription factor activates various genes that improve protein folding and degradation capabilities, which is essential for protecting cells and initiating responses like cell death when damage is severe (Du et al., 2020).  The findings showed that cells from naked mole rats are significantly more efficient in handling stress. These cells required higher doses of the stress-inducing chemicals, tunicamycin and thapsigargin, to trigger the splicing of XBP1, indicating that they can withstand more stress before their stress response is activated. Conversely, mouse cells activated this pathway at much lower concentrations of these chemicals. This demonstrates that naked mole rat cells have a higher tolerance to stress, giving the naked mole rat an advantage in its hypoxic environment. This finding shows that naked mole rat cells can handle more stress before they need to activate the unfolded protein response (Du et al., 2020). This ability could be beneficial for their longevity since it minimizes cellular damage and delays the onset of stress-related aging.  Additionally, Du and colleagues found that naked mole rat fibroblasts had a lower ratio of spliced (active) to unspliced (inactive) XBP1 across all levels of drug treatment (Figure 14), which indicates that there is less of the activated form of this protein relative to its inactive form, even when the cells are under stress. This suggests that the activation of the inositol-requiring enzyme type 1 pathway, which is crucial for managing cellular stress, is more controlled or delayed in these cells. This leads to reduced stress signaling, which means the cells do not react as quickly or intensely to stress and thus show greater resilience. Furthermore, the BLOC1S1 gene, which helps break down ribonucleic acid during stress responses, was more consistently expressed in naked mole rat cells. This indicates that these cells maintain better function under stress (Du et al., 2020).  
 Fig. 14.   Panel A displays gel electrophoresis results showing the levels of unspliced (Xbp1u) and spliced (Xbp1s) X-box binding protein 1 in naked mole rat (NMR) and mouse fibroblasts to reflect the differences in their response to tunicamycin (TU) and thapsigargin (TG) stressors. This visual data explains the delayed activation of the IRE1 pathway in naked mole rats. Panel B presents bar graphs comparing the spliced (Xbp1s) to unspliced (Xbp1u) ratios in both species across different concentrations of tunicamycin and  thapsigargin. This corresponds to the lower ratio of spliced to unspliced X-box binding protein 1 in naked mole rat cells, which indicates a more controlled response to stress. Panel C shows the expression levels of the BLOC1S1 gene, which is a part of the naked mole rat’s stress response.   This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the unfolded protein response in the naked mole rat and highlights its fibroblasts’ ability to tolerate higher levels of stress before activation. This enhanced resilience, demonstrated by their controlled response to the inositol-requiring enzyme type 1 pathway and consistent expression of the BLOC1S1 gene during stress, may contribute significantly to their longevity. By regulating protein homeostasis and avoiding premature cell death pathways, the naked mole rat effectively prevents the accumulation of cellular damage typically associated with aging in other species such as the mouse (Du et al., 2020).  Telomerase Activity and Longevity in the Naked Mole Rat   Telomere Length and Telomerase  Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences at the ends of chromosomes that protect genetic material during cell division. With each division, telomeres shorten, which limits how often a cell can divide. Moreover, limitation of cell division cycles is associated with aging. Telomerase is an enzyme that counters this process by adding telomere to chromosomes, which extends the lifespan of cells. High telomerase activity in long-lived species like the naked mole rat is linked to their longevity (Evfratov et al., 2014).  Genetic Features of Telomerase in the Naked Mole Rat  Researchers have identified two rare polymorphisms in the telomerase ribonucleic acid of the naked mole rat: the change of adenine to guanine in the pseudoknot region and guanine to adenine in the small Cajal body-specific ribonucleic acid domain. This assists in telomerase assembly and may enhance telomerase function (Evfratov et al., 2014). Promoter regions, which control gene expression, show two key transcription factor binding sites: a conserved site for the ETS family, a group of proteins that regulate cell growth and differentiation; and a unique SOX17 binding site, found only in the naked mole rat. These transcription factors regulate gene expression in development and stem cells.  Further analysis, which results are shown in Figure 15, identified the ETS family binding site as crucial for regulating genes involved in telomere maintenance, an essential factor in controlling cellular aging and lifespan. Additionally, the unique SOX17 binding site, absent in closely related species like guinea pigs and chinchillas, was located approximately 430 nucleotides upstream from where gene expression begins, which indicates it may play a regulatory role in gene activation. SOX17 is essential for gene regulation in early development and stem cell maintenance. Its presence in the naked mole rat may represent an evolutionary adaptation that supports enhanced telomerase activity, which ultimately contributes to the species’ longevity (Evfratov et al., 2014).  
 Fig. 15:  Illustration of the telomerase ribonucleic acid promoter regions across different species, including humans, guinea pigs, mole rats, and chinchillas. The figure shows the SOX17 binding site found specifically in the naked mole rat (H. glaber) and absent in closely related species like guinea pigs and chinchillas.  The SOX17 protein contains a specialized structural domain called the high mobility group box which enables it to bind to non-standard DNA structures such as kinked or unwound deoxyribonucleic acid. This high-affinity binding is essential for regulating genes involved in important processes, including the maintenance of telomeres. Hence, the ability of SOX17 to bind and regulate these processes may be a crucial factor in helping the naked mole rat to preserve telomere length and resist cellular aging (Evfratov et al., 2014).  Regulation of Telomerase and Its Impact on Longevity  The unique genetic features of telomerase in the naked mole rat, including rare polymorphisms and transcription factor binding sites like SOX17, are critical for maintaining telomere length and cellular integrity. By supporting telomerase activity and preserving stem cell function, these mechanisms are likely to contribute to the organism’s resilience to stress, prevention of cellular decline, and extended lifespan (Evfratov et al., 2014).  6.4 Link between metabolism and telomerase  The maintenance of youthful, age-independent metabolic pathways plays a key role in extending lifespan. The main pathways that remain stable include a consistent basal metabolic rate, prolonged neurogenesis, resilient cardiac and vascular health, and durable bone and body composition. The proposed biochemical strategy that delays the decline of these critical pathways is the maintenance of unchanged gene expression in vital organs, in which genes continue to express at levels typically associated with youthful physiology due to the increased telomerase activity. The extent to which these pathways deteriorate directly influences an animal’s longevity. Unlike other mammals, the naked mole rat’s metabolic pathways do not exhibit any significant age-related decline. This capacity to consistently sustain constant cellular function and regulate internal conditions contributes to its extended lifespan, in accordance with Demetrius’ theory on aging, called the “metabolic stability-longevity hypothesis.” This theory posits that a main factor contributing to a species’ longevity is a highly stable metabolic network that can return to equilibrium after an external stress (Olshansky & Rattan, 2009). The naked mole rat exemplifies this stability through the consistent regulation of its basal metabolic rate, fructose metabolism, and water and nutrient concentrations.  While their subterranean environment has necessitated the evolution of these alternative pathways to complete key cellular functions, it has also driven the development of advantageous adaptations to sustain metabolic homeostasis, which effectively delays aging (Buffenstein & Craft, 2021).    Conclusion  This paper focuses on the chemical mechanisms that contribute to longevity of the naked mole rat. The subterranean environments with limited light, oxygen, resources, and excess carbon dioxide, caused the naked mole rat to evolve and optimize its chemical mechanisms to survive. Through the design solutions used to adapt to this environment, the naked mole rat has evolved features that contribute to longevity as a byproduct.   The design solutions include:   
 Reducing levels of T4 hormones to reduce their metabolic rate.  
 Sustaining high levels of glycolysis to ensure continuous ATP generation in hypoxic environments by avoiding the use of phosphofructokinase.   
 Generating water through metabolic processes and reduce water loss by increased concentration of vasopressin.  
 Storing calcium in their teeth and bones by increasing the mineral density in these structures as they grow, which maintain mineral homeostasis when dietary calcium availability is lower.  
 Absorbing calcium and excreting pyrophosphate due to their increased concentrations of the klotho hormone, which regulate the intake and disposal from transport proteins.  
 Increasing their rate of autophagy to reduce oxidative damage while eliminating unnecessary cellular components.  
 Resisting systemic acidosis by using anaerobic respiration in critical organs when oxygen availability is low.  
 Minimizing sensitivity to acid-induced pain and neuronal damage by acid via smaller voltage-gated Na +  channels in their nerves.  
 Evolving several mechanisms that enhance their DNA repair pathways to sustain damage from their hypoxic environment via upregulation of these DNA repair proteins.  
 Exhibiting longer hyaluronan polymers via increased production and decreased degradation of these polymers to maintain stiffer and more damage-resistant cartilage.  
 Managing protein stress effectively through delayed activation and precise regulation of the unfolded protein response.  
 Enhancing telomerase activity and maintenance with the presence of SOX17 binding site.  
 Maintaining age-independent metabolic pathways through unchanged gene expression.  
 By studying the biochemical mechanisms of the naked mole rat, certain chemical pathways were found to increase its longevity and resist its process of aging.  Although this paper set out to investigate how the naked mole rat evolved remarkable longevity, it revealed that this extended lifespan is not a direct evolutionary goal but rather a byproduct of numerous chemical pathways adapted for survival in its unique environment.

title: Unlocking Locust Survival: A Chemical Analysis of Locusts
authors: Frederic Koran, Claire Leader, Alexandra Stoilova, Alina Weng
abstract: The complex chemical properties of locusts are responsible for the development, adaptability, and survival. Key factors such as hormones —including the juvenile hormone and [His7]-corazonin—and physiological functions enable the locust to respond to environmental cues. The juvenile hormone regulates growth and coloration, while neurotransmitters like dopamine and serotonin influence behavior and phase changes. Chemical communication, through pheromones and other signals, governs social interactions, reproductive synchronization, and swarm formation during both solitary and gregarious phases.  Understanding these chemical mechanisms provides insight into their function and place in the natural world and develop strategies for managing their impacts on agriculture and ecosystems.
content:
Unlocking Locust Survival: A Chemical Analysis of Locusts  Frederic Koran, Claire Leader, Alexandra Stoilova, Alina Weng Abstract The complex chemical properties of locusts are responsible for the development, adaptability, and survival. Key factors such as hormones —including the juvenile hormone and [His7]-corazonin—and physiological functions enable the locust to respond to environmental cues. The juvenile hormone regulates growth and coloration, while neurotransmitters like dopamine and serotonin influence behavior and phase changes. Chemical  communication , through pheromones and other signals, governs social interactions, reproductive synchronization, and swarm formation during both solitary and gregarious phases.  Understanding these chemical mechanisms provides insight into their function and place in the natural world and develop strategies for managing their impacts on agriculture and ecosystems.  Introduction Locusts, infamous for their destructive swarms, belong to the Acrididae family, which includes about 20 species known for phase transformations (phase polyphenism). This trait enables them to switch between two phases in response to environmental challenges: the solitary phase, where locusts behave more like individual grasshoppers, and the gregarious phase, in which they form swarms and are more attracted to other locusts. The environmental cues could be anything from population density to resource availability. While adaptability is behavioural, it goes further to chemical processes that regulate development, physiology, and interactions with the environment.  One of the locusts’ most fascinating abilities is their capacity to thrive in diverse environments, from lush grasslands to arid deserts. By exhibiting specific chemical processes through experience, the locust can make these necessary adaptations for their survival. For instance, chemical signals influence whether offspring develop into solitary or gregarious forms, altering their physical traits and behavior without changing their DNA.  In the locust’s nymphal stages, hormones are central and direct their growth and maturation. The juvenile hormone, secreted by the corpora allata, an endocrine gland near the brain, regulates the timing of development.  A decline in juvenile hormone levels triggers molting and development of adult characteristics such as wings or reproductive organs (Riddiford, 2012). As you may imagine, any disruption in timing can lead to developmental abnormalities or premature maturation, so precise timing is essential. The hormone [His₇]-corazonin is a neuropeptide that drives pigmentation. [His₇]-corazonin and juvenile hormone work together to determine locust coloration, influenced by factors such as camouflage, predator avoidance, and ecological interactions (Pener & Yerushalmi, 1998). Their precise interaction is essential to proper and specific development of physical traits at the right time.  Neurotransmitters like dopamine and serotonin play an important role in locusts’ behavioral and phase changes. Dopamine influences movement, arousal, and motivation of a locust and elevated dopamine levels are associated with increased locomotor activity and motivation, which promote social behaviors and swarming (which is a good thing for locusts) (Ma et al., 2011). Serotonin controls the sensory perception and behavior in locusts, promoting both solitary and gregarious phases depending on the species of locust (desert locusts react differently than migratory locusts). These chemical messengers drive the locust to adapt to its surroundings, changing based on specific conditions (Anstey et al., 2009).   Body-colour polymorphism  
 Life cycle of the locust  The life cycle of a locust begins in the  egg  phase. Female locusts lay their eggs inside holes made of damp soil and sand called pods (Fig. 1). Mothers produce a frothy liquid that fully envelopes the egg, protecting it from dehydration and predators (Agriculture Victoria, 2024). Phase change has been shown to accumulate generationally through the froth; it contains water-soluble factors known as aggregation pheromones that have been shown to influence whether a locust will hatch gregarious or solitary. Hormones and epigenetic factors, like pheromones, can modulate the expression of genes controlling gregarious colouration, either activating or repressing them. (Simpson, 2005).  The egg hatches into a nymph, the growth phase. Insects and arthropods have exoskeletons, hard outer shells that do not grow with them. As they increase in size, the exoskeleton must be shed and replaced by a new one; this process is known as ecdysis. The period between ecdyses is called an instar. The locust goes through five instars before reaching adulthood (Fig. 1) (Belles, 2020).   During the early instars, the body secretes the juvenile hormone, which helps control the maturation of the nymph. Increased hormone levels allow the insect to remain in a juvenile state—growing larger without developing adult features—by influencing the expression of genes associated with nymph characteristics. The juvenile hormone suppresses another hormone, ecdysone, which induces moulting or ecdysis. As the nymph grows, the concentration of juvenile hormone begins to decline and ecdysone is released to trigger the development of adult features like wings and reproductive organs, preparing the locust for adulthood (Singh Kaleka et al., 2019).  In adulthood, the locust feeds and migrates. While it is normally a solitary critter, adult locusts can travel in swarms if they become gregarious, which is dependent on environmental triggers. During the adult phase, male and female locusts mate; female locusts will then lay eggs, and the cycle will repeat itself (Fig. 1) (Agriculture Victora, 2024).   
 The juvenile hormone  The juvenile hormone is secreted by the corpora allata, an endocrine organ located beneath the aorta. The corpora allata contains many neurosecretory neurons that generate action potentials, but instead of secreting neurotransmitters into a synapse, they secrete hormones into the hemolymph (the bloodstream of the locust). The hormones are secreted as lipid droplets that reach receptors and interact with them (Gilbert, 1973). The basic structure of the juvenile hormone contains a cis oxirane ring (triangular ring containing two carbons and oxygen) and a trans double bond on the sixth carbon (Fig. 2). The natural hormone is not racemic (meaning there is an excess of a single enantiomer within the mixture), containing chiral centres at the tenth (R) and eleventh (S) carbons (Fig. 2). The hormone is synthesized through the terpenoid pathway, which involves the linkages of three five-carbon units called isoprenoids in a long chain  (Nouzova et al., 2018).   These chemical features and functional groups help the juvenile hormone perform its function within the locust. The terpenoid backbone and the oxirane ring allow interaction with nuclear hormone receptors and  proteins  that are involved in gene regulation, notably the Methoprene-tolerant (Met). Within the cytoplasm of a cell, the juvenile hormone bonds to the Met protein, which attracts coactivator proteins that help the complex translocate to the nucleus. There, the complex targets the promoter regions of specific genes and binds to them, working as a repressor or an inducer, preventing or facilitating their expression within the locust, respectively. Regulated genes are involved in the maturation of the nymph, but they are also related to its appearance, specifically its colour. The ester functional group before carbon one (Fig. 2) allows for the juvenile hormone’s hydrolyzation. Once the hormone has been secreted and performed its function, it can be broken down using water, which ensures that its effects are finely tuned according to developmental and environmental signs (Applebaum et al., 1997; Nouzova et al., 2018).  Locust colouration  Because juvenile hormone influences the transcription of genes affecting locust coloration, it plays a crucial role in the body-color polymorphism of gregarious locusts. Solitary locusts have green and brown colourations, usually earth-coloured, to adapt the individual to the background of its habitat. Gregarious locusts display black and vibrant red colors, along with yellow and orange tones. Their gregarious appearance is a design solution that allows them to ward off predators. Their colouration is a warning signalling that they are part of a large swarming group, making them potentially less palatable and more dangerous. The bright colours are similar to those of inedible toxic organisms, especially those that consume toxic flora. Although some species of locusts consume these plants, others that do not have also evolved the evolutionary strategy of mimicry, allowing them to appear toxic when, in reality, they are not (Sword et al., 2000; Tanaka, 2001). Both the juvenile hormone and another hormone called [His 7 ]-corazonin influence locust colour.  The release of hormones that change the colouration of the locust is dependent on many factors, including population density and environmental factors, like temperature and humidity (Tanaka, 2001). Body-colour polymorphism in locusts is reversible, and insects can switch between solitary and gregarious phases. During the growth phase, locusts with higher levels of juvenile hormone develop a green colour, while those lacking the hormone have a gregarious body colouration. Green nymphs with elevated levels of the juvenile hormone never showed gregarious colouration as adults. Therefore, the juvenile hormone only controls the green pigment, and there must be another factor controlling the dark colours in gregarious locusts. Implantation of the corpora allata of a black locust into a green one increased the amount of black expressed in the originally green locust, which points to a specific dark-colour-inducing compound also originating from the corpora allata (Tanaka, 2001).   
 An albino strain of locusts was used to identify the black-inducing factor (Tanaka, 2001). Different treatments were conducted on the compound, which was then implanted into the albino locust that was monitored for colour change. The treatments proved that the factor was a string of heat-stable neuropeptides that were then matched to the identical hormone [His 7 ]-corazonin (Fig. 4), which was previously isolated from a species of locust but had no known function. Injections of synthetic [His 7 ]-corazonin had the same colour-changing effect. The amount of the hormone injected changed the pigmentation of the locust. More of the hormone led to a darker colour. It was also shown that the timing of the secretion was related to the colouration. Locusts injected with [His 7 ]-corazonin at the beginning of an instar turned completely black after ecdysis (Fig. 3); those injected in the middle of an instar developed black patterns with an orange background, and locusts injected towards the end of an instar became brown or purple following ecdysis. None of these locusts entirely resembled gregarious insects in the wild (Fig. 3); therefore, it is hypothesized that both the juvenile hormone and [His 7 ]-corazonin control the locust’s solitary and gregarious colourations (Tanaka, 2001).   [His 7 ]-corazonin  The mechanism of action of [His 7 ]-corazonin differs significantly from that of the juvenile hormone, which influences the expression of specific genes. Instead, [His 7 ]-corazonin binds to specific receptors in the locust’s epidermal cells, which leads to the upregulation of pigments, especially melanin (Tanaka, 2001). The hormone modulates enzymes involved in its synthesis.   
 
 [His 7 ]-corazonin is a relatively short peptide, containing a string of 11 amino acids that help it perform its function (Fig. 4) (Tanaka, 2001). Histidine at the seventh position (Fig. 4) (in its name) allows the peptide to fit into the binding pocket of the corazonin receptor, a G-protein-coupled receptor. G-protein-coupled receptors are membrane proteins that respond to extracellular stimuli and initiate signal cascades (Fig. 5) (Predel & et al., 2007). Upon binding, the hormone activates the receptor by inducing a conformational change, enabling it to interact with G-proteins on the intracellular side, causing them to exchange GDP for GTP (Fig. 5). This activates the G-protein, which is now able to interact with secondary messengers like cyclic AMP or Calcium  ions  that trigger enzymes through phosphorylation or a change in membrane potential, respectively (Fig. 5).   The juvenile hormone and [His 7 ]-corazonin function in different ways affecting the type of colour regulation. The juvenile hormone works long-term because it regulates gene transcription, the first step in protein synthesis. On the other hand, [His₇]-corazonin activates specific enzymes that act quickly, enabling short-term regulation in response to environmental triggers. This allows locusts to rapidly switch from solitary to gregarious phases following external stimuli.  Locust behavioral phase change  Solitary locusts are less prone to locomotion, more sedentary and live in isolation. Gregarious locusts are more active, more social and, thus, live in swarms (Pflüger & Bräunig, 2021). There are two sensory pathways that trigger the phase change of locusts from solitary phase to gregarious phase. First, there is the thoracic pathway stimulated by mechanosensory when locusts get in contact with each other. Second, there is the cephalic pathway driven by the olfactory and visual stimuli (Anstey et al., 2009). Thus, sight, smell and touch are the main stimuli to locust phase change. Furthermore, not all locust species have been analyzed in dept. The most studied locust species are the migratory locust,  Locusta migratoria , and the desert locust,  Schistocerca gregaria  (Pflüger & Bräunig, 2021). A time-related variation in phase changes is distinguished between these two species. The migratory locust has slower gregarization and faster solitarization, whereas the desert locust crowds more rapidly and has slower solitarization (Guo et al., 2013).   Dopamine   Dopamine is a neurotransmitter that controls movement, pleasure, motivation, arousal and memory in organisms. Through gene observation and  analysis , it was determined that the catecholamine metabolic pathway was the most affected one in the fourth stadium of gregarious development for migratory locusts (Ma et al., 2011). Two gene expressions were analyzed extensively: the  pale  gene and the  vat1  gene. The  pale  gene encodes the enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase which is the rate-limiting enzyme for the synthesis of dopamine. The  vat1  gene encodes a protein responsible for the synaptic release of dopamine (Fig. 6). The development of locust was divided into five stadiums and genes were detected through quantitative PCR analysis of locust head tissues. During the five stadiums of development for a gregarious locust, the  pale  gene had a high expression in the first stadium and a weakening of the gene expression was observed by the end of the development stages. For the  vat1  gene, low expression was observed in the first stadium and there was an increase of expression by the fifth stadium. The time-related gene expressions demonstrate an early stage of dopamine synthesis and a late stage of dopamine release (Ma et al., 2011). With an increase in crowding, an increase in gene expressions can be seen. In solitary locust, both genes were less expressed. The reduction in dopamine synthesis and release explains the reserved and less active behavior of the solitary locust (Ma et al., 2011)  
 Fig. 6  Schematic representation of dopamine metabolic pathway. [Adapted from Ma et al., 2011]  Experiments using contrast microscopy showed higher dopamine levels in the metathoracic ganglia of isolated desert locusts compared to long-term crowded ones. Dopamine was injected into different test subjects which were then subjected to crowding. Two control groups injected with saline were set: gregarious locusts and solitary locusts. 60% of the gregarious control group reacted to stimuli and 38% of the solitary control group reacted. 32% of the gregarious locusts injected with dopamine reacted to the stimuli and 20% of the injected solitary locusts reacted (Alessi et al., 2014). Thus, it is observed that dopamine injections decrease the number of locusts reacting to the stimuli. This makes dopamine a key neurotransmitter responsible for the induction of behavioral change from gregarious to solitary. Dopamine reduced efficacy of synaptic inputs to the thoracic neurons controlling insect flight and locomotion, thus explaining the less active behavior of solitary locusts (Alessi et al., 2014). This decrease in activity helps locusts maintain a lifestyle of high endurance and optimize their food-intake in harsh environments.  Serotonin  Although dopamine plays a significant role in locusts behavioral phase transition, the shift of phase is incomplete without the involvement of other chemicals, such as serotonin. Serotonin is a neurotransmitter that controls mood, appetite, sleep and reproduction.   Amid crowding, the solitary desert locust can turn to the gregarious phase in less than two hours. With the identification of the sensory stimuli triggering behavioral change, the central nervous system is divided between the brain, subject to olfactory and visual stimuli, and the thoracic ganglia, subject to the mechanosensory stimulus. The brain controls the thoracic ganglia which regulates locomotion (Guo et al., 2013). During the behavioral change of a solitary desert locust, there is an increase in serotonin levels in the thoracic ganglia of the central nervous system. A positive correlation between serotonin levels and gregarization of the desert locust was determined through different manipulations. A binary logistic regression model with probabilistic metric was set with P greg  of 0 representing the solitary phase and P greg  of 1 representing the gregarious phase (Anstey et al., 2009). First, serotonin receptor antagonists were injected into the solitary locust to block the action of serotonin. The locust failed to change phase with a P greg  of 0.27 for the thoracic pathway and 0.07 for the cephalic pathway (Fig. 7). Second, serotonin precursor was injected into solitary locusts, and they were observed for thirty minutes. The control solitary locust was subject to crowding and showed some behavioral change after thirty minutes. The injected locust who remained isolated had a similar result from the control. The injected locust put into a crowded environment went through significant gregarization. Thus, serotonin accelerates behavioral gregarization when in contact with sensory stimuli (Anstey et al., 2009).   
 Fig. 7  Behavior of locusts injected with serotonin receptor antagonists that block the action of serotonin and then exposed to sensory stimuli that normally induce gregarization (left column) is shown. Saline-injected controls are shown in the right column. Locusts injected with serotonin-receptor antagonists ketanserin and methiothepin (1 mM) and given either 1 hour of femoral mechanosensory stimulation or 1 hour of olfactory and visual stimulation from other locusts. [Adapted from Anstey et al., 2009]  In contrast, the opposite correlation was found in migratory locusts. The serotonin neurotransmitter enhanced the behavioral change of gregarious locusts to solitary locusts. The injection of serotonin in an isolated gregarious locust accelerated its change to a solitary locust. Since the brain controls and instructs thoracic ganglia, researchers decided to measure serotonin levels in the brain. The results of the experiment are an increase in serotonin during isolation of gregarious locusts and no change in serotonin levels during crowding of solitary locusts (Guo et al., 2013). From previous reviews, the increase in serotonin decreases sensory reactivity and protects against overstimulation. Thus, this would explain the slower locomotion and isolation of solitary locusts. Serotonin would reduce responses and activities of the locust to exterior factors. Furthermore, an increase in serotonin 5-HT 2  receptor expression during crowding was revealed. The low expression of the receptor partially induces gregarious behavior, but a rapid increase in expression activates serotonin  signaling  pathways and inhibits the phase change of the solitary locust (Guo et al., 2013).   The contradictory role of serotonin and dopamine in locusts can be explained by several factors. The locusts analyzed in these separate studies are of different species, thus resulting in a species-specific behavioral pattern. The research conducted with desert locusts measured serotonin levels from the thoracic ganglia whereas the research conducted with migratory locusts measured them from the brain. The duration of the experiment differed where one was a short-term application of serotonin and the other a long-term and systemic application. Each experiment used different methods and manipulations ranging from direct injection of the neurotransmitter to gene analysis (Guo et al., 2013).  Gene expression  The phase change of locusts is due to polyphenism, the occurrence of different phenotypes in a population influenced by their environments and not their genes. In the specific case of the locust, population density is the factor influencing the phenotype of the locust. Gene expression levels of 532 genes vary depending on the solitary and gregarious phase of the locust (Guo et al., 2011). From bioinformatics analysis, several chemosensory proteins genes and the  takeout  gene  LmigTO1  were expressed at a much higher level in the gregarious phase than the solitary phase. These genes are related to the transition of attraction or repulsion behavior of the locust towards other individuals. Through RNA  interference , the removal of a chemosensory protein gene in a gregarious locust made it transition to a solitary phase and the removal of the  takeout  gene in a solitary locust led it to its gregarious phase (Guo et al., 2011). Thus, the expression levels of chemosensory proteins gene and the  takeout  gene correlate to the level of attraction or repulsion of a locust. Gregarious locusts have a higher gene expression for chemosensory proteins which leads to the behavioral change of attraction. Solitary locusts have a higher gene expression of the  takeout  gene for a repulsive behavioral change. Since these genes do not affect the locomotor activity of locusts, chemosensory proteins and  takeout  genes only initiate the transition process.  Chemical Communication  Locusts, including the desert locust  Schistocerca gregaria , use chemical communication extensively in modulating numerous behavioral events, including but not limited to courtship, reproduction, and aggregation. These behaviors follow from the interaction of pheromones, cuticular hydrocarbons, hormones, and volatile compounds that allow both individual interactions and group dynamics to take place. Chemical signals are involved in all of these, from mate attraction up to the coordination of large swarms. These chemical processes give a better understanding of how locusts reproduce and aggregate, and the biochemical underpinning of their complex behavioral ecology.  Pheromones and Mate Attraction  Generally, in locusts, pheromones are considered the seminal chemical signals controlling sexual reproduction. In the case of the locusts, females emit sex pheromones to attract males; this in turn allows mate recognition in very high-density aggregations, such as the swarms of  S. gregaria . In general, these are long-chain aldehydes, alcohols, and esters, synthesized from the fatty acids through a series of biochemical reactions involving oxidation, reduction, and elongation (Coombes et al., 2018). The pheromones are usually emitted by special glands near the abdomen, which diffuse into the air and are recognized by males on antennal chemoreceptors (Fig. 8).  
 Fig. 8  Subsections of the male antennal chemoreceptors, and the pathways that take them to the receiving area of their brain (Stern et al. 2012).  Once these pheromones are detected by a male locust, he is lured towards the female and starts with  displaying several courtship postures like the vibrating of wings, the movement of antennae, and the copulatory postures. Because of this type of chemical signaling, males can target future mates among the tumult of big aggregations. Juvenile hormones, therefore, initiate the production of sex pheromones whereby such chemicals are synthesized and released during the female’s fertile period (Ferenz et al., 2003). Accordingly, females timed their mating availability to correspond with the release of sex pheromones so that copulation occurs at the best reproductive time.  Cuticular Hydrocarbons and Sexual Recognition  Apart from sex pheromones, cuticular hydrocarbons or CHCs also play a significant role in sexual recognition and mate choice. These are derived from the locust cuticle and not only act as species-specific markers but also provide information on reproductive status. For example, in the females of  S. gregaria , CHC profiles change during their reproductive cycle and give information on their sexual receptivity to males. These hydrocarbons are produced by fatty acid elongation and can undergo modifications, like methylation or saturation, that affect their volatility and hence their detectability (Hassanali et al., 2005).  The males of  S. gregaria  detect receptive status via a CHC profile, thereby avoiding courtship that would be inappropriate. Non-receptive females usually have normal CHC patterns which signal their status and inhibit the useless efforts of the males. The chemical signaling prevents wasting mating effort on females in non-receptive physiological status, increasing reproductive efficiency, and preventing unwanted copulation (Coombes et al., 2018).  Courtship Inhibition and Sexual Conflict  Locusts also employ chemical signals in courtship inhibition, wherein females regulate mating opportunities. Female locusts release pheromones for courtship inhibition if they are not in the receptive state or want to avoid mating with lower-fitness males. Such pheromones inhibit sexual behavior in males and prevent any undesired mating attempts (Seidelmann et al., 2002). Understanding the mechanism of courtship inhibition is important in managing sexual conflict, where the male, under the strong drive to mate, can pursue courtship even when the female is unreceptive. Females avoid harassment through the release of inhibitory pheromones and thus ensure that copulation occurs only when it is most advantageous to their interest. This subtle modulation in courtship enables females to maintain control over their reproductive decisions and results in optimized mate selection.  Hormonal Control of Pheromone Production  Sex pheromones and courtship-inhibiting pheromones are released in response to a change in hormonal state, notably juvenile hormones and ecdysteroids. Juvenile hormone-which governs reproductive maturity-triggers the biosynthesis of sex pheromones during the fertile phase of the female reproductive cycle (Ferenz et al., 2003) (Fig. 9). As shall be discussed below, this same hormone increases the receptivity of females so that mating can occur precisely during this period. In addition, ecdysteroids-that regulate molting-regulate the time course of reproductive behavior and influence the release of both sex pheromones and courtship-inhibiting pheromones. High ecdysteroid levels correlate the female’s behavior with her reproductive physiology and form a tight mechanism for the control of mating.  
 Fig. 9 Juvenile Hormone and its resulting effects in the brain and receptors of the reproductive system.  Locust Aggregation  Besides courtship and reproduction, locusts also show a strong aggregation behavior, particularly in the gregarious phase when they take the form of huge swarms. Aggregation plays an important role in locust survival and reproductive strategies, wherein chemical signaling is at the center. Locusts aggregate because of environmental cues and the chemical signals, especially aggregation pheromones, from individuals themselves that attract other individuals. These chemical signals ensure that the movements and activities of locusts are coordinated with one another; large swarms are therefore easily formed, and this in turn assists the transition from solitary to gregarious behavior.  The volatile compounds initiating an aggregation response are produced both by immature and mature locusts. The chemicals are typically cuticular hydrocarbon derivatives, which are then detected by conspecifics via specialized antennal chemoreceptors. For instance, in  S. gregaria , aggregation pheromones trigger increased locomotion and attraction, thereby making individuals aggregate. Aggregation is related closely with density-dependent effects-increasingly, as locusts are more in number, aggregation pheromones are produced more intensively, enhancing attraction among individuals and therefore encouraging swarm development  (Seidelmann et al., 2002).  It also mediates behavioral synchrony in these groups, which maintains the locusts in proximity to one another and travel together. Swarm capability forms the very foundation of successful migration whereby locusts can cover long distances in search of food and suitable breeding grounds. The aggregation pheromones may also allow for reproductive synchronization among conspecifics, since individuals of a similar age and reproductive condition come together, thereby providing the opportunity to maximize mating.  Chemical Factors in Oviposition and Aggregation of Females  Chemical signaling at oviposition also plays a vital role in the aggregation of locusts, especially females. Ovipositing females in  S. gregaria  release specific pheromones attractive to other females to the site of oviposition. Such oviposition-related pheromones serve as recruitment signals, guiding other females to suitable egg-laying sites (Norris et al., 1970). Aggregation of females onto these sites depends on two factors: locust density and chemical signals prevailing in the environment.  In one study, it was demonstrated that during the gregarization phase of locusts, females that oviposit release a pheromone which elicits a positive aggregative response among conspecific females (Ferenz et al., 2003). The effect of such pheromones is that of synchronizing egg-laying activities, aggregating females in large numbers at an oviposition site. This is advantageous because, with such high density, eggs hatch more easily. Such aggregation allows for efficient use of space and resources, maximizing reproductive output in swarming locust populations.  Cannibalism and Chemical Signalling  Cannibalism is one of the interesting aspects of locust behavior, which is involved at the level of chemical signaling, particularly under conditions of crowding. Locusts have been recorded under specific conditions to exhibit cannibalistic behavior caused either by stress or scarcity of resources. Chemical signals on alarm pheromones provide information about potential danger or carcasses and, therefore, serve as stimuli for cannibalistic behavior. Their chemical nature is still under investigation, but it is considered that volatile compounds from injured or dead locusts are implicated in the induction of this behavior (Couzin et al., 2023).  Although it does not relate directly to either mating or aggregation, locust cannibalism is a response to extreme environmental stress and may be influenced by the same chemical pathways as other social behaviors such as aggregation and courtship. We gain from this an understanding of how such chemical signals can trigger such behaviors and widen our view on the locust’s chemical ecology to include complex social dynamics and survival strategies.  Conclusion Locusts must survive in environments with fluctuating resources, population stresses, and  predation  pressure. Through their complex chemical adaptations, locusts have evolved to adjust behavior, development, and social interactions to survive and thrive. Locusts must develop and adapt to environmental cues with precise timing. Through the use of the juvenile hormone and [His 7 ]-corazonin, locusts’ development, molting and pigmentation are regulated in responses to environmental conditions. With controlled life cycle stages and physical traits, the locust has smooth transitions through developmental stages and appropriate features for survival.   The resources and environment around locusts are everchanging and require constant adjusting behavior and activity to cope with possible challenges. Dopamine and serotonin are neurotransmitters that adjust the behavior, movement and social interactions of locusts. These transmitters are the driving force behind the locust responding to its surroundings, seeking resources, and adapting its social behavior, all to help balance energy conservation with necessary increased activity.   Locusts must navigate social dynamics and coordination to survive and reproduce. Pheromones – chemical signals communications – facilitate  foraging , predator avoidance, and swarm formation through both solitary and gregarious phases. These  evolutionary adaptations  provide effective, adaptive solutions to potential environmental challenges.  Understanding the interconnected chemical system in locusts offers valuable insights for comprehending and potentially managing their impacts on ecosystems and agriculture.
