title: The Chemistry of Pistol Shrimp and Antarctic Krill
authors: Alaia Krishnan Claveras, Celina Moukarzel, Chloe Chan Lam, Julia Purdue, Lina Benchekor
abstract: This paper investigates the chemistry behind the adaptive design solutions of krill and pistol shrimp. First, the exoskeleton that these crustaceans rely on for protection, structural support, and survival will be analyzed. Composed of organic substances such as chitin and inorganic minerals like calcium carbonate and fluoride salts, exoskeletons have been optimized for both flexibility and rigidity. Then, we will examine acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter that induces muscle contractions, facilitating the pistol shrimp’s rapid claw snap. Next, a discussion of omega-3 phospholipids will dive into the importance of maintaining membrane homeostasis and supporting cellular functions in cold environments. Finally, we will analyze the bioluminescence used by krill to camouflage themselves from predators. Through the luciferin-luciferase enzymatic reaction, krill photophores produce light that minimizes the silhouette effect created by solar light.
content:
The Chemistry of Pistol Shrimp and Antarctic Krill  Alaia Krishnan Claveras, Celina Moukarzel, Chloe Chan Lam, Julia Purdue, Lina Benchekor Abstract This paper investigates the chemistry behind the adaptive design solutions of krill and pistol shrimp. First, the exoskeleton that these crustaceans rely on for protection, structural support, and survival will be analyzed. Composed of organic substances such as  chitin  and inorganic minerals like calcium carbonate and fluoride salts, exoskeletons have been optimized for both flexibility and rigidity. Then, we will examine acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter that induces muscle contractions, facilitating the pistol shrimp’s rapid claw snap. Next, a discussion of omega-3 phospholipids will dive into the importance of maintaining membrane homeostasis and supporting cellular functions in cold environments. Finally, we will analyze the  bioluminescence  used by krill to camouflage themselves from predators. Through the luciferin-luciferase enzymatic reaction, krill photophores produce light that minimizes the silhouette effect created by solar light.  Introduction Pistol shrimp and krill share a common ancestry as members of the subphylum Crustacea, which are characterized by their hard exoskeletons, segmented bodies, and jointed limbs. Antarctic krill play a pivotal role in the Southern Ocean’s ecosystem, thriving along the continental shelf and in deeper oceanic regions (Grinnell, 1988). Despite their small size, their combined biomass is immense, making them one of the most abundant animal species on Earth alongside nematodes, insects, and fish (Shao et al., 2023). Krill, a keystone species, is the primary food source for a wide variety of marine animals, from fish to large whales. Pistol shrimps (Kingston, 2022), known for their asymmetrical front claws capable of producing powerful cavitations, inhabit tropical and temperate coastal waters, often dwelling in coral reefs and sponge cavities (Bohnenstiehl, 2016). This paper explores the key chemical components and processes that allow for the existence of krill and pistol shrimp. How does the pistol shrimp exoskeleton allow for the  strength  and flexibility it requires for both protection and growth? How are pistol shrimp able to snap its claw shut with so much force? How do krill manage free radical accumulation to avoid damage caused by oxidative stress? How are they able to camouflage themselves from predators during the daytime? By answering these questions, we aim to deepen our understanding of the complex interplay between chemistry and survival strategies in these remarkable crustaceans.  Chitin exoskeleton: the structural foundation  The most fundamental chemical component of crustacean exoskeletons is chitin, a long-chain polysaccharide (a type of carbohydrate or sugar) composed of repeating units of N-acetylglucosamine, a derivative of glucose with an additional nitrogen group. The long chitin molecules are organized into fibrous layers that provide structural support through interactions with other components (Horst, 1983; Peng, 2022). See Figure 1A for a planar view of chitin fibers and Figure 1B for a cross-sectional view showing the layered arrangement. This arrangement displays the Bouligand, or “twisted plywood,” structure, where linear chitin fibers form thin sheets that stack helically across multiple layers. Each layer is slightly rotated relative to the one below it, creating an anisotropic (directionally dependent) assembly that enhances toughness and fracture resistance by redistributing mechanical stresses. This structure provides resilience against impacts and compressive forces in natural environments (Peng et al., 2022). Figure 1B highlights the helicoidal stacking of chitin fibers, crucial for maintaining structural integrity and protection against mechanical stress (Horst, 1983).  
 Fig.1.  Microscopic structure of the chitin surface of the Antarctic krill cuticle treated with sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid ( A  plane structure of chitin;  B  structure of cross section) (Peng, 2022).   Although Figure 1 illustrates this structure in krill, the Bouligand arrangement of chitin fibers is also common across crustaceans, including pistol shrimp, where it serves a similar function in supporting exoskeletal strength and durability under environmental pressures (Peng et al., 2022).  Protein reinforcements  Chitin is combined with specific cuticular  proteins , including proteins that contribute to structural reinforcement called Rebers-Riddiford proteins and stabilizing proteins called obstructor proteins, which bind to chitin to reinforce the exoskeleton (Bentov, 2016; Skinner, 1992). These cuticular proteins cross-link with chitin fibers, forming covalent bonds between amino groups on chitin molecules and specific side chains on the protein molecules, creating a stable, interconnected network that greatly strengthens the structure. By chemically bonding with chitin, these proteins provide additional rigidity and durability to the exoskeleton (Bentov, 2016; Skinner, 1992).  In krill, proteins involved in exoskeleton formation, such as gastrolith matrix proteins (proteins that assist in calcium storage and exoskeletal calcification), play a critical role during molting by helping rebuild the exoskeleton after it is shed (Nicol, 1992; Skinner, 1992). Additionally, proteins in the exoskeleton undergo sclerotization—a hardening process that chemically strengthens proteins through cross-linking reactions. This reaction begins with the enzyme phenoloxidase, which catalyzes the oxidation of phenolic compounds into reactive quinones. These quinones then react with specific amino acids, such as lysine and tyrosine, on adjacent protein molecules, forming covalent cross-links between the proteins. This cross-linking transforms the softer, flexible protein matrix into a rigid, durable network that enhances the exoskeleton’s resistance to mechanical stress and damage (Terwilliger, 1999). This chemical hardening enables the exoskeleton to provide robust protection under environmental stress (Bentov, 2016).  Mineralization  Another essential part of the exoskeleton’s chemistry is mineralization, the process of depositing minerals to enhance hardness and durability. In both krill and pistol shrimp, calcium carbonate is the primary mineral that crystallizes within the exoskeleton, providing the hardness and mechanical support necessary for protection and structural integrity (Bentov, 2016). Krill exhibit an additional adaptation: their exoskeleton incorporates elevated levels of fluoride, which combines with calcium and phosphate to form fluorapatite, a calcium phosphate mineral. This fluorapatite mineralization significantly increases the rigidity of the exoskeleton, as fluorapatite is known for its extreme hardness and durability. In Antarctic krill, this calcium phosphate mineral consolidates the cuticle, making it highly resistant to mechanical wear and predation, ensuring the krill can effectively avoid predators and maintain its protective structure (Peng, 2019). In contrast, the pistol shrimp relies primarily on calcium carbonate to harden its snapping claw. This mineralization process involves embedding calcium carbonate within the claw’s chitinous matrix, creating a reinforced composite structure. Concentrated at the claw’s tip, the calcium carbonate provides compressive strength, which helps the claw resist deformation under high pressure. The crystalline structure of calcium carbonate also disperses impact forces across the claw, reducing the likelihood of fractures and enabling repeated, forceful snaps without compromising structural integrity (Amini et al., 2018).  Molting and growth  Molting is a critical process for both krill and pistol shrimp, allowing these organisms to shed their old exoskeleton and form a new, larger one that accommodates growth. The molting cycle includes distinct phases: pre-ecdysis, ecdysis (shedding), and post-ecdysis, each involving unique physiological and chemical changes.  In the pre-ecdysis stage, specific enzymes, including chitinase and phenoloxidase, begin breaking down the inner layer of the old exoskeleton’s chitin-protein matrix. Chitinase hydrolyzes chitin chains, while phenoloxidase generates reactive quinones, which help to weaken protein bonds within the matrix. This enzymatic breakdown facilitates the detachment of the old exoskeleton, creating space for the new, flexible structure underneath to expand (Peng, 2022; Bentov, 2016).  At ecdysis, the krill or shrimp sheds its old exoskeleton, revealing the soft, newly formed cuticle underneath. This cuticle is initially fragile and requires rapid mineralization during the post-ecdysis phase. In krill, the new exoskeleton absorbs calcium and fluoride ions from hemolymph (internal fluids) and seawater, allowing these minerals to be incorporated as calcium carbonate and fluorapatite, which harden the cuticle. Fluorapatite provides additional rigidity, enhancing the exoskeleton’s ability to withstand environmental pressures and predation (Nicol, 1992; Peng, 2022).  Pistol shrimp also undergo molting, though less frequently than krill. During their post-molt phase, calcium carbonate is deposited across the exoskeleton, with significant focus on the snapping claw. This deposition provides the claw with the durability necessary for hunting, enabling it to perform high-impact snaps repeatedly without compromising structural integrity. The calcium carbonate concentration at the claw tip enhances its resilience under mechanical stress, ensuring that the pistol shrimp retains an effective predatory mechanism (Amini, 2018; Bentov, 2016). This multi-stage molting process not only allows for growth but also plays a vital role in maintaining the exoskeletal properties that are essential for krill and pistol shrimp survival.  Astaxanthin: oxidative stress defense  Astaxanthin (AX), also known as 3,3′-dihydroxy-β,β-carotene-4,4′-dione, is a lipid-soluble pigment that is part of the xanthophyll carotenoid group. Its chemical formula is C40H52O4, its molar mass is 596.84 g/mol and it consists of two oxygenated β-ionone-type ring systems linked by a chain of conjugated double bonds (polyene chain). The ionone rings each carry hydroxyl (-OH) and a carbonyl-C=O) groups. AX is primarily found in the exoskeleton and imparts the vibrant orange-red hue to shrimp and krill because of the 13 conjugated double bonds in its molecular structure. This structure lowers the energy gap between the ground state and the excited state, making it possible to absorb the lower-energy (longer wavelength) light of the blue-green region and reflect the higher-energy (shorter wavelength) light of the red-orange region. However, AX can form aggregates when bound to other proteins like crustacyanin that cause it to exhibit different optical properties, hence the appearance of colors such as brown or yellow. In shrimp specifically, three optical isomers of AX are found in the lipid bilayer of cells: (3R,3′R), meso, and (3S,3′S) (Figure 2) (Nishida, 2023).    
 Fig. 2.  The three stereoisomers of astaxanthin found in shrimp (Nishida, 2023).  AX has a unique molecular structure with polar groups at both ends and a nonpolar middle section. This structure allows it to span the entire width of the cell membrane. The two ionone rings at the ends of the molecule bear polar groups which can interact with the hydrophilic heads of the phospholipids, while the non-polar polyene chain in the middle, containing methyl groups, interacts with the hydrophobic fatty acid tails. Crustaceans obtain AX directly by consuming algae and other marine organisms that produce and accumulate this pigment naturally or produce it from β-carotene. They can convert β-carotene into AX through a series of enzymatic reactions that is also often obtained from algae. The proposed pathway of β-carotene to AX found in krill and shrimp is demonstrated by the orange arrows in Figure 3. After obtaining or producing AX, Crustaceans then store it in their tissues, exoskeletons, hemolymph, and eggs (Šimat et al., 2022). This is important for their survival, as AX plays a vital role in protecting these organisms from oxidative stress, particularly from reactive species like singlet oxygen and free radicals generated by UV exposure.  
 Fig. 3.  Conversion pathways of beta-carotene to astaxanthin. The orange arrows display the chemical pathway for most crustaceans, including shrimp and krill. The yellow and blue arrows indicate a less common, alternative pathway (Šimat et al., 2022).   AX has strong antiangiogenic (inhibition of the formation of new blood vessels), anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant activities. In fact, it is a stronger antioxidant compared to β-carotene and vitamin E. AX can gather and neutralize reactive chemical species, including reactive oxygen species (ROS), effectively deactivating these highly reactive molecules. This is useful for krill and shrimp, since it prevents cellular damage caused by metabolic processes and UV radiation exposure in polar waters.  Singlet oxygen  AX’s antioxidant properties are particularly important in combating harmful reactive species like singlet oxygen (¹O₂), which form when sunlight is absorbed and can pose a threat to the cellular integrity of these organisms. Singlet oxygen is an excited state of O₂ in which two unpaired electrons become paired, resulting in electrons with opposite spins (Figure 4). The formation of singlet oxygen can occur through the absorption of sunlight by photosensitizer molecules (such as chlorophyll) which then transfer this energy to ground state molecules to excite them (Ossola, 2021).   
 Fig. 4.  Molecular orbital diagram of ground state triplet oxygen and excited singlet oxygen (Ormond, 2009).   The generation of singlet oxygen can be detrimental to biological tissues. Since the molecule has a high reactivity, it can react within an organism and modify DNA, proteins, and lipids. Nevertheless, carotenoids are amazingly effective at quenching singlet molecular oxygen, especially AX. Once the molecules make Van der Waals contact, the oxygen binds to the center of the carotenoids. They do this by forming a weakly bound complex with singlet oxygen through the donation of electron density from the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) to the pi orbitals of the singlet oxygen (Figure 5).  
 Fig. 5.  Process of singlet oxygen (red spheres) quenching by carotenoids (orange & white spheres). Orbitals are represented by the red and orange lines (Tamura, 2020).  This is called a Dexter-type super exchange mechanism, where the intermediate, in this case, involves a radical positively charged carotenoid and a radical negatively charged oxygen. This intermediate state is significantly higher in energy compared to the initial state (Figure 6), making it inherently unstable. Consequently, the system is driven to proceed to form new products. These products are triplet oxygen, the ground state of molecular oxygen, as well as triplet AX, meaning there are two unpaired electrons with parallel spins. The larger the length of the conjugated double bonds and the higher the HOMO level, the lower the energy gap between the initial and intermediate state, meaning a faster quenching of the singlet oxygen. While AX does not have the highest HOMO level, it efficiently quenches singlet oxygen because of the strong electronic coupling that occurs between both reactants (Tamura, 2020).  
 Fig. 6.  Energy diagram of the reaction of singlet oxygen quenching. As seen, the intermediate state is significantly high in energy (Tamura, 2020).  Free radicals   AX is also important in mitigating the harmful effects of free radicals, including lipid peroxyl radicals, which can cause significant cellular damage in shrimp and krill. Free radicals are defined as molecular species with unpaired electrons, which can exist in different atomic orbitals. This makes these species highly unstable and reactive. For instance, singlet oxygen is not a free radical because it has all its electrons paired. In shrimp and krill, lipid peroxyl radicals could be damaging to the cells. They both have a high amount of polyunsaturated fatty acids ( PUFA s) in their lipids, which are important for energy storage. However, when subjected to external stressors like fluctuations in temperature and light, these lipids can change to form free radicals which can cause cellular damage, particularly membrane damage (Ormond, 2009). While the exact mechanisms by which carotenoids scavenge free radicals are not fully understood, it’s possible that some may act as pro-oxidants (Krinsky, 2003), potentially generating even more reactive oxygen species and free radicals in the process. Nonetheless, AX has demonstrated very little pro-oxidant activity (Nishida et al., 2023).  In summary, AX is essential for the survival and general health of shrimp and krill as it provides substantial antioxidant effects. Hence, not surprisingly, shrimp fed AX for 4–8 weeks had a 91% survival rate, while shrimp fed no antioxidant had a survival rate of just 57% (Yamada et al., 1990). Interestingly, even microscopic organisms like  cyanobacteria  (Bai et al., 2023) and  tardigrades  (Jabbour et al., 2023) exhibit similar antioxidant mechanisms to prevent DNA damage from UV radiation.  Omega-3 phospholipids: extreme temperature survival  In the icy waters of the Southern Ocean, where temperatures plunge to near freezing, Antarctic krill showcase one of nature’s most remarkable chemical adaptations for surviving these extreme conditions. At the core of their adaptation is the intricate chemistry of their cell membranes, which rely on omega-3 PUFAs such as eicosatetraenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) (Figure 7). This ingenious design allows krill to maintain membrane fluidity and ensure proper cellular function in a sub-zero  environment .    
 Fig. 7.  Structural components of phospholipids found in cell membranes (Alberts, 2002). The phospholipids, with their glycerol backbone, polar head, and long-chain omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (EPA and DHA), introduce kinks in the fatty acid chains due to double bonds, enhancing membrane fluidity. These kinks are essential for maintaining flexibility and ensuring proper cellular function in the cold.  Krill membranes contain omega-3 phospholipids (Burri, 2012), which are molecules perfectly suited for cold adaptations. The chemical components of a phospholipid include a glycerol backbone, shown in Figure 6, which forms the scaffold of the molecule, two fatty acid chains, often EPA (C₂₀H₃₀O₂) and DHA (C₂₂H₃₂O₂), both of which are long-chain omega-3 PUFAs, and a phosphate group with a polar head. The polar head of the phosphate is hydrophilic ( water -attracting), allowing interaction with the aqueous environment outside the cell (Burri, 2012).  Membrane flexibility  What differentiates omega-3 fatty acids such as EPA and DHA from saturated fats is their degree of unsaturation. Unsaturation refers to the presence of double bonds between carbon atoms in the fatty acid chain. The double bonds create bends or curves (kinks), shown in Figure 8, in their H-C chain, which prevents the fatty acids from packing tightly together. This molecular disorder maintains membrane fluidity at low temperature, which is critical for maintaining the function of membrane-bound proteins and enzymes.   
 Fig. 8.  Chemical structure of EPA and DHA. EPA has five double bonds along its 20-carbon chain and DHA has six double bonds along its 22-carbon chain (Chan Lam, 2024).   The double bonds in EPA and DHA typically adopt a cis configuration, where the hydrogen atoms attached to the carbon atoms at the double bond are on the same side. The  cis  configuration creates a pronounced bend in the hydrocarbon chain. The spatial arrangement in  cis -configuration disrupts Van der Waals forces, preventing a rigid, crystalline-like structure in the membrane. Additionally, the  cis  double bonds reduce  intermolecular forces  between adjacent phospholipid molecules, maintaining lateral mobility of the lipids within the membrane bilayer. The  cis -kink structure that is found in the krill cell membrane is crucial because it prevents the fatty acids from aligning perfectly, therefore increasing fluidity of the membrane.    The chain length and the number of double bonds present in DHA further enhance flexibility. DHA contains 22 carbons and six double bonds, and is more unsaturated than EPA, shown in Figure 11. This degree of unsaturation leads to more kinks in the chain, enhancing membrane fluidity at even lower temperatures. The flexibility introduced by omega-3 fatty acids can also affect the movement of cholesterol and proteins within the membrane (Falch, 2023). Cholesterol normally acts to modulate fluidity, but in frigid conditions, its effects are mitigated by the high concentration of unsaturated fats.   The hydrophilic nature of the phosphate head allows it to interact with the water molecules surrounding the cell, stabilizing the membrane in two ways:   
 The negative charge of the phosphate group can form electrostatic attractions with positively charged ions in the aqueous environment, further stabilizing the structure.   
 The interaction with water creates a hydration layer that provides a physical buffer, protecting the membrane from mechanical stress caused by changes in external conditions (e.g., ice formation).   
 In freezing environments, membranes with high levels of saturated fats would effectively “freeze,” compromising cellular processes like nutrient transport, energy production, and signal transduction. Antarctic krill do not synthesize these essential omega-3 PUFAs on their own, but ingested through their diet of phytoplankton, microscopic marine plants that are rich in EPA and DHA. Phytoplankton, through photosynthesis, synthesizes omega-3 fatty acids, which krill consumes and incorporates into their own cellular membranes. This creates a biochemical cycle in which omega-3s, derived from primary producers, fuel the cold-resistant survival mechanisms of organisms higher up in the food chain.   The survival of Antarctic krill in freezing water demonstrates the ingenious design solution of nature. The incorporation of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids like EPA and DHA into their membranes is a finely tuned chemical strategy, enabling krill to maintain the flexibility and fluidity in their membranes under extreme cold. This structural adaptability ensures that vital cellular processes, driven by membrane-bound proteins and enzymes, continue without interruption, even in extreme conditions. The chemical adaptation displays how Antarctic krill can flourish in the Southern Ocean through complex and elegant chemical solution.  Chemical camouflage: bioluminescence in krill  Bioluminescence is the production of light from living organisms. One third of species in the  Arthropoda phylum , as well as most marine dwellers, are bioluminescent, including jellyfish, krill,  copepods ,  Radiolaria , and dinoflagellate. The purposes of bioluminescence vary, ranging from attracting mates or prey to evading predators through camouflage and blinding tactics (Tsarkova, 2021). In this paper, we will be specifically discussing bioluminescence as a design solution for krill’s need to camouflage itself from predators.   This form of bioluminescence, used by some marine animals to blend into their environment and avoid detection by predators, is known as cryptic bioluminescence. It is often achieved through a method called counter-illumination, where the animal produces light from its underside to match the ambient light from above, effectively erasing its silhouette when viewed from below (Warner et al., 1979).   Photophores  The production of this light takes place in organs called photophores. In the transparent euphausiid shrimp, there are 10 photophores widely spaced along the ventral surface of the body as seen in Figure 9. There is one on each eyestalk, two pairs placed laterally on the thorax, and four arranged along the mid-line of the abdomen under the cephalothorax and the gut, the least transparent structures (Grinnell, 1988).  
 Fig. 9.  Photographs of  M. norvegica  (Fregin, 2002). In the left photo, the photophores can be seen in relation to the eyes, thorax, and abdomen. In the right photo, the photophores can be seen brightly luminescing in the dark.  The general structure of krill photophores is similar between species. Light-producing cells and refractive rods are positioned in the center of the light organ, forming a striated structure called the lantern. The lantern functions as a sinus and about 30 capillaries drain oxygenated hemolymph into it. A filamentous cuff wraps around the opening of the capillaries and functions as a sphincter (Kronstrom et al., 2009). Sphincters are circular muscles that open and close passages in the body to regulate the flow of substances, thus the filamentous cuff expands and contracts to control how much oxygenated hemolymph drains into the lantern. Electron microscopy shows that the filamentous material consists of thick and thin muscle filaments arranged in perpendicular blocks around the opening of each capillary (Figure 10).   
 Fig. 10. a.  Cross-section of photophore from M. norvegica. (Kronstrom, 2009) The lantern (la) is composed of processes from light-producing cells (lc). Light is reflected against the inside of the organ wall (r reflector) and passes through a lens (le) before leaving the photophore.  b.  Representation of a capillary emptying into the lantern (la). The sphincter cells (sc) that act as cuffs lay at the ends of the capillaries and contains filamentous material (hatched area).  Luciferin and luciferase enzymatic reaction  Inside the light-producing cells of the lantern, a chemical reaction occurs to produce bioluminescence. The enzyme luciferase catalyzes the oxidation of the substrate luciferin in the presence of oxygen, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) (Xia, 2021), and either magnesium or calcium ions. In the oxidation process, luciferin loses some of its electrons to oxygen as it is a strong oxidative agent that is very electronegative. Within the luciferin molecule, electrons are forced to rearrange at higher energy levels, but not all of them are lost to oxygen. Instead, some of the electrons jump to higher orbitals (energy states) but then return to their lower initial energy state. The difference in energy between the two energy states is released as light. Thus, the luciferin-luciferase reaction releases the molecule oxyluciferin in an excited state in addition to other products like carbon dioxide and pyrophosphate. Light in the wavelength region of 530 to 640 nm is emitted when the excited luciferin relaxes to its normal state. It is important to note that the luciferin utilized by krill is structurally similar to the luciferin found in dinoflagellates (Tsarkova, 2021), one of the many types of phytoplankton that krill feed on. This suggests a dietary dependence on dinoflagellates; krill obtain the luciferin and luciferase they need for bioluminescence from the dinoflagellates that they eat.  Counter illumination  Animals that live in the mesopelagic region, the region of the ocean that extends from 200 meters to 1000 meters below the surface, like krill, spend the daylight hours at depths where the light-level is extremely low,   and less. However, even under those low-level light conditions they are not completely hidden by the darkness of their environment. Deep-sea fish have functional  vision  at light-levels as low as   (Clarke, 1963), which is far below the levels of light found in the environment of the deep scattering layers. Other predators associated with these low-level light layers likely have functional vision too. Under the down coming light, krill, when seen from below, would appear as a dark spot to predators. This detection from below would be the optimal situation for predators as they could catch the krill off guard and eat a large amount of them at once.   However, krill adapted and developed the ability to minimize the silhouette effect by matching the light produced by photophores on their ventral surface to the down-coming solar light as shown in Figure 11 (Warner, 1979). This process, known as counter-illumination, was proven by an investigation into the spectral composition of the  luminescence  in two species of krill (Clarke, 1963). The investigation concluded primary peaks of krill luminesce in the 470 to 480 nm range, which is very close to the 478 nm peak of blue light in the mesopelagic region, demonstrating that the purpose of the photophores is to produce light that is the same colour as the down-coming solar light.  
 Fig. 11.  Demonstration of photophores eliminating body silhouette  ( Fregin, 2002)  The mechanism that controls bioluminescence in krill is not completely understood, though some believe that regulating the supply of hemolymph to the light-producing cells may be part of it. Relaxation of filamentous cuffs that encircle the base of the capillaries leads to an increased supply of the hemolymph, and thus oxygen, to the lantern, which may be sufficient to stimulate light production. Serotonin or 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) is suspected to be the substance that relaxes or triggers another substance to relax the cuff structures. 5-HT is a monoamine that functions both as a neurotransmitter and a hormone and is synthesized from L-tryptophan by the enzymes tryptophan hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase. For krill, serotonin functions more as a neurotransmitter as it is likely carrying a chemical signal to the filamentous cuff that initiates its relaxation. Just as light exposure triggers release of serotonin in humans, the increase in light exposure that krill experience in the daytime may also trigger the release of serotonin and allow for continuous bioluminescence to be produced. As a result, krill are able to camouflage themselves from predators during the day through counter-illumination.  Conclusion In conclusion, there are many chemical characteristics of shrimp and krill that allow them to overcome various challenges and thrive in their respective environments. We first discussed how crustacea’s need for a flexible, yet tough exterior, is solved by the chitinous exoskeleton, which minimizes dehydration while providing vital structural support. Next, we demonstrated how the oxidative stress caused by UV rays is addressed by the brilliant antioxidant astaxanthin, a molecule that protects shrimp and krill through the quenching of singlet oxygen and the mitigation of free radicals. The freezing conditions of the Antarctic also present a challenge to krill; however, PUFAs cleverly allow krill to maintain cell membrane integrity, growth, and reproduction. Lastly, the essential need of krill to evade predators during the day was addressed by the ability to produce bioluminescence and counter illuminate their silhouette. Collectively, these chemistry-based design solutions enable shrimp and krill to succeed in diverse marine environments.

title: Hydrozoans and Bryozoans: Chemical Engineers of the Sea
authors: Aizaz Ahsan Wahla, Ocean Burland, Dante Daniel Garcia Perez & Jessica Michalski
abstract: Hydrozoans and bryozoans are two diverse colonial clades with a rich evolutionary history dating back millions of years. Over time, hydrozoans and bryozoans have come to play crucial structuring roles in the aquatic environments they inhabit. Furthermore, they have developed numerous adaptations, on a zooidal and colonial level, which have allowed these fascinating aquatic organisms to thrive. From bioluminescence and venom in hydrozoans to biomineralization in bryozoans, as well as cell plasticity in both groups, many of the evolutionary traits found in hydrozoans and bryozoans involve chemistry principles. In hydrozoans, bioluminescence serves as a communication tool with other organisms, warding off potential predators or luring prey. Moreover, venom released from specialized stinging cells in hydrozoans acts as additional methods of prey acquisition and chemical defense. In bryozoans, biomineralization is a multifaceted bioindicator, providing insight into the conditions bryozoans live in and their response to the changing climate. In fact, both hydrozoans and bryozoans exhibit cellular and phenotypic plasticity, which may be a key aspect behind their survival up until this point in time and could provide invaluable insights into the effects of climate change on marine organisms. Ultimately, developing an understanding of the chemical processes underlying the adaptations of hydrozoans and bryozoans is essential to fully appreciate these incredible organisms.

Hydrozoans and Bryozoans: Chemical Engineers of the Sea  Aizaz Ahsan Wahla, Ocean Burland, Dante Daniel Garcia Perez & Jessica Michalski Abstract Hydrozoans and bryozoans are two diverse colonial clades with a rich evolutionary history dating back millions of years. Over time, hydrozoans and bryozoans have come to play crucial structuring roles in the aquatic environments they inhabit. Furthermore, they have developed numerous adaptations, on a zooidal and colonial level, which have allowed these fascinating aquatic organisms to thrive. From  bioluminescence  and venom in hydrozoans to biomineralization in bryozoans, as well as cell plasticity in both groups, many of the evolutionary traits found in hydrozoans and bryozoans involve chemistry principles. In hydrozoans, bioluminescence serves as a communication tool with other organisms, warding off potential predators or luring prey. Moreover, venom released from specialized stinging cells in hydrozoans acts as additional methods of prey acquisition and chemical defense. In bryozoans, biomineralization is a multifaceted bioindicator, providing insight into the conditions bryozoans live in and their response to the changing climate. In fact, both hydrozoans and bryozoans exhibit cellular and phenotypic plasticity, which may be a key aspect behind their survival up until this point in time and could provide invaluable insights into the effects of climate change on marine organisms. Ultimately, developing an understanding of the chemical processes underlying the adaptations of hydrozoans and bryozoans is essential to fully appreciate these incredible organisms.  Introduction Bryozoans and hydrozoans have much to contribute to our understanding of biological complexity, cell biology, species development, and evolutionary processes. Indeed, scientists have extensively investigated their role within the marine ecosystem, from their respective colony-level distribution and organization to their diets and much more. For instance, bryozoan complexity lies in their structures which are composed of individual modules called zooids, where a colony can have one or many types of zooids that differ both functionally and structurally. Among the feeding zooids (autozooids), they feed on phytoplankton, diatoms, and  bacteria  using lophophore filter feeding, and commonly inhabit kelp forests and rocky shores. At the colony level, hydrozoans in benthic and pelagic environments remain interconnected through continuous epithelia and a shared gastrovascular cavity. Their polyps feed on zooplankton and phytoplankton via tentacle trapping or by capturing fish, eggs, and pellets through filter suspension (Nawrocki & Cartwright, 2012). However, rapid technological advancements now feasible at more modest costs have allowed scientists to uncover the micro-evolutionary and chemical processes that occur from within the bodies that make up this phylum and class, discovering how many species have engineered themselves on a chemical level to allow for higher-level organization and complexity in marine ecosystems.   Bryozoans  Bryozoans make use of a process called biomineralization, a mechanism by which organisms produce skeletal structures from minerals (Clark, 2020). Biomineralization has a rich evolutionary history within the bryozoan phylum, having evolved in the two calcified clades,  Cheilostomata  ( Gymnolaemata ) and  Cyclostomata  ( Stenolaemata ), millions of years apart. Today, bryozoan biomineralization can provide valuable insight into the effects of climate change, and thus, is essential to understand from a chemical standpoint (Taylor et al., 2015).  Hydrozoans  Many hydrozoan species also exhibit bioluminescence, producing light as a lure for their prey or as  camouflage  from predators lurking below. Different flashing patterns and colors are used in hydrozoan species to communicate signals for attracting mates or confusing enemies. Though there is still much to uncover about the ecological role of bioluminescence, the process itself can be understood at the chemical level following the production and use of green fluorescent proteins (GFP) in fluorescence (Singer et al., 1963). Toxicity in hydrozoans through specialized and unique methods of venom production, maintenance and deployment in nematocytes are extremely crucial to their predation and defensive techniques.   Hydrozoans and Bryozoans  In conjunction, hydrozoans and bryozoans shed light on many mechanisms allowing them to have phenotypical plasticity. Phenotypic plasticity is their “engineering” ability to produce different phenotypes in response to their  environment . They do this through their highly flexible stem cells, and in the case of hydrozoans, make use of this trait in their ability to regenerate despite their harsh surrounding environments. Indeed, we can observe these via rapid technological advances such as genome sequencing, large-scale gene expression/transcriptomics studies, as well as tracking using transgenic lines carrying diverse fluorescent reporters which we will further discuss within the paper.   Biomineralization in  Bryozoa   As biomineralizers, bryozoans occupy a crucial niche in the marine ecosystem. Not only do their intricate skeletal structures promote biodiversity, but the integration of CaCO 3  into their skeletons helps sequester atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) entering the ocean (Clark, 2020; Lombardi et al., 2020). In recent years, biomineralization processes and the responses of calcifying organisms to climate change have become increasingly active areas of research, as they can provide insight into the mechanism and effects of climate change. Despite their importance, the calcification mechanisms of bryozoans have historically been less intensely studied than other biomineralizers (Taylor et al., 2015). This section will explore the role of bryozoans in the ocean’s chemical equilibrium, their skeletal structure, their mechanism of calcification, and their responses to environmental change.  Carbonate chemistry in the ocean  The ocean has absorbed approximately 24% of anthropogenic CO 2  emissions since the Industrial Revolution, which is sequestered in deep-sea sediments or as the calcified skeletons of marine organisms (Middelburg et al., 2020). Structurally, walls are classified as interior, exterior, or compound walls, which are a variant of exterior walls.  The interior walls are internal partitions that divide the body cavity and can be shared between adjacent zooids. These walls have secretory epithelia on both sides and lack a cuticular layer. In contrast, exterior walls grow from a secretory epithelium along their outer edges from one side, with the skeletal layer sandwiched between the secretory epithelium and the cuticle. Compound walls are formed by two back-to-back exterior walls, with the cuticles facing each other at the centre of the wall (Taylor et al., 2015).

Cheilostomate bryozoans form aragonitic or bimineralic skeletons, while stenolaemates form uniquely calcitic skeletons. In the case of bimineralic cheilostomes, calcite is always deposited first, with the aragonitic layer acting as a ‘frosting’ on top of the calcite. Further, magnesium (Mg) can be substituted for calcium in calcite, as in other biomineralizing phyla. Interestingly, the amount of Mg substitution can vary not only between species and colonies, but also within the skeletal elements of a single zooid. The calcite found in bryozoans can be classified as low Mg-calcite (0-4 mol%), intermediate Mg-calcite (4-12 mol%), and high Mg-calcite (>12 mol%). While low to intermediate Mg-calcite is the most common among bryozoans, the cheilostome  Membraniporopsis tubigera  has ~14 mol% MgCO 3 . The proportion of magnesium present in calcite affects the solubility of the skeleton, which increases as the Mg/Ca ratio increases. Further, high Mg-calcite is typically more prevalent in bryozoans living in warmer water, the implications of which will be further discussed (Figuerola et al., 2023; Taylor et al., 2015).   The organic component of bryozoan skeletons is the cuticle, or the periostracum, which is typically less than 5µm thick and is generally persistent throughout the life of healthy zooids. The cuticle originates from undifferentiated epithelial or palisade cells at the growing edge of the colony (Figure 2). There are three types of cells associated with the growth of the cuticle, beyond the palisade cells, although this section will focus on only the cuboidal epithelial cells and vesicular cells. The former cells, which arise from the differentiation of palisade cells, are found on the proximal side of the terminal cap (right side of Figure 2). These cells are also responsible for the secretion of the mineral component of the skeleton. Vesicular cells are found adjacent to the palisade cells in the medial zone, which are rich in vesicles containing secretion droplets (Taylor et al., 2015).

(Taylor et al., 2015).  Mechanism of calcification in bryozoans  Although little is known about the biomineralization process specific to bryozoans, hypotheses can be formed in comparison with better studied calcifying organisms, such as corals (Taylor et al., 2015). The conditions required for the formation of crystals are well understood and assumed to be required in biomineralization. For crystallization to occur, a supersaturated solution is required (Ω > 1.0), as well as nucleation, or the formation of the initial crystals that triggers crystal growth (Myerson & Ginde, 2002). To better understand the potential mechanisms of calcification in bryozoans, the site of mineralization must be considered first, which is the cuticle. As new epithelium is generated, the palisade bell cap moves in the distal direction (Figure 2), which is adjusted to the growth of the cuticle. The oldest part of the cuticle is left as a cover for newly generated cells. Meanwhile, the new epithelium initially exudes cuticle, followed by an irregularly developed electron-dense sheet, which is suggested as a seeding surface for the first crystallites of the mineralized skeleton (Figure 3). Therefore, the cuticle, an organic matrix, acts as a nucleating template, which aligns with biomineralization processes occurring within the cell as in other taxa. In this case, the biominerals either leave the cell as individual units or as preassembled structures. In bryozoans, the biominerals would likely be transported through the epithelium via vesicles located in the vesicular cells discussed above, before being released into the extracellular environment. Once released, the biominerals interact with an  extracellular matrix (ECM)  to form an ordered, crystalline structure. Alternatively, biomineralization may occur outside of the cell, wherein calcium ions are stored temporarily in vesicles, released into intercellular spaces, and gradually infiltrated into the cuticle. This process would be consistent with a later crystal growth, due to the continuous transfer of calcium ions (Taylor et al., 2015).

Evidently, the addition of CO 2  to seawater impacts the chemical equilibria governing the carbonate chemistry of the ocean; higher concentrations of CO 2  drive the formation of carbonic acid, which increases bicarbonate and hydrogen ion concentrations. The latter decreases the pH and carbonate ion concentration in the water. A direct consequence of this shift in equilibria is the decrease in calcium carbonate saturation state. As previously discussed, when Ω < 1.0, calcium carbonate will begin to dissolve (Doney et al., 2009). Moreover, the accumulation of CO 2  has caused an increase in seawater temperature of 0.76℃ (Taylor et al., 2015). Not only are more soluble forms of CaCO 3 , such as high Mg-calcite, are more prevalent in warmer waters, but rising global temperatures may prompt low and intermediate Mg-calcite bryozoans to switch to high Mg-calcite skeletons (Figuerola et al., 2023; Swezey, Bean, Ninokawa, et al., 2017). As such, calcifying marine organisms, including bryozoans, are particularly vulnerable to OA and rising temperatures caused by climate change.  The response and vulnerability of bryozoans to ocean acidification and rising temperature is multi-faceted, and the effects of climate change are often interactive. A study by Swezey and colleagues (Swezey, Bean, Ninokawa, et al., 2017), examined the interactive effects temperature, dissolved CO 2  concentrations, and food availability on the growth and mineralogy of  Jellyella tuberculata  ( Cheilostomata ), an encrusting bryozoan found in most temperate and tropical seas that weakly regulates skeletal Mg content. Contrary to expectations, growth efficiencies were maintained across all treatments, at the cost of zooid longevity. Although the saturation state of aragonite (Ω arag ), which was used as an estimation for the saturation state of high Mg-calcite, was approximately the same across high CO 2  treatments, 0.997 and 1.082 for low and high temperatures, respectively, there was notable dissolution at the higher temperature. Thus, it is likely that an increase in the skeletal Mg content of zooids grown in higher temperature conditions was a dominant cause of dissolution. Overall, these results suggest that  J. tuberculata  reallocates limited energy resources from maintenance and repair functions towards the generation of new zooids under strenuous conditions (Swezey, Bean, Ninokawa, et al., 2017).  Despite the increased vulnerability of some bryozoans, such as  J. tuberculata , to climate change, the colonial structure of bryozoans may allow them to better respond to changing conditions, due to organizational modularity and successive asexual generations found within the same colony. In another study by Swezey and colleagues (Swezey, Bean, Hill, et al., 2017), the role of phenotypic plasticity in shielding  Celleporella cornuta  ( Cheilostomata ) against the negative impacts of rising temperatures and ocean acidification caused by climate change was analyzed. Sample colonies were examined under high and low CO 2  concentrations, which serve to approximate ocean acidification. Several plastic responses were identified in  C. cornuta , including reproductive investment, changes in zooid morphology, and shifts in zooid calcification. In response to higher concentrations of CO 2 , the growth of  C. cornuta  populations increased, in contrast to predictions, with the new colonial growth being characterized by a higher investment in the production of autozooids (feeding zooids) in comparison to reproductive zooids. This response is suggested as a strategy to increase caloric intake to compensate for the increased energetic stress caused by low pH conditions. While increasing caloric intake may partially offset reductions in growth and calcification during short term occurrences of low pH, it may not convey a significant advantage during prolonged exposure to higher CO 2  conditions. Similarly, a decrease in carbonate mass, which is associated with a lower energy investment in calcification, was observed in the populations studied, as  C. cornuta  is composed of low Mg-calcite, the solubility of which should not be affected by increased CO 2  concentrations. Finally, the new zooids formed in populations under high CO 2  concentrations demonstrated an increased occurrence of organic coverings, which may serve to protect the calcium carbonate from dissolution in response to changing equilibria. This shift in morphology suggests that younger zooids have morphological flexibility, allowing the formation of new organic coverings, which is not possible in zooids of a certain age. Alternatively, more significant organic coverings found in younger zooids may reflect an energetic trade-off, wherein resources are diverted from older zooids to younger members of the colony (Swezey, Bean, Hill, et al., 2017).  In spite of the relative lack of knowledge on the specific mechanism of biomineralization of bryozoans, the study of these colonial organisms can provide a wealth of information on the effects of climate change on marine calcifiers as well as possible ways to combat these changes. The adaptations of bryozoans in response to changing seawater chemistry include the reallocation of energy towards the production of new zooids, the thickening of the organic cuticular layer to protect the skeleton from dissolution, and changes in calcification, through the variable energy investments into calcification mechanisms and differing mineralogies. As bryozoans adapt to changes in their environment, they can serve as important bioindicators, which provide insight into the effects of changing conditions on other organisms as well. Thus, bryozoans can be invaluable to future climate-based research and should not be ignored as crucial members of marine ecosystems.  Bioluminescence in Hydrozoans  Bioluminescence is the emission of light by organisms via chemical reactions. It has been observed in several marine as well as a few terrestrial species across many unrelated phyla, such as certain cephalopods and cnidarians. In the ocean, light is involved in many kinds of interactions, such as predation and parasitism, as well as intraspecific functions like communication and mating. More precisely, it is mostly observed among species living in the deep sea rather than benthic or shallow environments (Haddock et al., 2010).   Since bioluminescence is a form of chemiluminescence that occurs via biochemical reactions, it can be modelled with the following generic equation, which can be applied to all bioluminescent processes:   (7)      where luciferin, a light-emitting molecule, is oxidized by the enzyme luciferase and the rate of the reaction is controlled by luciferase as well. The energy released by the oxidation of luciferin is absorbed by its electrons, which after being brought to higher energetic levels, release the acquired energy in the form of light emissions (Gonzalez Jr, 2007; Haddock et al., 2010; Morse, 2013).  Since bioluminescence evolved independently across many unrelated taxa, it must be important as well as relatively easy to evolve. The ease with which it can be developed can be attributed to the availability of light-emitting luciferins in luminous and nonluminous prey. If present, predators of luciferin-bearing prey need only to evolve the proper luciferase enzyme to catalyze their oxidation (Shimomura, 1987).   Of the hydrozoans, bioluminescence is observed in both hydromedusae (Figure 5) and siphonophores (Figure 6). Although light emission can serve as a form of communication in some marine species, such as squid, it is unlikely that hydrozoans use bioluminescence for this purpose, as they are not known to possess light-sensing organs (Haddock et al., 2005). Rather, luminescence in these marine creatures is thought to have mostly evolved for defense and warning purposes. Almost all siphonophores are luminescent except for one or two genera, and some of them use it to attract prey to their stinging tentacles or couple it with fluorescence (Figure 4) (Haddock et al., 2010; Morse, 2013).

Because of its relative stability, a photoprotein can be isolated in complex (Figure 9) (Morse, 2013). The binding of Ca 2+  ions to the photoprotein at the C-terminus causes a conformational change, which triggers the oxidation of coelenterazine via a nucleophilic attack, a reaction in which an electron-rich group replaces another leaving group at an atom (Fourrage et al., 2014; Head et al., 2000). This allows hydrozoans to control their emission of light without having to compartmentalize the reactants or allosterically inhibiting the luciferase enzyme, as opposed to other bioluminescent organisms like fireflies. The photoprotein can after be regenerated by binding to any available coelenterazine (Haddock et al., 2010; Morse, 2013).

Deep-sea fish and shrimp are sensitive to light ranging between 470nm and 490nm, which corresponds to the 470nm wavelength peak emitted by photoproteins like aequorin in  A. victoria . Generally, it is thought that light emissions cause predators to hesitate by startling them (Haddock & Case, 1999; Haddock et al., 2010).  Siphonophores notably employ bioluminescence to create smoke screens, clouds of glowing particles or fluid that misdirect predators by making it difficult to locate the prey. Using the same effect of distracting predators, they may also detach from photophores, light-emitting organs. After escaping a predator, these may be regenerated in most hydrozoans. This ensures the survival of the colony despite losing a few individuals (Haddock et al., 2010).   Similarly, they may also employ photophores as sacrificial tags: if the photophore can still glow for hours after being ingested, light will be emitted from within the predator’s stomach, thus increasing the likelihood of being spotted and eaten in the deep sea where transparency is a common trait. In fact, it is thought that many predators evolved red or black stomachs that absorb blue light to avoid this precise issue. Thus, sacrificial tags allow a colony to escape a predator suffering from having ingested the photophore (Haddock et al., 2010). Some siphonophores of the genus  Erenna  use bioluminescence with red fluorescent proteins as lures to attract prey. Their heavily modified tentacles equipped with stinging cells are flicked to mimic the movement of small, crustacean prey (Figure 10). This suggests that some  Erenna  siphonophores prey on larger fish that are sensitive to longer wavelengths, an uncommon feature in the deep sea where blue light is typically employed (Haddock & Case, 1999).

(Banagouro et al., 2022)

 Fig. 17  Measurement of mouse paw edema (%) before and after the injection of  Macrorhynchia philippina  venom showing significant edema peaks at 5-10 minutes and 30 minutes post-injection (p < 0:05)  The venom of  M. philippin a lacks protein toxins, and the toxic effects are due to low molecular mass compounds. This data explains the lack of cytotoxic/hemolytic activity by  M. philippina , which contrasts with other similar cnidarians. In conclusion, the  M. philippina  venom contains peptides and several low molecular mass compounds that can trigger fast inflammatory and nociceptive reactions typical of envenomation and antimicrobial activity, which are essential for animal defense (Banagouro et al., 2022).  Hydrozoan Stem Cell Plasticity  One of the major traits recognized in hydrozoans is their extensive phenotypic plasticity and regenerative capabilities (Galliot et al., 2006). Indeed, many biologists are familiar with  Hydra ; an experimentally tractable, model-like hydrozoan species that can suitably display developmental plasticity and regeneration among multicellular organisms. At the microscopic anatomical level, the  Hydra  polyp cells differentiate from three stem cell populations found along their body column (Bosch, 2009); (Martin & Archer, 1997). Of these stem cell lineages, there are the multipotent and fast cycling interstitial cells which provide progenitors for proliferating nematoblasts to differentiate into migratory nematocytes, as well as precursors for the creation of neurons, gland cells and germ line cells that differentiate into sperm and eggs (Martin & Archer, 1997). In addition to the i-cells, they also have slower paced epithelial stem cells, either ectodermal to make up the outer layer of the polyp or endodermal to line up the gastric system (see Figure 18). After many investigations through controlled  Hydra  feeding, amputation and dissociation, we can better understand the roles of these different cell types and conclude that epithelial cells drive morphogenetic events whereas interstitial cells tune them (Galliot et al., 2006).  
 Fig. 18  A scheme depicting the three cell compartments in hydra: myoepithelial endodermal, interstitial and myoepithelial ectodermal. Each compartment shows the different differentiation pathways that the stem cells take, along with the appropriate genes and proteins expressed of each differentiation. Gene expression in somatic cell lineages without any known regulation during differentiation or regeneration are not indicated (Galliot et al., 2006).  For instance, upon amputation of a Hydra hypostome (the oral tip of the  Hydra  head), there is almost immediate upregulation of endodermal digestive cells that differentiate into blastema-like cells to regain organization. Post bisection, there is intense cell proliferation after 24 hours, and tentacle buds will reform after 40 hours post-bisection. Moreover, through  Kazall  gene silencing (a gene which codes for a serine-protease inhibitor expressed in gland cells of digestive function) biologists discovered that it would induce massive animal death, suggesting that endothelial cells are necessary in self-preservation. Upon recombination of epithelial and interstitial cells, as well as experimental disconnect of neurogenesis in  Hydra  leading to the lack on interstitial lineage derivatives, nerve-free  Hydra  still bud and regenerate, confirming that the former stem cells play a minimal role in morphogenetics (see Figure 19) (Galliot et al., 2006).  
 Fig. 19  Successive cellular and molecular phases displayed by head-regenerating tip. The ectodermal cells are displayed with light-blue nuclei. Endodermal cells are digestive cells at the time of bisection displayed with red nuclei and transform into blastema-like cells displayed as dark cells with blue nuclei. Tentacle buds will appear after 40 hours post-bisection along with the beginning of the hypostome formation. For each phase, the genes and proteins upregulated during head-regeneration are  displayed for every cell lineage (Galliot et al., 2006).  Interestingly, cells of the three lineages cannot transform from one lineage into the other, and this may be attributable to specific gene expression like PcG family or PRC2 components in the different lineages which prevents and regulates the transitions into the different somatic cell types (Bosch, 2009).  Role of Interstitial Stem Cells Hydrozoan Planulae Growth  As previously mentioned, i-cells play a major role in the proliferation and the creation of hydrozoan neural plexus, contributing neurites from dark and light ganglionic cells. Light ganglionic cells have electron-lucent cytoplasm and fewer mitochondria whereas dark ganglionic cells have electron-dense cytoplasm and numerous mitochondria. In the larva stage, “neural” interstitial cells will begin to differentiate once they have fully migrated from the endoderm to the ectoderm through the mesoglea to form light ganglionic cells around 8 hours post fertilization and will begin to fully differentiate in the ectoderm after 24 hours. At 48-96 hours post fertilization, dark ganglionic cells are distributed in the head and anterior mid-sides of the planula. Furthermore, both ganglionic cells contributing to the neural plexus and exhibit combined morphological features of interneurons and neurosecretory cells, suggesting that neuron cells are also primitive “stem” cell from which multifunctional nerves can be derived and specialized (Martin, 1988).     Effect of Phenotypical Plasticity on the Hydrozoan Life Cycle Complexity  The typical life cycle of hydrozoans is comprised of a motile larva, sessile polyp and pelagic sexual medusae stage generated by polyp budding. However, due to the remarkable plasticity of hydrozoans, some will lose their medusae or polyp stages, and can include sexual and/or asexual reproduction. Moreover, connected polyps may specialize in different functions—such as budding, feeding, reproduction, defense, and  swimming —and colonies of the same species can fuse or reject one another through allorecognition complexes composed of Alr1 and Alr2 proteins. Thus evolutionary selection in this context may act at the level of stem cells (Leclère et al., 2016).  Plasticity Within Bryozoan Ecophenotypic Variability  In terms of the differentiation of functional zones in colonies, there exists three major zones known as the “edge zone” for growth of young zooids using polypides, the “middle zone” containing active feeding zooids and polypides, and the “basal zone” with degenerating(ed) polypides. Through protein analysis based on the different zones, we can better understand functional differentiation.  That is, that a majority of zone-specific proteins in the colonies of studied species were confined to the distal and proximal regions. There are little to no characteristic proteins in the middle regions (Figure 20).  Yet, specificity of proteins within the zone of astogenetic repetition was determined by either a proximal-distal gradient, or a distal-proximal gradient, with zone specific proteins. This may be an engineered design resulting from morphological changes of zooid in the course of ontogenesis. (Kutyumov et al., 2016)  
 Fig. 20  Distribution of zone-specific proteins across categories in  F. hispida  (a),  membranaceotruncata  (b) and  S. securrifrons  (c). Overlapping areas correspond to proteins characteristic of multiple locations. (Kutyumov et al., 2016)  Differential Gene Expression Hydrozoan Zooids  Morphological differences between specialized zooids forming a polyp colony have been said to be due to axial patterning during development. However, recent studies suggest that polymorphic polyps are the result of differentially expressed functional, structural, and patterning genes (Sanders et al., 2014). We can take the case of the  Hydractinia symbiolongicarpus  to analyze the difference in gene expression of different zooids. Indeed, this polyp colony is comprised of dactylozooids which are used for defense and chemosensory, gastrozooids which are a feeding polyp, and gonozooids which are reproductive polyps.(Mills et al., 2007) Upon differential analysis of their respective contigs, they found that dactylozooids and gastrozooids share the fewest number of DE transcripts, and that gonozooids have the largest number of polyp-specific transcripts. In terms of homeobox genes, that is, the genes that recognize specific DNA and regulate target genes, toxin and myosin transcripts, they were found to be differentially expressed in each polyp type. Finally, through  in situ  hybridization (a laboratory technique used to localize a sequence of DNA or RNA in a biological sample), polyp specific DE transcripts were analyzed depending on the polyp type (see table 3) (Sanders et al., 2014). This shows that the differences in gene expression between these zooids allows for specialization within a colony for efficient survivability.  Table 3  Polyp-specific DE transcripts analyzed with whole mount  in situ  hybridization (Sanders et al., 2014) 
 Differential Gene Expression Between Polymorphic Bryozoan Zooids  Like hydrozoan polyps, bryozoan species also exhibit differential gene expression between different zooid colonies. Indeed, the division of labor allows for an increase in biological efficiency in these multicellular organisms as they remain connected and share resources within the colonies. All bryozoan colonies are comprised of autozooids, the feeding and reproductive zooids, as well as non-feeding zooids for other functions known as heterozooids (Edu, 2024). Upon comparing autozooid, avicularium tissues and rhizoids (two types of non-feeding zooid) at different life stages, it was found that there was a significant difference in gene expression. Significant meaning, of 1597 genes differentially expressed in a reference transcriptome, an analysis by pairwise comparison showed the greatest differential expression occurs in autozooid and aviculrium contrasts and comparison between rhizoid networks and autozooids (see Figure 21). Moreover, the highest differential expression was found when comparing the zooid types rather than zooids in their respective life stages. (Treibergs & Giribet, 2020)  
 Fig. 21  Pairwise comparison of 1597 genes of a reference transcriptome. Y-axis shows the numbers of significantly upregulated genes for representatives of each pairwise. Up-regulated genes in the first representative of the contrast are shown in blue and up-regulated genes in the second representative of the contrast are shown in the graph as green on the x-axis. Sample abbreviations are as follows: ‘AutoBud’ = autozooid bud, ‘AutoMat’ = mature autozooid, ‘AvicBud’ = avicularium bud, ‘AvicMat’ = mature avicularium, ‘RhizAuto’ = rhizoid autozooid, and ‘RhizStol’ = rhizoid network. (Treibergs & Giribet, 2020)  Gene Expression Through the  Bugula Neritina  Bryozoa   Bryozoan life cycles make it unclear whether tissue cells are pre-determined according to their adult fate, or whether the cells are undifferentiated and pluripotent stem cells. This proposed hypothesis was rooted from the idea that the bilaterian adult stage evolved through cells distinct from the larval cells, known as “homologous set-aside cells”. Upon further investigation through the gene expression of 13 developmental genes in the larval stage of Bugula neritina, it was found that 11 of those genes were expressed in discreet and reproducible regions in the tissues that form during larval metamorphosis, suggesting blastemas are not pluripotent, set-aside cells are pre-patterned according to their future fate. For example, one of the most important genes is that of BnTropomyosin, which is expressed in the larvae stage of  Bugula neritina  at the upper edge of the apical disc, as well as the ciliated cleft and around the glandular area of the pyriform organ (meaning way before adulthood is reached) (Fuchs et al., 2011).  Conclusion  From a chemistry-focused perspective, this paper explored the solutions developed by hydrozoans and bryozoans to the unique challenges posed by their environments. Bryozoans need to somehow shelter their zooids throughout the life of a colony using any available, dissolved materials. To solve this issue, they evolved biomineralized exoskeletons made of calcium carbonate whose relevant formation and dissolution reactions, structure, growth and chemical responses to the effects of climate change are discussed. The discussion then dives into the dark, deep sea to answer how vulnerable hydrozoans, particularly siphonophores and hydromedusae, avoid or protect themselves and their offspring against predators. Their solution consists in leveraging the light-emitting oxidation of coelenterazine to ward off predators and, in some cases, to attract prey. In addition, Hydrozoans are even more vulnerable because of their relatively limited mobility, making the capture of prey very difficult. Their evolution led to the development of powerful formulations of venom that allow them to immobilize prey. Finally, this paper brings the reader to consider the problem of zooid differentiation of bryozoans and hydrozoans and how a colony organizes itself. The answer to this rests on molecular signals and transcriptomics of different zooids that govern their specialization throughout colonial superorganisms.   In conclusion, the research presented here aspires to give readers a sense of the intricate, astonishingly precise solutions developed by both groups, leveraging chemistry to produce light, build structures, synthesize weapons and coordinate a whole colony.
