title: Survival Through Synthesis: The Chemical Tactics of Fungi
authors: Edison Luke, Felix Gamper, Lea Bleibel, Vasily Ignatov
abstract: This paper investigates the survival strategies of fungi through their chemical tactics and metabolic processes. We explore how fungi utilize complex biochemical pathways, such as glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway, to generate energy and synthesize vital compounds, including antibiotics like penicillin, which are crucial for their defense mechanisms and survival. The role of enzymes in fungal metabolism will be examined, highlighting their contributions to degrading environmental pollutants, facilitating nutrient absorption, and their role in fungi’s survival. Additionally, we discuss the ecological significance of compounds like psilocybin and psilocin, including their potential therapeutic applications and interactions within ecosystems. By understanding these chemical tactics, we reveal how fungi adapt to environmental stresses and contribute to ecological balance, emphasizing their crucial role in both natural and engineered ecosystems.
content:
Survival Through Synthesis: The Chemical Tactics of Fungi  Edison Luke, Felix Gamper, Lea Bleibel, Vasily Ignatov Abstract This paper investigates the survival strategies of fungi through their chemical tactics and metabolic processes. We explore how fungi utilize complex biochemical pathways, such as glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway, to generate energy and synthesize vital compounds, including antibiotics like penicillin, which are crucial for their defense mechanisms and survival. The role of enzymes in fungal metabolism will be examined, highlighting their contributions to degrading environmental pollutants, facilitating nutrient  absorption , and their role in fungi’s survival. Additionally, we discuss the ecological significance of compounds like psilocybin and psilocin, including their potential therapeutic applications and interactions within ecosystems. By understanding these chemical tactics, we reveal how fungi adapt to environmental stresses and contribute to ecological balance, emphasizing their crucial role in both natural and engineered ecosystems.  Introduction Fungi are nature’s recyclers, breaking down organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the soil, a process that supports plant life and, consequently, all terrestrial food chains. Beyond their ecological contributions though, fungi are constantly fighting for survival, needing to survive harsh environments and outcompete other organisms. Fungi possess an arsenal of chemical defenses, ranging from metabolic byproducts and adaptive enzymes to lethal compounds. With the use of these chemical tools, fungi overcome the many challenges that seek to remove it from their ecosystems.  Fungi exhibit remarkable metabolic versatility, allowing them to thrive in diverse environments. For instance, the yeast  Saccharomyces cerevisiae , commonly used in baking and brewing, has been harnessed for centuries to produce bread, beer, and wine. However, fungal metabolism is more than just a means to produce food; rather, it is the source of various survival strategies. Metabolism defines how fungi can survive in aerobic or anaerobic environments. It is the production pathway for alcohols, antibiotics, which can be used to eliminate competition, and is the source of hallucinogens, which can be used as a defense strategy.   Fungi’s ability to synthesize a wide array of bioactive compounds makes them sophisticated chemical tacticians. Using their chemical synthesis abilities, fungi can produce potent antibiotics like penicillin, as well as psychoactive compounds such as psilocybin and psilocin, found in certain mushroom species. Additionally, fungi can adapt to extreme environmental conditions through unique biochemical pathways, enabling them to degrade pollutants and absorb heavy metals, making them invaluable allies in bioremediation efforts. Overall, whether synthesizing bioactive compounds to outcompete rivals, adapting biochemically to harsh climates, or absorbing and breaking down pollutants, fungi exemplify a unique mastery over their chemical surroundings.  Metabolism Fungal metabolism occupies a central role in ecological and industrial processes, driving the degradation of organic pollutants and facilitating the absorption of heavy metals from the  environment . Fungi not only contribute to the biogeochemical cycles of carbon and nitrogen, but also play a vital role in the production of fermented beverages, biofuels, antibiotics, and sterols. In biotechnology, yeast species stand at the forefront of recombinant DNA technology, synthesizing human therapeutic  proteins  such as insulin.  
 
 Fig. 1  Fungal metabolism in ecosystem and industry: (top) fungal processes facilitate biogeochemical cycles (Behera & Das, 2023) and (bottom) diverse fungal metabolic enzymes offer many industrial uses (Hyde et al., 2019). As chemoorganotrophs, fungi rely on the oxidation of environmental nutrients to sustain their complex biosynthetic pathways, enabling them to thrive in diverse ecological niches (Kavanagh, 2005).  
 Fig. 2  Photograph showing the saprotrophic lifestyle of   several fungi.  Stereum fasciatum  (middle),  Trametes hirsuta  (right) and  Lenzites betulina  (left) are capable of decomposing cellulose and lignin into their glucose and phenolic subunits (Photographed by Felix Gamper).  The structure of the fungal cell wall is highly specialized; its porousness allows the absorption of molecules up to 300 daltons while selectively retaining larger molecules around 700 daltons (Kavanagh, 2005). This structural feature limits fungi’s absorption of basic macromolecular components, necessitating extracellular breakdown of these larger structures. To achieve this, fungi have evolved hydrolytic enzymes and active transport mechanisms, allowing them to extract essential nutrients such as monosaccharides (typically 180 daltons) and amino acids (up to 200 daltons). These mechanisms are integral to their survival and offer insights into their bioremediation and mycoremediation capacities.   Anabolic processes require energy input. Fungal biosynthesis relies on interconnected pathways as glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). Glycolysis is primarily catabolic in nature, after an energy investment phase it yields NADPH and ATP, at the cost of converting glucose to pyruvate. Further energy is extracted from the products of glycolysis in respiration and fermentation. PPP also produces NADPH during the oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate, the product of phosphorylation of glucose on the sixth carbon during the energy investment step. However, the pathway does not further break down the molecule, instead it produces ribose-5-phosphate, which can be used in nucleotide production. Side pathways produce different products. The Shikimate pathway produces aromatic precursors to aromatic amino acids such as tryptophan, but also to many other secondary metabolites. (Masi, Mach, & Mach-Aigner, 2021). Even the synthesis of vitamins and some antibiotics originates from these precursors (Roberts et al., 2002). Together, these two processes illustrate the balance within the organism’s metabolism. Depending on cellular needs, food can be directed towards energy production or the building of molecules.  
 Fig. 3  Glycolysis and Pentose Phosphate Pathways (Masi, Mach, & Mach-Aigner, 2021).  Tandem processes up- and down- regulated to meet the fungal cells’ energetic and synthetic needs.  While these tandem processes are performed by other organisms, they are extremely important to fungi who actively use their metabolism to change the environment around them. PPP is used in fungi to manage oxidative stress, support cell wall biosynthesis and to produce secondary metabolites (Masi, Mach, & Mach-Aigner, 2021).   While fungi have mitochondria, and many rely on respiration for the bulk of their energy, anaerobic pathways remain essential to fungi’s life cycles. Fermentation allows fungi to survive under various conditions—at different oxygen concentrations, with diverse carbon sources—and to produce important secondary metabolites.  Alcohol production is a key survival mechanism of  Saccharomyces cerevisiae . In low oxygen conditions, the Krebs cycle, left without a final electron acceptor, oxygen, cannot function. As a result, pyruvate produced in glycolysis is further metabolized into ethanol. Yet yeasts may also produce alcohol in environments with a surplus of oxygen as a mechanism evolved to prevent colonization of food sources by other organisms more sensitive to ethanol. Evolving self-harming traits to control competition is common in the microbiotic world, known as the Crabtree effect (Pfeiffer & Morley, 2014).   
 Fig. 4  The relationship between Glycolysis, Respiration and Fermentation. The Krebs (TCA) Cycle requires oxygen for oxidative phosphorylation, while Fermentation is anaerobic. Despite breaking down pyruvate, fermentation produces no further ATP, only NADH (Pfeiffer & Morley, 2014).   Enzymes   Fungi’s success is largely attributable to the complex synthesis they can perform from decomposing materials. This process is enabled by enzymes, which work by reducing the activation energy needed for a particular chemical reaction. Fungal enzyme function can be broadly characterized as lytic, oxidoreductive, transferring, isomerizing, and ligating.  Lytic enzymes are essential to the carbon catabolizing processes, cleaving bonds between macromolecule subunits. Next, oxidoreductases play a role in catabolizing and synthesis while addressing environmental dangers. Fungi are exposed to reactive oxygen species produced during respiration, radiation exposure, and by plant defense mechanisms. By managing peroxides, some fungi can even use these mechanisms to degrade complex substrates like lignin (Conesa, Punt & Hondel, 2002). Furthermore, fungi can reduce nitrate to nitrite and to ammonium, which they can then use for organic synthesis or exchange with other organisms. Similarly, fungi with nitrogenase enzymes can reduce elemental nitrogen to ammonium; in fact, around 80% of terrestrial plants associate with nitrogen-reducing mycorrhizal fungi, demonstrating how fungi’s unique chemical characteristics open up certain mutualistic niches (Di Martino et al., 2022). Finally, transferases, enzymes responsible for transferring functional groups, and isomerases, enzymes that ensure the particular chirality of synthesized molecules, enable the synthesis of specific molecules. In tandem with ligating enzymes, fungal synthesis can be very specific and complex. For example, antibiotics underline how specificity draws the line between organisms’ life and death; with even a small change in chemical structure enhancing or reducing the killing potency of the compound. Through enzymatic activity,  evolution  has refined fungal metabolism into a survival toolkit for species’ ecosystems.    Chemical Warfare on the Environment   A fascinating characteristic of fungi is their diverse range of enzymes and metabolites utilized to solve many environmentally imposed problems. Particularly, fungi has the ability to degrade compounds such as polyethylene, highlighting their potential in addressing plastic pollution. Fungi can also degrade pharmaceutically active compounds (PhACs), making them valuable for bioremediation efforts. Additionally, fungi play a crucial role in mitigating pesticide pollution through the production of specific enzymes that break down harmful pesticides, reducing their toxicity and environmental impact.   Heavy metal contamination is another significant environmental problem that fungi can help address through mechanisms like biosorption and bioaccumulation, absorbing and detoxifying heavy metals from polluted environments. This multifaceted capability of fungi offers sustainable solutions to some of the most pressing environmental issues, contributing to the restoration of soil and  water  quality and promoting healthier ecosystems.  Bioremediation    Bioremediation involves removing pharmaceutically active compounds (PhACs) from contaminated environments due to their harmful effects on ecosystems and human health (Amobonye et al., 2023). PhACs have a low octanol/water partition coefficient, making them highly mobile and resistant to biodegradation, particularly in wastewater (Samal et al., 2022). PhACs’ hydrophilic nature allows them to dissolve easily in water, facilitating their transport through aqueous environments without significant retention. Moreover, PhACs often contain stable chemical moieties, such as aromatic rings and halogenated groups (see  Fig. 5 ), which are resistant to microbial degradation. These structural features hinder the breakdown processes typically carried out by microbial communities in wastewater treatment systems, leading to the persistence of PhACs in the environment (Bangia et al., 2023).  
 Fig. 5  Chemical structure of Fluoxetine commonly known as Prozac and a PhAC (aromatic rings are circled in red and halogens, here fluorine, are highlighted in blue)  Fungal bioremediation is an emerging solution regarding PhAC contamination; based on the use of high recoverability and reusability fungi (Kuppan et al., 2024). In other words, these organisms must be able to thrive in diverse and extreme environments, relying not only on pollutants as a nutritional substrate, but also on other compounds or on trophic interactions with plants for sustenance. Fungi perfectly meet this criterion– in fact, our  physics  paper on the mechanisms of adaptation and Interaction of fungi with the Physical World directly addresses and explains how fungi interact with their surroundings. White rot fungi  White rot fungi, classified as Basidiomycetes, are known for their ability to degrade lignin using extracellular enzymes such as laccases and peroxidases. This special feature is what makes them useful for reducing pollutants like polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and synthetic dyes through bioremediation. Some notable species include  Pleurotus ostreatus, Phanerochaete chrysosporium, Trametes versicolor  ( fig. 6 (f) ),  Ganoderma lucidum  ( fig. 6 (d) ) and  Irpex lacteus  ( fig. 6 (e) ) (Mir-Tutusaus et al., 2018).  
 Fig. 6  White-rot fungi of species (a) Abortiporus biennis, (b) Ceriporiopsis subvermispora, (c) Coriolopsis trogii, (d) Ganoderma applanatum, (e) Irpex lacteus and (f) Trametes versicolor. (Ginns, 2017).  White rot fungi secrete the enzymes laccase, lignin peroxidase, manganese peroxidase (MnP)  and versatile peroxidase. These enzymes are classified as lignin modifying enzymes (LME) ( Fig. 7 ). Lignin peroxidase (LiP) oxidizes di-methoxylated aromatic compounds to radical cations, often leading to lignin polymerization  in vitro . The enzyme’s catalytic cycle involves veratryl alcohol, which is oxidized to radical cations that mediate lignin oxidation. LiP activity is regulated by phenolic compounds, which can transiently inactivate the enzyme, suggesting a feedback control mechanism. This regulation favors degradative ring-opening reactions rather than polymerization. In the presence of low concentrations of hydrogen peroxide and veratryl alcohol, LiP can also catalyze the partial depolymerization of synthetic hardwood lignin, highlighting its potential in bioremediation (Harvey et al., 1992). MnP system generates reactive radicals that break down recalcitrant lignin and other complex pollutants (Hofrichter, 2002). Versatile peroxide degrades complex and recalcitrant pollutants as it shows both LiP-like and MnP-like activities, allowing it to break down a wide range of aromatic and phenolic compounds. It oxidizes non-phenolic substrates, such as those found in lignin, via radical formation (similar to LiP), and converts Mn²⁺ to Mn³⁺, which in turn oxidizes organic pollutants (a typical MnP function). Additionally, versatile peroxidase can degrade synthetic dyes such as Reactive Black 5, which are commonly found in industrial wastewater and resistant to many other microbial degradation processes (Camarero et al., 1999).  
 Fig. 7  Degradation of organic pollutants by white rot fungi (WRF) and their oxidative and extracellular ligninolytic systems (Zhuo & Fan, 2021).  How does Fungi Bioremediation compare to other potential Bioremediations?  Similar to fungi, plants and  bacteria  also play significant roles in bioremediation, each with unique advantages and limitations. For instance, hyperaccumulator plants like  Thlaspi caerulescens  can absorb heavy metals from soil, and bacteria such as  Pseudomonas putida  can degrade hydrocarbons (Medić & Karadžić, 2022; Milner & Kochian, 2008). While fungi go through mycoremediation ( Fig. 8-B ), plants go through phytoremediation ( Fig. 8-D ); they absorb, accumulate, and detoxify pollutants via their roots and shoots; this makes them especially good at degrading metals just like fungi. This mechanism earned them the title of liver of nature (Nabi & Dar, 2022). While phytoremediation is a captivating subject to study, it falls short as it is generally slower and limited to a plant’s root zone. Root systems extend only a few feet into the soil and restrict their ability to access and remediate contaminants located deeper underground. Interestingly, combining fungi and plants in bioremediation can enhance the overall effectiveness of the process. In fact, fungi can degrade complex organic pollutants and heavy metals, making them more accessible for uptake by plant roots. This synergistic approach leverages the strengths of both organisms: the deep soil penetration and enzymatic capabilities of fungi, and the stabilization and accumulation abilities of plants (Tomer et al., 2021). Bacterial bioremediation (seen in Fig. 8 A), rather, competes with fungi in the biodegradation of PhACs and hydrocarbons. They are often used in synergy with mycoremediation due to their limitation: dependency on some environmental factors such as pH, temperature, and presence of particular nutrients (Thirumalaivasan et al., 2024).  
 Fig. 8  An overview of bioremediation approaches (in the case study of cadmium contamination into soil by (Kumar et al., 2021)).  Fungus biodegradation of polyethylene  Polyethylene (PE) is widely utilized as a synthetic polymer, especially known as plastic, due to its strong and resistant nature against deterioration. These strengths, however, cause it to be a major environmental contaminant, as PE builds up in garbage dumps and ecosystems, endangering animals and biodiversity (Britannica, T., 2024). Nonetheless, specific types of fungi, notably  Aspergillus flavus ,  Aspergillus oryzae , and  Penicillium simplicissimum,  have exhibited significant capabilities in breaking down PE, presenting a hopeful solution to this enduring issue (Bautista-Zamudio et al., 2023). Biodegradation of PE by fungi seems to be a combination of physical and chemical processes. The initial step involves the colonization of the PE surface by fungal hyphae (see   Fig. 9 1) to increase the surface area of the polymer and create a point of access to enzymatic action (More about fungi hyphae systems are discussed in our  physics  paper on the mechanisms of adaptation and Interaction of fungi with the Physical World).  
 Fig. 9  Steps involved in the biodegradation process performed by white-rot fungi (Bautista-Zamudio et al., 2023).  The enzymes involved in this process are cutinases, lipases, and lignocellulolytic enzymes like laccases and peroxidases (Srikanth et al., 2022), similarly to mycoremediation. These enzymes start the degradation of PE by adding oxygen to the polymer structure. In other words, oxidative degradation occurs   (Fig. 9 3). This results in the creation of functional groups such as carbonyls and hydroxyls, which enhance the polymer’s hydrophilicity and lower its molecular weights (Srikanth et al., 2022). The smaller fragments with low molecular weight are easier to be broken down by enzymes (Fig. 9 4), eventually resulting in complete biodegradation into carbon dioxide and water.  A remarkable fungi species is  Cladosporium halotoleran  (See   Fig. 10) that has the ability to break down high-density PE (HDPE) by binding to the plastic through its hyphae and releasing oxidoreductase enzymes (Di Napoli et al., 2023).

Scale bars: 50µ (A, B, D). 100µ (C) (Di Napoli et al., 2023).  Thermal stress adaptations  Most fungi are mesophiles who thrive in temperatures of 20 to 30℃ but can survive in environments between 5 to 35℃. Similarly, most other organisms prefer these ranges because high temperatures cause their proteins to denature and aggregate (Fig. 11 A). Denaturation refers to the unfolding of proteins and the loss of their three-dimensional shape which leaves them dysfunctional. Denatured proteins can form aggregates which are structures of accumulated dysfunctional proteins. Despite this, certain fungi have developed strategies to help them tolerate and even thrive in hot environments. For instance, the  Chaetomium thermophilus  can exist in composts that reach 58℃ due to high substrate decomposition rates. For these fungi, the ability to tolerate high temperatures is critical for survival and competition with other organisms. Thermotolerant and thermophilic fungi can occupy extreme niches that other creatures simply cannot tolerate (Dix and Webster, 1995). However, heat-shock adaptations are also critical for mesophilic fungi, which often face precarious situations. Since fungi have limited locomotion, escaping environmental stressors is not a viable survival strategy. This section will discuss a two-step defense protocol found in  Saccharomyces cerevisiae  (brewer’s yeast) that helps them persevere through heat-shock. However, these mechanisms can be applied to other fungi as well.  
 Fig. 11  Thermal stress response in  S. cerevisiae  (Singer and Lindquist, 1998) .    Damage mitigation  Firstly, brewer’s yeast produces trehalose as the primary line of defense against denaturation. This sugar is composed of two glucose molecules linked at their 1-carbons. Initially, it was hypothesized that yeast produces trehalose to serve as an energy reserve, similar to glycogen. However, studies have shown that  S .  cerevisiae  prefers to metabolize glycogen during starvation and only use trehalose as a last resort. This preference shows that the disaccharide has a primary biological function that is not simply energy storage. Moreover, in normal conditions, yeast cells only produce trehalose during the stationary (non-growth) and spore phases. However, heat stress causes the sugar to be produced during the growth phase as well. In these circumstances, trehalose can amount to 20% of dry cell weight (Singer and Lindquist, 1998). This is a substantial amount, which indicates that trehalose must play a non-negligible role in heat protection. Indeed, a study by De Virgillio et al. showed that elevated trehalose levels were correlated to cell survival in adverse conditions. The researchers compared wild type yeast to cells with defective trehalose synthases and incubated them at 52℃ for 20 minutes and at 54℃ for 4 minutes. The mutant cells showed 100 times and 800 times less survival rates respectively than wild types (De Virgillio et al., 1994). Trehalose is proposed to mitigate denaturation and aggregation by surrounding proteins, similar to how dogs herd sheep (Fig. 11 B). Unlike denaturation protection mechanisms in other organisms, trehalose does not inhibit unfolding by trapping structural water within the protein. Instead, the disaccharide forms  hydrogen bonds  with sensitive amino acid groups, thereby inhibiting their interaction with other unstable species (Allison et al., 1999). This strategy ensures that protein shape is conserved while already denatured enzymes are blocked from forming aggregates with each other (Singer and Lindquist, 1998). However, these mechanisms do not allow the cell to resume normal functions, rather they simply mitigate the damage. For a viable stress response, the trehalose requires a teammate: Heat-shock proteins (Singer and Lindquist, 1998).   Cell recovery  Heat-shock proteins (HSPs) work with trehalose to recover cell function after thermal stress. Most HSPs act as janitors by degrading proteins that have been irreversibly damaged or as stabilizing agents that inhibit denaturation and aggregation during heat-shock (Singer and Lindquist, 1998). However, certain HSPs, like the Hsp104, can reactivate damaged enzymes. This unique ability was demonstrated by Parsell et al., who conducted a study which compared wild-type yeast cells to mutants that lack Hsp104s. First, both groups were made to produce bioluminescent luciferase enzymes. Then, the cells were incubated at 37℃, heat-shocked at 44℃, and allowed to recover at 25℃. The ability to produce new proteins was blocked in the mutant cells. Surprisingly, the WT cells were able to reactivate 70% of luciferases in the next 2 hours, where these mutants could only recover about 5% (Parsell et al., 1994). The results demonstrate that Hsp104s are vital for the heat-shock response as trehalose in brewer’s yeast. Moreover, this enzyme seems to be the more elegant design solution to thermal stress. Instead of simply degrading useless proteins and making new ones, Hsp104s fix them.  S. cerevisiae  may have developed this mechanism because fixing broken enzymes could demonstrate a lower energy investment than building anew. In contrast, other fungi and organisms prefer Hsp70s, which lack the disaggregating abilities of Hsp104s. The former enzyme acts in a similar way to trehalose by stabilizing proteins during heat stress. This dichotomy illustrates that both approaches are viable and depend on the specific needs of the organism. Mechanisms that utilize Hsp104s could be better adapted to heat shocks, while those that use Hsp70s could function better during prolonged heat exposure (Parsell et al., 1994).    Fungal chemical weaponry   Although fungi face many challenges in surviving their ecological environments, fungi are always fighting a constant war of survival and competition with other organisms. Fungi come well-equipped to their battles, wielding chemical weapons like antibiotics and hallucinogens. These fascinating weapons allow fungi to have effective means of survival and propagation against both microscale and macroscale organisms, ensuring fungi will have a chance to continue in the game of life.  Antibiotics  Imagine that one day your  skin  just stopped repairing itself. Quickly, your skin deteriorates, becoming fragile and leaky, with any small impact causing lesions. Eventually, your skin becomes so weak that it bursts, and your organs leak out! You might imagine that there was some catastrophic bioweapon of mass destruction let loose – and for bacteria, this is often the reality they face when encountering fungi; the factories of these destructive bioweapons. These “bioweapons” are antibiotics, one of the most critical chemical weapons produced by fungi to kill or reduce competitor microorganisms, ensuring the survival and propagation of a fungal colony (Grenni et al, 2018).  The first antibiotic was discovered in 1928 by Alexander Fleming, produced by a mold of the genus  Penicillium  (Gaynes, 2017). While Fleming was talking to a colleague, he noticed that on an agar plate, an invading fungus was surrounded by a zone where no bacteria grew (see  Fig. 12 ). After isolating  Penicillium , Fleming obtained an extract from it, determining this extract was what caused the region to be bacteria free. After medical testing, it was determined that the active ingredient of this extract, penicillin, had the capacity to destroy bacteria. (Gaynes, 2017) Many new antibiotics would be discovered from this point on, often found being produced by different species of fungus.  
 Fig. 12  Alexander Fleming’s Agar dish. Around the  Penicillium  colony at the top of the agar plate, there are no staphylococcal bacteria colonies due to the presence of penicillin antibiotic (Brown, 2024)  Fungi produce antibiotics through their metabolic processes, specifically fermentation (Binod et al., 2023). Antibiotic creation starts with the synthesis of amino acid precursors, which can be created as a result of metabolic reactions or other biosynthetic pathways. With enough precursor concentration, specialized enzymes catalyze chains of reactions, called pathways, to form intermediates and products. At the end of the pathways, the antibiotic product is formed, ready to be used by fungi (Brakhage, 2006).  Biosynthesis of Penicillin  The synthesis of penicillin is one of the most understood biosynthetic pathways of antibiotic creation in fungi. It occurs over three major steps, recruiting three or four main enzymes (Brakhage, 2006; (Mestrovic, 2023). Due to its well understood nature, it is a model pathway for understanding antibiotic biosynthesis.  The pathway begins with the amino acid precursors L-α-aminoadipic acid, L-cysteine and L-valine (ACV). Fungi can obtain L-cysteine and L-valine from their own respective pathways, and L-α-aminoadipic acid, an intermediate produced in the L-lysine biosynthetic pathway (Brakhage, 2006). With the presence of the precursors, the first catalytic step begins; the enzyme ACV synthase chemically condenses the three precursors into the tripeptide ACV (Mestrovic, 2023). Next, the second enzyme isopenicillin N synthase causes oxidative ring closure of the ACV molecule. In other words, the isopenicillin N synthase causes a four-membered beta-lactam ring as well as a five-membered thiazolidine ring (see  Fig. 13 ). The resulting compound is isopenicillin N, or IPN, which has weak antibiotic activity. From here, the pathway can diverge depending on the fungi. For  Penicillium  and other penicillium-producing fungi, the third step is catalyzed by acyl coenzyme A, where a lateral L-alpha-aminoadipate chain is replaced by a hydrophobic lateral chain. Comparatively, fungi of genus  Acremonium  converts IPN to penicillin N in a two-enzyme system involving the enzymes acyl-CoA-synthetase and acyl-CoA-racemase (Mestrovic, 2023). Although there are different types of penicillins each with their own structural differences, caused by slight differences in the biosynthesis processes of various fungi, in general all penicillins have a reactive β-lactam ring system and reactive cyclic amide group (Fernandes et al., 2012).  While various fungi may synthesize different antibiotics with vastly different pathways, fungi generally synthesize antibiotics through a similar process to that of penicillin; that being through catabolic reactions of amino acid precursors forming antibiotic products.  
 Fig. 13  The biosynthetic pathway of penicillin (Mestrovic, 2023).  Chemical mechanism of antibiotics  Just as fungi are diverse, so are the antibiotics they produce. Despite the diversity of antibiotics, they generally work in one of the five ways: inhibition of cell wall synthesis; impairment of the cytoplasmic membrane; inhibition of nucleic acid synthesis; inhibition of protein synthesis; and metabolic antagonist action (Fernandes et al., 2012). β-lactam antibiotics, including antibiotics like penicillin and amoxicillin, use the mode of action ‘inhibition of cell wall synthesis’ to kill bacteria.  β-lactams themselves are also diverse; in fact, synthesis of β-lactams is actually widespread in nature (Brakhage, 1998). However, their common feature, the β-lactam ring (shown in  Fig. 14 ), is what plays the defining role in antibacterial activity. β-lactam rings are composed of a four-membered ring structure containing a carbonyl group and an amide group (Nangia et al., 1996). Since the bond angles of β-lactam rings are less than 109.5°, they experience ring strain, a type of bond instability, which is further exacerbated by being fused to another ring structure (Gevorg, 2024). The high instability makes β-lactam rings readily hydrolyzed, meaning their bonds can be broken by water (Iwata et al., 1990). When hydrolyzed, the carbonyl-amide group can covalently bond to the serine residues of enzymes, termed penicillin-binding-proteins (PBPs) (Nangia et al., 1996).  PBPs are crucial for the biosynthesis and linkage of peptidoglycans, a key component of bacterial cell walls. With the covalent linkage of β-lactams, PBP activity is inhibited, causing the loss of vitality in bacterial cell walls, and eventually, death by cell lysis (Pandey & Cascella, 2023).   
 Fig. 14  Structure of the β-lactam ring (Nangia et al., 1996).  Hallucinogens  While fungi can secrete antibiotic compounds to actively remove microorganism competitors, some species also use a fascinating strategy to deter, or interestingly, encourage, microorganism  predation – mind manipulation! More specifically, various fungi can produce metabolites with psychoactive and hallucinogenic properties (Meyer & Slot, 2023), such as psilocybin or lysergic acid (LSD) (Cleveland Clinic, 2024). While the ecological role of hallucinogens is not yet fully understood, several hypotheses exist regarding how fungi may benefit from their production (Meyer & Slot, 2023).  Psilocybin and Psilocin  Psilocybin is a naturally occurring tertiary amine found in many species of fungi (Glatfelter et al., 2022). It is the prodrug of psilocin, meaning once ingested, psilocybin becomes activated as psilocin. Psilocin is a four-substituted simple tryptamine, meaning its structure is built around a fused double ring consisting of a benzene ring and a pyrrole, as well as a 2-carbon side chain and a hydroxy group substituent on position 4 (Greene, 2013; PubChem, 2005). Psilocin induces psychedelic effects by acting as a serotonin agonist; since psilocin’s structure is chemically very similar to serotonin, serotonin receptors bind with psilocin instead of serotonin causing psychedelic effects (Glatfelter et al., 2022). Notably, the differences between psilocin and serotonin are the primary amine of serotonin being replaced with a tertiary amine, and the indole ring of psilocybin is substituted on position 5 for serotonin instead of position 4 (See  Fig. 15 ) (Zanjani et al., 2023).   
 Fig. 15  The differences in the structures of psilocin and serotonin (Zanjani et al., 2023).  Ecological role of Psilocybin  While antibiotics prove to be an effective means to control competition on a microorganism scale, fungi often need ways to defend themselves from macro-scale aggressors. Fortunately for fungi, the synthesis of hallucinogens, such as psilocybin, are one of many design solutions fungi use to defend themselves with! The most straightforward way fungi weaponize psilocybin is using it as a form of direct toxicity against fungivorous species (Meyer & Slot, 2023). In mouse models, ingestion of large doses of psilocin (293 mg of psilocin per kg of mouse body weight) caused mortality, and even low doses (10 mg/kg) could cause oxidative DNA damage to neural tissues. Similarly for invertebrates, while not extensively tested, psilocin ingestion likely causes fatal oxidative damage (Meyer & Slot, 2023). Fungi also use psilocybin as a deterrent from ingestion by modulating  gut  microbiomes of fungivorous species (Meyer & Slot, 2023). Psilocybin can suppress appetite by regulating the expression of dual oxidase, an enzyme responsible for regulating gut microbiomes (Zeng et al., 2022). Thus, consumption of psilocybin-producing fungi reduces the appetite for fungi. In a similar vein, psilocybin can cause immune system depression, directly causing selection against mushroom consumption. Psilocybin downregulates and upregulates various immunomodulatory factors that are crucial for defense against bacterial infections in  Drosophila  (Meyer & Slot, 2023). Furthermore, psilocybin further discourages fungal consumption by disruption of social behavior, particularly for colonial organisms. Hallucinogens like LSD produce asocial behavior in ants such as decreased group formation, food sharing, and nest return rates of foragers, limiting colony growth. Psilocybin may have similar effects on colonial insects, selecting for psilocybin-producing-fungi avoidant behavior (Meyer & Slot, 2023).   While fungi use psilocybin to protect against predation for the above reasons, a complementary hypothesis suggests that some fungi use psilocybin to facilitate interactions with animal vectors for spore dispersal. For example, in a study conducted by Hibicke and Nichols (Hibicke & Nichols, 2022), fruit flies were demonstrated to travel more, which would allow for greater spore dispersal in a naturalistic setting (Meyer & Slot, 2023).   Overall, fungi cleverly implement the use of chemical weapons to gain a competitive advantage in its respective niches. When dealing with competition in the form of microorganisms, fungi can produce antibiotics such as penicillin to kill off bacteria. For larger organisms, fungi can use hallucinogens, such as psilocybin, as a solution to deter predation, or sometimes encourage predation for greater propagation. Despite the effectiveness of these design solutions, with the diverse array of fungi, there are still many more chemical weapons that fungi use to survive and compete with in their environments.  Conclusion Fungi live in a dangerous and hostile world. They must avoid both predators and environmental stresses. However, compared to other organisms, they are limited in their access to conventional means of survival. Fungi do not possess legs or wings they can use to flee, nor do they have any conventional weapons like claws or teeth that they can employ to defend themselves. Yet, they exist in virtually every ecosystem on earth. It is clear that the chemical solutions they have developed for attack and defense are just as effective as more conventional methods.    Firstly, fungi have developed complex metabolic pathways and enzymes that allow them to break down various substances in their environment. These design solutions are critical for the ecosystem and for fungi themselves who use them as both offensive and defensive measures. For instance, white rot employs a variety of enzymes to break down lignin for nutrients. Curiously, the same solutions are also used by the fungus to degrade organic pollutants such as dyes and aromatics. By protecting itself from harmful substances, white rot also contributes to bioremediation and mitigation of harm done by human activity. Moreover, fungi like brewer’s yeast utilize heat-shock enzymes to help them survive thermal stress. This adaptation is critical for efficient decomposition because it allows certain fungi to colonize composts with high internal temperatures.    Similarly, fungi also employ synthesis of molecules to ensure their survival. They can attack other organisms by producing chemical weapons, such as antibiotics, which kill bacterial pathogens and competitors. Fungi can also protect themselves by synthesizing hallucinogens that discourage predation. They do not let the lack of physical weapons stop them from defending themselves and their territory. Likewise, fungi also fight inanimate foes like thermal stress using synthesis. Brewer’s yeast produces sugar trehalose that allows it to withstand heat by inhibiting denaturation and aggregation of proteins.

title: Chemistry of Cohesion and Communication in Fish Schools
authors: Anne-Sophie Roy, Emma Warner, Hoi Ching Wat, Lucas Yatcyshyn
abstract: Over a quarter of the world’s fish school at some point in their life; many spend most of their lives apart of these groups. Fish rely on several different sensory systems to communicate and school, including bioluminescence, osmoregulatory, olfactory, gustatory, and chemosensory systems. These sensory approaches are crucial for survival and social interaction; for instance, bioluminescence can attract mates or deter predators, while the olfactory and chemosensory systems are essential for detecting pheromones and environmental cues. Ecological changes caused by heavy metal, pesticide, and many other forms of pollution interfere with the communication pathways required for fish to school and are thus detrimental to their survival. Examining the physiology, communication, and responses of fish to environmental stressors may lead to a better understanding of some of the complex mechanisms behind schooling.

Chemistry of Cohesion and Communication in Fish Schools  Anne-Sophie Roy, Emma Warner, Hoi Ching Wat, Lucas Yatcyshyn Abstract Over a quarter of the world’s fish school at some point in their life; many spend most of their lives apart of these groups. Fish rely on several different sensory systems to communicate and school, including bioluminescence, osmoregulatory, olfactory, gustatory, and chemosensory systems. These sensory approaches are crucial for survival and social interaction; for instance, bioluminescence can attract mates or deter predators, while the olfactory and chemosensory systems are essential for detecting pheromones and environmental cues. Ecological changes caused by heavy metal, pesticide, and many other forms of pollution interfere with the communication pathways required for fish to school and are thus detrimental to their survival. Examining the physiology, communication, and responses of fish to environmental stressors may lead to a better understanding of some of the complex mechanisms behind schooling.  Introduction Schooling is a distinctive social behavior that first evolved in teleosts (bony fish). It is a type of shoal, defined as an aggregation of fish, but is unique in that fish traveling in a school must do so parallel to each other and at a certain distance apart (Pavlov & Kasumyan, 2000). This structured behaviour allows fish to achieve numerous benefits that are often crucial for the survival of these fish.  Fish in a school learn advantageous reflexes from their schoolmates through imitation and gain greater  swimming  efficiency by swimming in the vortices created by their neighbours. They are also able to achieve higher defence, better nutrition, and safer migration; the increased number of individuals in a school provides advantages over solitary living. In addition to using pressure waves and electrical signals to detect their neighbours, fish are equipped with many other methods of communication which they rely on to school (readers are referred to  Nature’s Aquatic Ballet: The Physics and Synchronization of Schooling Fish  for more detail on the advantages of schooling).  To join a school, a fish must be able to identify other schooling fish that are phenotypically similar to itself. For a school to remain cohesive, all individuals must be able to adjust to changes in the movement of their neighbors (Pavlov & Kasumyan, 2000). The mechanisms by which fish detect and respond to these changes are diverse and range from an instinctual attraction based on sight to other similar fish (typically of the same species), to sense of smell and taste to detect chemical signals such as pheromones released by others in the school.  The ability of fish to communicate and receive these chemical signals is largely dependent on the environment. In fact, schooling behavior as a whole is largely influenced by ecological context. Environmental factors are considered to be more significant in the development of schooling behaviors than ancestry (Pavlov & Kasumyan, 2000), and sudden changes to these environments may have negative impacts on the health of fish and their ability to coordinate with their neighbours.   Physiology Fish physiology—including the gills, swim bladder, and osmoregulatory and chemosensory systems—is highly adapted to the diverse environments they inhabit. Among these systems, respiration is particularly important as it enables fish to harness energy from their surroundings.  Respiration Respiration in fish is a complex process facilitated by gills which are crucial to the absorption of oxygen and in supporting cellular respiration. The function of gills along with the metabolic processes involved in cellular respiration enable efficient energy production in fish, powering many other physiological processes necessary for the fish’s survival.  The energy currency of eukaryotic cells, including those in shoaling fish, is Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP), a nucleic acid. Organisms must be able to synthesize the glucose in the food they digest. The chemical equation for cellular respiration is noted below in Figure 1 (Kahwaty & Kahwaty, 2021).  
 Fig. 1    Chemical reaction for Cellular Respiration (Kahwaty & Kahwaty, 2021)  The first step in cellular respiration is glycolysis which occurs in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells. It is an anaerobic process which converts a single glucose molecule into two pyruvates, two ATPs molecules, and two NADH. The pyruvate then goes through an intermediate step while being transported to the mitochondria of the cell. There, it is converted into acetyl CoA and a CO 2  molecule is emitted (Kahwaty & Kahwaty, 2021).  In the mitochondrial matrix, the second step of cellular respiration occurs: the Kreb’s Cycle. This aerobic process releases a CO 2  while synthesizing two ATP, six NADH, and two FADH 2 . These compounds are necessary in the third step of the process: the electron transport chain.  Using the inner mitochondrial membrane as a barrier, the electrons from NADH and FADH 2  are used to generate a proton gradient by pumping H +   ions  into the intermembrane space of the mitochondria. ATP synthase uses this proton gradient to add a phosphate to ADP to make ATP as the H +  enters back across the membrane (Fig. 2). Finally, oxygen acts as the last electron acceptor, producing H 2 O. Overall, cellular respiration generates about 30 ATP molecules per glucose, contributing to the energy currency cells need to survive.  Though many organisms utilize this evolutionarily conserved process, fish are unique in that they use it while living in an underwater environment. To undergo cellular respiration, they have found a way to obtain oxygen using their innovative gills.  
 Fig. 2  The electron transport chain and ATP synthase (Kahwaty & Kahwaty, 2021)  Gills Oxygen is relatively insoluble in  water  and thus respiration under water requires a much greater amount of energy than respiration in air. As such, fish have evolved a unique system to increase the efficiency of gas exchange under water.  Gills are thin layers of thin, capillary-filled tissue primarily responsible for gas exchange. Water flows in through the fish’s mouth and passes over the surface of the gills as it leaves, allowing oxygen to diffuse into the bloodstream, and waste to diffuse back into the environment (Fig. 3) (Parenti & Weitzman, 2024a).  In order to increase the overall rate of diffusion, thin layers of tissue called lamella are evenly distributed across the gill filaments. Gill filaments are also covered by epithelial pavement cells with microvilli and microplicae structures. In combination, lamellae and pavement cells increase the surface area of the gills (the mean scaling exponent of gill area being 0.76) (Palzenberger & Pohla, 1992) allowing a higher overall rate of diffusion and increasing the efficiency of the gas exchange in gills (Baker et al., 2019; Evans et al., 2005). The rate of diffusion is defined by (Baker et al., 2019):    (1)      
 Fig. 3  The water flows through the gills for respiration to occur (Evans et al., 2005).   Bony fish and cartilaginous fish use different methods to pass water over their gills.   Cartilaginous fish use ram ventilation, the opening of their mouths during swimming to let water pass (Evans et al., 2005). Cartilaginous fish must be constantly moving for enough water to flow over their gills for them to respire. Bony fish, on the other hand, have evolved the operculum, a special bone that covers the fish’s gills. The operculum allows bony fish to use buccal pumping, meaning that fish actively swallow water in order to push water through its gills. Thus, teleosts do not need to be moving to respire (Parenti & Weitzman, 2024b;  Ferry & Hernandez, 2011;  U.S. Department of the Interior, n.d.).  In addition to being the site for respiration, fish gills are also a site for metabolism. Toxins, in addition to certain wastes, are also excreted at the gills. Thus, environmental pollutants, such as the 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo- p -dioxin (TCDD), often significantly damage the gills (Evans et al., 2005).   Swim bladder  Fish rely on gas absorption not only for respiration, but also for movement. The swim bladder is a hydrostatic organ found in most modern fish, which allows them to control their depth in water. Special glands release gas, mostly oxygen, into the bladder, which increases the buoyancy of the fish and decreases its depth. When the fish wants to increase its depth in water, the gas is absorbed into the bloodstream, decreasing the buoyancy of the fish (Parenti & Weitzman, 2024a).  Osmoregulation  Fish have adapted to live between opposite extremes of habitat osmodiversity, ranging from desert pools with concentration quadruple that of the ocean (128 ppt) to freshwater pools with nearly no ion concentration at all (Greenwell et al., 2003). Living cells require a constant osmotic environment to function and maintain their structure. While most of the fish is covered in scales and a thin mucus that renders it impermeable to water, the gills of the fish are semipermeable, thin, exposed to the environment, and designed to maximize the area over which gas exchange can occur. The semipermeable nature of gills also allows the transport of water across their membranes (Greenwell et al., 2003).    The greatest challenge to fish is therefore the regulation of internal water and electrolyte homeostasis in the face of extremely hypo- and hyper- osmotic environments (compared to the bodily fluids of the fish). Marine teleosts reside in hyperosmotic environments which contain a concentration of salt 2-4 times that of the bodily fluids of the fish (1000 mOsm/kg and 250-500 mOsm/kg, respectively). The higher concentration of salt in the environment poses chronic risk of dehydration and salt loading. Conversely, freshwater teleosts, which live in hypoosmotic environments (< 1mM as compared with 150 mM in their bodily fluids), are faced with constant challenges of volume loading, strain caused by excess fluid volume within the fish due to over-absorption of water and salt depletion (Greenwell et al., 2003). The differences in the respective osmoregulatory physiologies of marine and freshwater teleosts help highlight their specialized adaptations in response to their contrasting environmental challenges.  The main purpose of osmotic mechanisms in marine fish is to minimize dehydration through the constant intake of sodium chloride. This is primarily done by drinking seawater (Greenwell et al., 2003). Marine fish typically drink 10-20% of their body weight in sea water per day, though some may drink up to 35-40% of their weight in more saline environments. The ions are then absorbed, transported in a series of ion exchanges, and excreted, allowing for a net gain in total body water but generally no net gain in ions. The absorption and excretion of ions is primarily through the gills, gastrointestinal system, and urinary tract. Approximately 80% of sodium and chloride ions consumed are absorbed in the esophagus, which is impermeable to water, and the gut lumen, which is permeable to both water and monovalent ions, via diffusion along the concentration gradient. Other monovalent and divalent ions such as potassium, magnesium, and sulfate are also absorbed in the gut lumen via Na +  -K +  ATPase-driven basal membrane pumps and a Na +  -K +  -2Cl –  cotransporter system. Any excess of sodium, chloride, and potassium ions are excreted via a combination of active transport, cotransport and passive diffusion by mitochondria-rich chloride cells in the fish’s gills. Absorbed divalent ions are excreted by kidneys into the urine, though 80% of divalent ions are not absorbed and are simply excreted in the feces. Urine flow rates in marine fish are low (approximately 1-2% of their body weight) as the water is reabsorbed by the urinary bladder (Greenwell et al., 2003).  The osmoregulation in freshwater fish is designed to prevent overhydration. Due to the hypotonic environmental conditions, a large amount of water is absorbed through the gills—the influx of water may reach roughly 50% of the fish’s body mass per hour. To compensate, freshwater fish drink very little and excrete large amounts of dilute urine, facilitated by the kidneys which rely on high glomerular filtration rates to eliminate large volumes of water. Sodium and chloride ions are completely reabsorbed, facilitated by Cl –  exchange with HCO 3 –  in chloride cells and conductive channels driven by proton pumps in the outer cells of the gills. The chloride cells in freshwater fish are also located deeper in the gill tissues than in marine fish, which results in lower ion absorption in freshwater fish, making them more suitable to their hypoosmotic environment (Greenwell et al., 2003).  These adaptive osmoregulatory strategies are vital for the physiological stability and cellular function across a diverse set of aquatic environments. In addition to osmoregulation, fish have evolved various sensory tools to aid in navigating their environment, helping fish to school, even under less favourable conditions.  Flashlight fish and bioluminescence   Vision is the primary sensory basis for schooling; fish rely on vision to imitate the behaviors of their neighbors and respond to predators. In low light, the distance between fish gradually increases and the school eventually loses its structure, and thus schools often dissipate in low light to decrease the risk of  predation  (Pavlov & Kasumyan, 2000). Flashlight fish (Anomalopidae) are a family of fish that rely on bioluminescence as a light source to remain a school at night (Gruber et. al, 2019).   Bioluminescence is the emission of visible light by an organism via a chemical reaction (chemiluminescence). The energy released by the oxidation of a luciferin substrate by a luciferase enzyme is emitted as visible light as opposed to heat. Depending on the bioluminescent organism, the luciferin and luciferase involved may differ (Herring & Widder, 2001).  In flashlight fish, a symbiotic bioluminescent bacterium of the genus Vibrio is responsible for the light emitted by the fish. In these bacteria, luciferase is a heterodimer composed of alpha and beta subunits that catalyzes the oxidation of long-chain aldehydes (RCOH) and reduced flavin mononucleotides (FMNH2). The alpha and beta subunits of luciferase are encoded by luxA and luxB genes, respectively. Other luxCDABEG genes encode various proteins that catalyze different steps in the chemical pathways responsible for producing long-chain aldehydes and flavin mononucleotides. These pathways also include the production and recycling of fatty acids and the activation of AMP, an intermediate in ATP synthesis (Fig. 4) (Miyashiro & Ruby, 2013).  
 Fig. 4  (A) Genes involved in the production (luxA-G) and regulation (luxR and luxL) of  luminescence  in Vibrio bacteria (Miyashiro & Ruby, 2013).  Vibrio bacteria grow within masses of parallel, specialized tubules in the subocular bioluminescent organs of flashlight fish. These masses of tubules align at right angles to each other and run along the surface of the fish’s light organs (Fig. 5). Stacks of guanine crystals parallel to the surface of the organ are attached to the base of the tubules and act to reflect the light generated by the bacteria (Gruber et. al, 2019). Flashlight fish rotate or cover their light organ (depending on the species) in order to reduce the light output. They frequently rotate or cover and uncover their light organs to expose and hide the bioluminescent bacteria to create brief flashes of light that they use for defense, feeding, communication, and schooling (Gruber et. al, 2019).  
 Fig 5.  (A) An adult  Anomalops katoptron  and (B) a macro image of its bioluminescent organ (Gruber et al., 2019).     Chemosensory system  As water is a good solvent, the aquatic environment serves as a perfect medium for the dispersion of chemicals (Ward et al., 2008). Fish can detect minute concentrations of environmental chemicals, such as pheromones, through their chemosensory system, which consists of various types of chemoreceptors. The detection of chemical signals plays a crucial role in the behavior and survival of schooling fish (Sorensen, 1992). There are two major systems for detecting chemical signals, the olfactory and the gustatory systems.   Olfactory and gustatory systems  The olfactory system in fish is primarily responsible for detecting volatile substances in the environment, including those dissolved in water (Jónsson, 1980). While olfaction is generally concerned with the detection of food, it is also important for the detection of chemical signals by conspecifics (Liley, 1982). Fish typically possess paired nasal cavities located near the dorsal surface of the head (Fig. 6). However, some species, such as lampreys and hagfish, have only a single nostril and nasal cavity (Daghfous et al., 2012). The olfactory chambers (rosettes) in these cavities contain folds or lamellae lined with olfactory sensory neurons (Fig. 7) (Jónsson, 1980). The surface area and layout of these lamellae differ between species, and it was once thought they affected the sense of smell. However, new studies have shown that fluid flow and how odors move are more important for smell sensitivity (Daghfous et al., 2012).  
 Fig 6.  Olfactory pathway of a goldfish. Odors enter the nasal cavity and reach the olfactory epithelium. The olfactory information is then transmitted from the olfactory nerve to the bulbs. The bulbs transmit action potentials via the olfactory tracts to the telencephalon, where the behavioral control center is located (Kobayashi, 2020).  
 Fig 7.  Overview of the peripheral zebrafish olfactory system. A) Adult zebra fish B) View of the peripheral olfactory organ and connectivity to the brain. The olfactory system consists of two olfactory epithelia located on each side of the head. Each olfactory epithelium extends a short nerve, composed of olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) axons, to the olfactory bulb. C) Composition of olfactory rosette (chambers). D) A single lamella, Olfactory sensory neurons occupy the inner sensory region of each lamella. E) Different olfactory sensory neurons present in zebrafish (Calvo-Ochoa et al., 2020).  Olfaction refers to the chemical information detected through the specific chemoreceptors located in the olfactory epithelium, a sensitive tissue inside the nasal cavity (Sorensen, 1992). Inside the nasal cavity, ligands – specific stimulus molecule that can be bind to specific membrane receptors- bind to the chemoreceptors, activating the G proteins (proteins that can bind to guanosine triphosphate and guanosine diphosphate) on the cell membrane (Hara, 1994; Rehman et al., 2023). The activated G proteins in turn activate adenylyl cyclase or phospholipase C to produce secondary messengers. The secondary messengers activate the opening of ion channels, leading to the generation of an action potential across the olfactory tracts. Ions can also be directly transported across the membrane without involving the second messengers, leading to the generation of electrical signals to the central nervous system. By recording the generation of action potentials by different chemical stimuli, the electro-olfactogram (EOG) can be obtained (Fig. 8) (Hara, 1994).    
 Fig. 8  The electro-olfactogram of cichlid with different odorants. OB stands for olfactory bulb, OE stands for olfactory epithelium, and Vv stands for ventral telencephalon. Through the recording electrode and the reference electrode, the electric field and the action potentials can be recorded (Nikonov & Maruska, 2019).   While the olfactory neurons are more sensitive to several compounds—such as amino acids, sex steroids, bile acids/salts, and prostaglandins—they are less sensitive to alcohols, carboxylic acids, amines, and aromatic hydrocarbons (Hara, 1994). The highly complex olfactory systems help fish to distinguish between different types of pheromones, each eliciting specific behaviors (Stacey & Sorensen, 2002).  In addition to the olfactory system, fish also rely on the gustatory system to detect chemical compounds in water. Gustatory system is composed of epithelial gustatory cells. Different species are more sensitive to different amino acids. A fish’s gustatory system is also sensitive to carbon dioxide and certain toxins. Gustatory system might aid the fish to avoid poisons and dangerous environments in water (Hara, 1994).   Olfactory signals are one of the main determinants of whether a fish will join and remain in a shoal or school. For example, focal fish will stay in conspecific shoals even if they lack their vision, however, they do not when they lack on olfactory stimulus (Ward et al., 2002). Moreover, fish can also compare its own chemical signals from those of the other fish. Through this “self-reference”, it can find conspecific fish with size similar to itself. It is hypothesized that ontogenetic changes with respect to size produce chemical cues, aiding fish in finding conspecific fish with similar size and to form a more uniform school (Ward & Currie, 2013). Other chemical signals are used for communication and help schools remain cohesive and respond to external stimuli.  Pheromones  Pheromones are chemical signals released by fish as a form of communication that trigger behavioral or physiological responses in others of the same species (Stacey & Sorensen, 2002; Liley 1982). They can be in the form of amines, amino acids, prostaglandins, bile acids, and steroids (Fig. 9) (Bowers et al., 2023), compounds that the olfactory system is sensitive to (Hara, 1994). These chemicals are crucial in regulating key behaviors such as reproduction, migration, predator avoidance, and the maintenance of social hierarchies (Sorensen & Stacey, 2004). Pheromones are species-specific, meaning they affect only members of the same species, ensuring targeted communication (Liley, 1982).   
 Fig. 9  Chemical structure of different pheromones. For each chemical, the general structure is given followed by an example of fish pheromone (Chung-Davidson et al., 2011).  Reproductive pheromones  In some fish species, reproductive pheromones are essential for ensuring synchronized mating and reproductive success (Stacey & Sorensen, 2002). One of the most studied fish pheromones is prostaglandin, which functions as a sex pheromone in various species. Ovulating females release prostaglandin, and this chemical signal stimulates male courtship behavior, which increases the likelihood of successful reproduction (Fig. 10). Different species show unique responses to reproductive pheromones, with some fish relying heavily on these chemical cues to coordinate mating (Sorensen & Stacey, 2004).  
 Fig. 10  Female releases sex pheromones to find a male of the same species to mate with. (Wyatt, 2015)  Alarm pheromones  In fish, pheromones also play an important role in group behaviors, especially in species that form schools or shoals (Stacey & Sorensen, 2002). Alarm pheromones are released when a fish is injured or under stress, signalling danger to nearby fish (Chung-Davidson et al., 2011). This triggers an immediate group response aimed at enhancing the survival of individuals (Fig. 11). For example, the release of these alarm pheromones can cause the group to scatter or adopt defensive behaviors, such as darting, when faced with a predator (Sorensen, 1992; Masuda et al., 2024).  
 Fig. 11  (A) Fish uses reproductive pheromones to enable mating, (B) to senses alarm pheromones from predators, (C) to detects food pheromones, and (D) senses alarm pheromones from pollutants (Korsching, 2020).  In certain fish, such as those in the ostariophysan group (which includes minnows), injury causes the release of a chemical alarm signal from specialized skin cells called club cells. These cells store the alarm substance, which is released into the water when the fish is injured. Nearby fish detect this cue and react quickly, often by swimming away or forming tighter groups for protection (Daghfous et al., 2012).  Other fish species like gobies, salmon, cichlids, and perch also release alarm substances when injured, but the reactions differ between species. For instance, minnows respond by swimming faster, tightening their school, or freezing in place to avoid detection, while Crucian carp react by swimming down to the bottom and stirring up mud to hide (Daghfous et al., 2012). Although the specific behaviors vary, the common response across fish species is to avoid areas where alarm pheromones are present, thus reducing the risk of predation (Stacey & Sorensen, 2002).  Two specific molecules have been identified as the alarm pheromones in zebrafish: daniol sulfate, a sulfated bile alcohol with the molecular formula C 27 H 46 O 7 S   ; and the ostariopterin, a pterin derivative with a molecular formula C 11 H 13 N 5 O 5 . These molecular signals are perceived by the olfactory receptors on the fish’s  cilia  or microvilli. A signal is then transmitted to the olfactory bulb composed by glomeruli. The daniol sulfate activates the part of the glomeruli called dorsal glomerular cluster(dGa) and the ostariopterin activates the lateral glomerulus 4 (IG4) (Fig. 12). When the two substances are released together in the water, they activate the telencephalon, similar to mammalian amygdaloid nuclei, and trigger the panic reactions in zebrafish (Masuda et al., 2024).    
 Fig. 12  Daniol sulfate and ostariopterin are released by an injured fish and act as the dangers and conspecifics signals to alert the shoal of the potential dangers (Masuda et al., 2024).   Social and territorial pheromones  Pheromones are also used by fish for migration, to establish social hierarchies, and to defend territories. It is widely accepted that migratory fish “imprint their odor” onto their environment by the release of population-specific pheromone trails, which later provide information to the fish on the location of their return destination (Hasler, 1966; Liley, 1982). Furthermore, in schools with dominant fish, the dominant fish release pheromones that suppress reproductive activities in subordinates, ensuring only the strongest individuals have the chance to reproduce. This hierarchical control helps maintain balance within the population. In species like tilapia, pheromones play a role in defending nesting sites and establishing breeding territories, ensuring that individuals can successfully reproduce and defend their young (Stacey & Sorensen, 2002).  Food pheromones   For fish that do not rely on vision for hunting or foraging, chemosensory systems are crucial for locating food, capturing prey, and avoiding harmful substances. Fish detect amino acids released by prey and use them to initiate species-specific search behaviors. For example, in zebrafish, the amino acids trigger an appetitive swimming behavior, characterized by an increased number of turns as they search for food. However, in rainbow trout, amino acids induce bottom-searching behaviors (Daghfous et al., 2012).   Fish can detect amino acids at very low concentrations, from micro-molar to nanomolar levels, which are commonly found in natural waters. However, environmental pollutants can interfere with these olfactory-mediated behaviors. Fish may be attracted to contaminated areas due to the presence of amino acid-like substances, which could lead them into harmful environments. This highlights the importance of the chemical senses in fish survival and the potential risks posed by water contamination (Daghfous et al., 2012).  Environment chemistry and fish health  The presence of certain chemicals in the water is integral for fish survival while other elements act as toxins, detrimental to fish health. Each of these factors not only impact the survival of each individual fish but the ecosystem as a whole. Pollution, whether caused by human activities or natural disasters, leads to fundamental changes in aquatic environments. These include decreases in the amount of dissolved oxygen, changes in water pH, and the introduction of  toxic chemicals , impacting the health of fish and their ability to osmoregulate and communicate (Mustafa et al., 2024).  Heavy metals  Human activities such as smelting, mining, manufacturing, urbanization, and agriculture have led to the contamination of heavy metals in aquatic environments (Mustafa et al., 2024). Heavy metals such as mercury, lead, cadmium, and arsenic, accumulate within aquatic organisms, impacting many of their biological functions. Fish absorb heavy metals as part of ion exchange in their gills, skin and tissues, through osmoregulation and the consumption of contaminated food. These heavy metals are then carried through the bloodstream, spreading to vital organs where they bind to metal binding proteins. As the heavy metals accumulate, they damage tissues, organs, and cells. Some of these detrimental impacts include reduced reproductive capabilities, endocrine disruption, neurological disorders, and death (Mustafa et al., 2024). Such effects, especially endocrine disruption and neurological disorders, have severe impacts on the health of individual fish, carrying implications for the overall cohesion of shoals and schools.  Another impact of high levels of heavy metals is oxidative stress. Heavy metals generate free  radicals  and reactive oxygen species within cells. These highly reactive molecules cause damage to vital cellular structures such as proteins, lipids, and DNA, known as oxidative stress. Furthermore, these molecules may activate redox-sensitive transcription factors which affect DNA repair, apoptosis, cell growth, and cell differentiation (Mustafa et al., 2024).   Pesticides   Agriculture commonly uses pesticides, including fungicides, insecticides, and herbicides, to maximize crop output. However, runoff from farms contaminates waters, leads to changes in pH, nutrient content, and oxygen levels. These changes can negatively impact a fish’s ability to breathe and may also destroy their bodies on a cellular level.  Some pesticides are known to be toxic to fish. For example, acrolein, a well-known herbicide, is a highly toxic algaecide that causes severe damage to fish gills which are vital for respiration. Other pesticides introduce high amounts of plant nutrients. The runoff assists the growth of algae in aquatic environments, leading to eutrophication. Chemicals containing high amounts of nitrogen and phosphorus saturate the aquatic environment, creating a prime habitat for large algae blooms. This surplus in algae depletes the oxygen levels as well as blocks sunlight from reaching inhabitants below the surface. These impacts of eutrophication impact fish and their ability to survive such chemical changes (Mustafa et al., 2024).  Nanoparticles  Nanoparticles are molecules that can pollute the environment through waste discharge, runoff, and leaching (Mustafa et al., 2024). They are responsible for leading to oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and tissue damage through bioaccumulation, direct toxicity, and interfering with biological process.  Endocrine disrupting compounds  Endocrine Disrupting Compounds (EDCs) are chemicals that interfere with typical function of the endocrine system, impacting the creation and release of hormones in an organism. Some examples of such chemicals include phenols, estrogens, heavy metals, industrial intermediates, PAHs, pesticides, dioxins, and polychlorinated biphenyls (Mustafa et al., 2024). For example, the release of harmful EDCs in a phenomenon called red tide has serious implications for water chemistry and fish health.  Red tide: A case study   Red tide is a term for harmful algal blooms (US Department of Commerce, NOAA, 2019). As mentioned before, changes in water chemistry resulting from pollution may lead to eutrophication from algae blooms. Red tide releases neurotoxins into the surrounding environment, resulting in massive fish kills. Not only that, but the algae also deplete the oxygen supply in the water, further leading to death resulting from changes in water chemistry (Howard, 2023). With the pollution of aquatic environments and climate change, waters have become more susceptible to longer and more destructive red tides, indicating the delicate balance between habitat chemistry and the survival of different organisms, including fish.  For example, in recent years, Florida has been dealing with increasingly larger and longer lasting blooms of a toxic alga called  Karenia brevis . These algae release toxins that accumulate in shellfish, causing a condition called neurotoxic shellfish poisoning, leading to death. These toxins not only impact the predators that eat these organisms but also those living in the surrounding waters, including shoaling fish. Together, these lead to massive kills of wildlife as well as disrupting the Florida ecosystem (Fig. 13) (Rose, 2023).  
 Fig. 13  Red Tide Algae Blooms lead to massive fish kills in Florida (Jacobo, n.d.)   Surfactants  Surfactants are known to disrupt the function of important receptors involved in chemical communication, affecting a fish’s ability to school (Ward et al., 2008). Surfactants are components with an amphiphilic structure (Fig. 14), their amphiphilic properties cause them to assemble at interfaces between two phases or two substances, reducing the surface tension at the interphase (Unal et al., 2023).   
 Fig. 14  Structure of a surfactant molecule (Unal et al., 2023).   When juvenile Arctic charr ( Salvelinus alpinus ) are exposed to surfactants, they are less attracted to conspecific chemical cues. One vastly used surfactant in industrial and sewage processes is 4-Nonylphenol (4-NP). The levels of 4-NP near outflows across the world is currently around 1 to 2 μg 1 -1 .  Under these concentrations, shoaling killifish ( Fundulus diaphanus ) avoided the odor of their conspecifics and maintained a greater distance from its neighbors, compared to fish in an environment without 4-NP. The exposure to 4-NP thus affects the chemical signal of fish and impedes social recognition, this might be detrimental to the formation of a shoal if fish are no longer attracted to their conspecifics (Ward et al., 2008).   Carbon dioxide and ocean acidification  The current carbon dioxide concentration is the highest since the last 800 000 years and is projected to double by 2100 (Nadler et al., 2016). This drastic change in CO 2  levels may carry serious implications for fish, including impaired neurotransmission in fish, resulting in behavioral changes such as an inability to recognize predators. Certain neurotransmitters rely on the function of GABA-A receptors, which are linked to chloride and bicarbonate ion channels. Changes in the concentration of these ions within cells, potentially caused by elevated carbon dioxide levels in the water, can affect receptor function. Research has shown that gabazine, an inhibitory neurotransmitter of the GABA-A receptor, can treat the behavioral changes in fish being exposed to elevated concentrated CO 2  water (Chivers et al., 2013).   Under the projected future CO 2  concentration, the ability of fish to recognize olfactory cues will also be negatively affected. Increased  CO 2 levels lead to decreased shoaling instinct. It is postulated that the decrease in shoaling instinct is a result of elevated CO 2  concentration damaging the fish’s ability to detect olfactory social cues, and interfering with memory and the ability to learn (Nadler et al., 2016). Increased CO 2  concentration may also impact behavioral traits such as boldness, which may be fatal in the face of threats such as predators (Nadler et al., 2016).   Carbon dioxide  reacts with water to form carbonic acid which can dissociate to produce hydrogen atoms and increase the acidity of water (Fig. 15). As CO 2  concentration increases, more carbonic acid can be produced, leading to ocean acidification (Doney et al., 2009).   
 Fig 15  The reaction that CO 2  undergoes in water (Doney et al., 2009).   Ocean acidification affects fish lateralization. Lateralization describes the “handedness” of fish which affects the ability of fish to move in certain directions. At a lower pH, fish move randomly to the left or right when encountering a wall, and lateralization decreases. This can cause the schools to lose cohesion when making rapid maneuvers (such as when changing direction in response to predators).   Furthermore, increasing ocean temperature increases the boldness of temperate fish, so they only start escaping when they are at a closer distance to the predators (Fig. 15) (Mitchell et al., 2022).   These changes in behaviours due to ocean acidification can be detrimental to fish cohesion and the survival of shoaling fish, as shown in the figure 16.   
 Fig. 16  Shoaling behaviors are expected to change with the predicted carbon dioxide levels of the year 2100. Lateralization in fish will decrease and so fish will no longer turn in the same direction, will become bolder, and therefore will only escape predators when they are much closer (Mitchell et al., 2022).   Conclusion   Living in water is different from living on land. Water is much denser than air, and it transmits chemical information differently.    To live in water, even breathing becomes a difficulty due to the insolubility of oxygen in water. To obtain enough oxygen, fish use the gills with a high surface area for gas diffusion, and they use their swimming movements or swallowing of water to pass enough water through their gills. Moreover, fish need to adapt to osmodiverse environments with different ion concentrations. Marine fish consume high amounts of seawater to take in enough sodium chloride to avoid dehydration, while freshwater fish excrete dilute urine to avoid being overhydrated.    In addition to these basic survival strategies in water, fish rely on chemistry to cooperate with each other. At night, when lack of light becomes a problem, flashlight fish use bioluminescence to maintain their school structure in the dark. On the other side, water can easily disperse chemical particles. The fish’s olfactory and gustatory systems allow them to communicate, mate, and alert each other by releasing different pheromones.   Since fish rely heavily on their aquatic environment to survive, changes in the water compositions and the water pH can have a great impact on the health of individual fish, their behaviors and affect the shoal’s formation and cohesiveness.    Fish use a variety of chemical strategies and adaptations to ensure they survive and thrive in diverse waters. Any environmental change will not only impact the land and oceans but also has the potential to disrupt the balance that fish and their shoals maintain within their ecosystem, negatively affecting their survival. Given the complex and interconnected nature of the chemical strategies fish employ for survival, further research is needed to determine the future sustainability of fish and other aquatic  animals  under the growing uncertainties and threats of climate change.
