Euler Who? The Original Optimizers: Heterocephalus glaber and Their Algorithmic Society  Clayton Dame, David Bensemana, Lana Habhab Abstract Owing to its eusocial organization, the naked mole rat emerges as a model species exemplifying principle of biological  optimization . The design solutions associated with this behavior seamlessly translate into algorithmic capabilities: the positive feedback of workers achieving appropriate fitness to become breeders; the fittest breeders mating with the queen; the negative feedback of breeders getting demoted in the caste to become workers; the queen optimizing for the best possible breeder to mate with; and the cooperation and competition to determine rank in the colony which creates multiple interactions between males. These eusocial dynamics extend beyond their biological roots to address complex mathematical challenges. This paper examines the development and application of the naked mole rat Algorithm as a graph-theory-inspired optimization tool, rooted in these cooperative behaviors. It further explores the algorithm’s performance in unimodal, multimodal and fixed functions highlighting its versatility and effectiveness. Furthermore, compared with other nature-inspired algorithms, the naked mole Rat Algorithm offers unique strengths in achieving decentralized, scalable, and efficient solutions. Thus, through the lens of the naked mole rat algorithm and its efficiency in finding optimal solutions in a timely manner, this paper concludes that the representation of the eusocial caste system as an algorithm captures both the abilities and limitations of the colony’s mate optimization capabilities.  Introduction The naked mole rat ( Heterocephalus glaber ) inhabits complex, extensive underground tunnel systems in the arid regions of East Africa. These tunnels serve multiple functions beyond just travel pathways; they are carefully constructed to optimize temperature control, predator defense, and resource management (Sherman, Jarvis, & Alexander, 1991). Moreover, the naked mole rat is among the few vertebrates that exhibit eusociality, a complex social organization usually found among some insects like bees and ants (Jarvis, 1981). It exhibits a highly structured and rigid social hierarchy that supports its eusocial system, and this distinguishes it as one of the few mammals to show this level of social complexity. This form of social structure is characterized by a division of labor into reproductive and non-reproductive groups, the cooperative care of offspring, and a clear hierarchy that includes a dominant breeding pair (Salgotra & Singh, 2019).   In the case of the naked mole rat, the colony is typically led by a single breeding female, known as the queen (Salgotra & Singh, 2019). She is the only female in the colony that breeds and produces offspring, and she maintains her dominance through aggressive behaviors towards other females, effectively suppressing their reproductive capabilities (Hart  et al ., 2022). Beneath the queen are a few selected breeding males, who are allowed to mate with her. In naked mole rat colonies, most members are non-reproductive workers that are divided into castes based on their roles and tasks like  foraging  for food, defending the colony, supporting the tunnels, and caring for the queen’s offspring (Sherman, Jarvis, & Alexander, 1991).  The structure of the colony serves as a good model for studying cooperative and adaptive behaviors in living systems (Spinks  et al ., 2000). These complex social structures are supported by an efficient and adaptive caste system that can transition workers to breeders when necessary. The differentiation and specialization within these roles are crucial for the colony’s survival, since they ensure efficient resource utilization, defense against predators, and overall stability (Clarke & Faulkes, 1997). The dynamic transition of roles within the colony where non-reproductive workers can become breeders occurs when the queen dies or when there is a shift in the colony’s needs. Conversely, reproductive roles can be relinquished to ensure optimal task allocation and resource management within the colony (Spinks  et al ., 2000).   The queen’s role can be seen as a strategy to maximize the colony’s reproductive output, while the workers’ non-reproductive status minimizes internal conflict over breeding opportunities. The transition between roles in the naked mole rat colony is a key aspect of its  social behavior  and adaptability. When the queen dies and the colony faces internal pressures, non-reproductive females can transition to become new breeders, illustrating a flexibility in the naked mole rat’s rigid social order. As mentioned previously, this transition is accompanied by intensive competition among females, with the emergence of a new queen marked by shifts in aggressive behavior and social dominance (Hart  et al ., 2022). This competition and aggression over breeding rights is minimized due to the presence of the structured social hierarchy. On the other hand, most males are non-aggressive towards breeding opportunities as the queen selectively mates with a few males who are capable of  reproduction  (Clarke & Faulkes, 1997). This system of defined roles and controlled reproduction explains how conflict is minimized and how colony harmony is maintained.  Another interesting aspect of the naked mole rat’s social behavior is related to their  communication  system. The naked mole rat exhibits a complex vocal repertoire, in which distinct vocalizes are used for different purposes, including social bonding, recognition of colony members, and alerting others to threats (Barker  et al ., 2021). Each colony has its own dialect that helps the colony members to distinguish its members from others. This shows that they can recognize and protect themselves against external threats. This communication system not only supports efficient coordination but also helps maintain the rigid social hierarchy, as interactions with the queen and higher-ranking members are often marked by specific behaviors and vocal cues. Communication extends beyond just vocalizations since the naked mole rat depends on other aspects, such as tactile cues and scent marking with their intricate tunnel systems to convey information related to territory boundaries, food availability, and reproductive status (Brett, 1991).  The naked mole rat also has remarkable physiological adaptations that support their lifestyle and contribute to its colony’s resilience. It has a highly efficient metabolism that allows it to thrive in hypoxic environments (Park  et al ., 2017). This metabolic adaptation ensures that all members, regardless of their caste, can perform their tasks even under conditions such as limited oxygen availability. These physiological traits contribute to the longevity and stability of the colony, reinforcing the strict division of labor and ensuring that the queen’s reproductive output is maximized. This combination of behavioral, communicative, and physiological adaptations allows naked mole rat colonies to function as highly organized and efficient units that can adapt to a wide range of environmental and social pressures.    The cooperative and adaptive behaviors of the naked mole rat, including efficient task allocation, role transitions, and environmental responsiveness, makes it an excellent model for the development of computational algorithms due to its ability to optimize complex systems and adapt to changing conditions. These behaviours lend themselves to the creation of optimization algorithms inspired by natural processes (Salgotra & Singh, 2019).  Graph Theory Preface Before exploring the intricacies of graph theory and the significance of this field of mathematics, it is important to understand its historical context. In 1735, Leonhard Euler sought to solve the Königsberg bridge problem. This problem posed a deceptively simple question: Is it possible to walk through the city of Königsberg, crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once? (Editors of www.encyclopediabritannica, 2024).   
 Fig. 1 : The map of Königsberg and its 7 bridges. The challenge was as follows: visitors would attempt to explore the city of Königsberg whilst only crossing each of the 7 bridges once.  Euler’s proved this feat was impossible with a rudimentary form of graph theory, in which he represented each landmass as a node and each bridge as an edge and set mathematical constraints according to this challenge. This elegant solution to the optimization problem that stumped mathematicians for many years thus laid the foundation for a novel field of mathematics. As this field evolved, it became integral to various disciplines, including computer science, biology, and social network  analysis . These algorithms are often inspired by biological processes, which have the intrinsic ability to solve complex optimization challenges. These nature-inspired algorithms rely on principles of cooperation, adaptation, and efficiency, in which they mimic phenomena like foraging, flocking behavior, and genetic  evolution . However, to fully appreciate the elegance and utility of these algorithms, the jargon surrounding this field of mathematics must be explored.  Basic graph theory terminology   Graph theory is defined as the branch of mathematics and computer science that studies the relationships between objects connected by edges. The objects can be seen as individual entities or points on a graph and are represented by vertices or nodes. The connections between nodes are called edges or links. These edges can be used to show the relationships between different nodes, as seen in Figure 2 below (Diestel, 2018).  
 Fig. 2  Pictorial representation of vertices and edges to start the reader’s intuition on graph theory. The vertices are represented by the circled letters and the edges are represented by the lines connecting these circles (Rote, 2023).  Directed versus undirected graphs are another important concept to understand. In an undirected graph, edges have no direction, which means that the connections between nodes are bidirectional. In contrast, a directed graph features edges with a defined direction, called arcs, which represent one-way connections. These graphs are crucial for modeling directional processes like resource flow or information transfer. The distinction is illustrated in Figure 3 below (Diestel, 2018).  
 Fig. 3  Pictorial representation of directed versus undirected graphs. Notice that directed graphs have arrows which indicate the direction of flow whereas undirected graphs do not have any directionality in their edges ( Editors of  https://cs226fa21.github.io/notes/26-graph/step05.html , 2024) .  Another similar concept can be seen in the difference between weighted and unweighted graphs. Unweighted graphs are graphs in which all edges are treated as equal, without any preference or cost associated with a specific edge. Weighted graphs are graphs where each edge has an associated numerical value or weight: the weight represents costs, distances, or other metrics. The weight placed on a certain connection is important for modeling real-world scenarios like transportation networks or communication systems, as it specifies the relative favorability or efficiency of certain routes over others (Diestel, 2018). The concepts of weight and directionality can be combined to represent complex systems, as seen in figure 4 below.  
 Fig. 4  This graph shows the difference between weighted and unweighted graph while also building on the previous concepts on directionality. On the left, notice the numerical values, or weights, placed on each edge. On the right, notice that the edges do not have a specific weight associated with them, which means that any edge can be taken without a bias (Editors of  https://afteracademy.com,  2020).  Characteristics of a graph  Now that the basic kinds of graphs have been established, there are certain characteristics used to describe graphs, which are important to develop a sense of intuition with graph theory. The degree of a node is described as the number of edges that are connected to a specific node. A node with a large degree has many connections to other nodes. For example, in Figure 2, node B has a degree of 3 since it has three incident edges.   The path is the sequence of nodes where each consecutive pair is connected by an edge. To put this concept into context, the Königsberg bridge problem is set to find a path connecting all 7 nodes where each node is passed once. Additionally, a cycle is a specific type of path that starts and ends at the same node without repeating any edges or vertices. Thus, all cycles are paths, but not all paths are cycles. The difference between a path and a cycle can be understood through a simple analogy: walking your dog to your friend’s house represents a path, as it has a clear start and endpoint, whereas walking your dog around the block represents a cycle, as it begins and ends at the same point (Diestel, 2018).  The final term to understand is the distinction between connected and disconnected graphs, in which connected graphs have paths connecting all nodes whereas disconnected graphs do not possess this characteristic. This difference can be seen in Figure 5 below (Diestel, 2018).  
 Fig. 5  The difference between connected and undirected graphs. Notice the difference in connected nodes between these two graphs. On the left, notice the connected graph where all the vertices are connected by edges. On the right, notice the disconnected graph where the right-most vertex is not connected to the rest of the graph by an edge (Rote, 2023).  Optimization in graph structures   It is very easy to get lost in the graph theory jargon and lose sight of the big picture. It is important to remember the goal of an algorithm, which is to solve an allotted problem. Now that a basic understanding of the framework of this theory was established, the more interesting aspects that this field of mathematics unlocks can be explored.   Optimization solutions find the most efficient solution to a problem, such as the shortest path between two nodes, by leveraging the structural relationships and characteristics of the specific graph. Just like in calculus, the best overall solution is referred to as a global optimum (maximum or minimum), as seen in figure 6. Accordingly, the local optimum refers to a solution that is better than its immediate neighbours but may not be the best overall solution.    
 Fig. 6  This graph shows the difference between a local maximum and global maximum in a 3-dimensional function. This representation can be extended to a local optimum versus a global maximum (Luo, 2022).  However, algorithms are not without limitations and often face challenges. One such challenge is premature convergence, in which the algorithm quickly settles on a suboptimal solution. These suboptimal solutions can cause the algorithm to stagnate and cease its progression, as it gets stuck oscillating around a suboptimal solution space. Thus, these challenges highlight the importance of balance in an algorithm: it must maintain sufficient exploration, which is the algorithm’s active search for new areas of the solution space, while ensuring effective exploitation, in which the algorithm refines already-known optimal solutions (Gentile  et al ., 2021).  Dynamic interactions help algorithms explore solutions effectively and adapt to complex problems. These interactions involve repulsion and attraction, which allow an algorithm to balance its exploration and exploitation. Attraction draws solutions closer for refinement, while repulsion spreads them apart to explore diverse regions to ultimately prevent premature convergence. Fluctuations, which are random variations or disturbances, introduce a sense of randomness to the algorithm. This randomness allows algorithms to escape local optima by enabling the exploration of alternative solutions. Multiple interactions, which refer to the simultaneous influence of various factors, create a dynamic landscape in an algorithm. This landscape creates adaptability and enables algorithms to respond to a problem’s complexity while it adapts its search strategy (Gentile  et al ., 2021).   Nature-inspired algorithms mimic biological processes to maintain diversity, escape local optima, and dynamically adjust parameters. These changes to the structure of a typical algorithm led to more robust optimization strategies. One advantage of these algorithms is their initialization techniques, in which they ensure diverse starting points and introduce random perturbations to further enhance their ability to achieve global optimization (Gentile  et al ., 2021). Through nature’s inspiration, these algorithms achieve solutions that closely emulate the efficiency found in natural systems.  Swarm-inspired algorithms: a bridge to the naked mole rat algorithm  Swarm-inspired algorithms are a subset of nature-inspired optimization techniques that model the collective behavior of decentralized systems. These algorithms excel at solving complex optimization problems by mimicking self-organization and cooperative behavior found in biological phenomena such as ant foraging and bird flocking.   Central to swarm algorithms is the concept of fitness values, which measure the quality of a solution. Fitness is an important concept that guides the balance between exploration and exploitation in SWARM algorithms. Successful algorithms can dynamically adapt this balance, as they leverage the collective intelligence of agents to escape local optima and converge on the global optimum.  By incorporating mechanisms such as repulsion, attraction and fluctuations, Swarm algorithms are particularly well-suited to addressing challenges like premature convergence and stagnation, which often arise in traditional optimization methods (Gupta, 2021).  The naked mole rat algorithm  The algorithmic behaviour of the naked mole rat colony  The naked mole rat colony exhibits self-organization and division of labor, which is characteristic of a swarm inspired algorithm.  Self-organization can be subdivided into positive and negative feedback, fluctuations, and multiple interactions. In the context of eusocial behavior, positive feedback is the increase in probability of males mating with the queen. The magnitude of the probability increases as workers become breeders and eventually mating with the queen.  Negative feedback is the decrease in probability of males mating with the queen. If a breeder is not fit to breed, he is demoted to the worker caste: this fall in the hierarchy can be recognized as negative feedback.  Fluctuations in the colony are demonstrated by both the randomness of the male with the highest initial probability of mating and the choice of the queen in the colony. Multiple interactions are displayed by the cooperation among the colony.  As a result of the cooperation, the naked mole rat colony displays a complex division of labor.  By having members of the colony perform specialized tasks, all tasks can be simultaneously performed, which is more beneficial than unspecialized members performing tasks sequentially.  This drastically improves the efficiency of the colony (Salgotra and Singh,2019).  
 Fig. 7  The naked mole rat caste system.  This figure demonstrates the movements within the caste system to find the most optimal mate for the queen.  This system can be modeled as an algorithm to solve optimization problems. The colony modelled as an algorithm  In 2019, Solgota and Singh proposed a naked mole rat algorithm that focuses specifically on the mating  patterns  of the naked mole rat colony, built upon four rules inspired by these mating patterns.  The proposed algorithm uses a colony with a population of 50. This creates a connected graph with 50 different vertices. A female queen divides the population among breeders and workers, with no overlap between the roles of breeders and workers. It should be noted that the queen is identified as the vertex with the highest degree. The edges connecting workers to the queen are assigned higher weights than those connecting breeders to the queen to reflect their differing probabilities of interaction. In this algorithm, edge weight directly influences the likelihood of traversing a solution, with higher weights decreasing the probability of a path being taken. The colony structure is dynamic: the best-performing workers are promoted to breeders, while underperforming breeders are demoted to workers, which leads to continuous updates in edge weights as the algorithm progresses. Ultimately, the top-performing breeders are selected to mate with the queen: this makes the graph unidirectional, with all edges converging toward the queen. This iterative process mimics optimization, as the algorithm seeks to identify the “best breeder,” or the optimal solution to the problem it addresses.   The algorithm begins by analyzing the male population and dividing members into the worker caste and breeder caste.  The fitness of the breeders and workers is continuously reassessed, and the weights of the different edges are continuously updated.  The worker’s fitness is constantly artificially improving, to increase the probability that they will become a breeder. In terms of the graph, the edge weights between workers and the queen are artificially improved to increase the likelihood of workers being promoted to breeders. On the other hand, the breeders’ fitness is determined by their probability of mating with the queen.  If a breeder’s probability falls below a certain threshold, they are demoted to the worker caste: this threshold dictates whether a vertex is associated with workers or breeders and evolves throughout the algorithm. The fittest workers then replace demoted breeders to maintain a dynamic cycle of reassessment and optimization (Salgotra and Singh, 2019).    The phases of the algorithm   The algorithm contains three distinct phases: initialization, worker, and breeder. In initialization, the population of the naked mole rats is uniformly distributed, and each member is defined as a vector (1,2…n). The number of dimensions of the vector is determined by the number of variables or parameters present in the problem.  The initialization of each naked mole rat can be described by the following equation.          The variables can be defined by the following: i ϵ [1,2,…n], j ϵ [1,2,…n] where NMR i,j  is the i th  solution in the j th  dimension, NMR min,j  and NMR max,j  are the lower and upper bounds of the problem and  U (0,1) is a random number responsible for the fluctuations within the algorithm.  Upon initialization, the objective function is evaluated, and its initial fitness is calculated. Breeders and workers are identified depending on an individual’s relative fitness.  The breeder with the best fitness is recognized as the best initial solution.    The next phase, referred to as the worker phase, can then begin.  In this phase, the workers’ fitness gradually improves as a factor of the workers’ experience, as well as new local information. If the experience and local information can provide the members with better fitness, the old solution is discarded and the new solution is integrated.  This mechanism is determined by the following equation:          The variables can be defined by the following:   is the i th  worker in the t th  interaction whereas   is the new solution. Furthermore,   and   are two random solutions chosen from the pool of workers, and λ is a uniform distribution from [0,1].    Finally, the breeder phase determines the final and most optimal solution.  The breeders update themselves in a similar fashion.  However, in conjunction with fitness, the breeders are sorted on their breeding probability with respect to the best solution. Breeding probability is determined by a random number in [0,1].  If the fitness of the breeder is too low, they will be pushed back down to the worker caste.  These mechanisms are determined by the following equation.          The variables can be defined by the following:   is the breeder i in the t th  iteration; λ is a factor that controls mating frequency, which helps define the new breeder  .  Initially, the breeding probability (bp) is set at 0.5. If U (0,1) is greater than the bp, the breeder phase is performed.  The algorithm will cycle through these phases in multiple iterations until the best solution is found.  Thus, the naked mole rat Algorithm leverages graph theory concepts to represent the colony as a directed graph where vertices signify individuals, and weighted edges reflect dynamic relationships. This algorithm then employs mathematical equations to model fluctuations in edge weights, which simulate optimization and hierarchical changes within the colony (Salgotra and Singh, 2019).  Performance of the algorithm  Algorithm performance is generally evaluated by its ability to find optimal solutions efficiently and consistently across various test scenarios. To test the performance of the naked mole rat algorithm, Salgota and Singh used a twofold approach. The researchers evaluated the algorithm’s performance on test problems by comparing its results to those of standard algorithms and conducting a rank-sum test to identify statistically significant differences. The standard algorithms the researchers used were the differential evolution algorithm, the firefly algorithm, the flower  pollination  algorithm, and the bat algorithm.  They used a variety of test problems ranging from unimodal, multimodal, and fixed dimension functions.  The unimodal functions have no local solution and only contain a single global solution.  Unimodal functions are helpful to determine convergence rate, since there is no risk of the algorithm stagnating at a local minimum.  The multimodal functions had many local minima, which allows the researchers to determine the algorithm’s ability to avoid local minima and show the algorithm’s balance between exploration and exploitation. The fixed dimension functions maintain a consistent number of dimensions, which tests the algorithms consistency in finding optimal solutions.    To evaluate the naked mole rat algorithm’s rate of convergence, nine unimodal functions were tested: one of which was the Tablet function, which can be seen below.          The naked mole rat algorithm performed very well, with a final fitness value of 2.22 x 10 -9 . Furthermore, it converged to its solution much faster than the other algorithms, as seen in Figure 8.  
 Fig. 8  Results from the Tablet function test of the naked mole rat (NMR), differential evolution (DE), firefly (FA), flower pollination (FPA), and the bat (BA) algorithms.  A lower fitness value signifies a more optimal solution. As illustrated by the graph, the NMR algorithm demonstrated faster convergence toward the optimal solution compared to the other algorithms, highlighting its superior optimization efficiency. Of the eight other unimodal tests done, the naked mole rat algorithm showed the fastest convergence rate in seven: it should be noted that it was outperformed by all the other algorithms in only one of the functions tested. Thus, these results demonstrate that the naked mole rat algorithm possesses a great convergence rate in optimization problems.   In terms of multimodal tests, one of the functions tested was the Ackley function, seen in the equation below.          The simulation of the algorithm applied to the Ackley function showed that the naked mole rat algorithm was the only one to find an optimal solution, as seen in figures 9 and 10.  The fitness value, in which lower values denote more optimal solution, was only 3.76×10 -12 , whereas the next best algorithm, being the firefly algorithm, was 2.82×10 -2 . Of the twelve multimodal functions tested, the naked mole rat algorithm achieved the best performance in nine and demonstrated comparable results in the remaining three. This outstanding performance in the multimodal tests shows that the naked mole rat algorithm’s ability to effectively avoid local minimum.   
 Fig. 9  Results of the Ackley function test of the naked mole rat (NMR), differential evolution (DE), firefly (FA), flower pollination (FPA), and bat (BA) algorithms.  Best, worst and mean signify the associated fitness values, in which a lower fitness value identifying a more optimal solution.  
 Fig. 10  Results of the naked mole rat (NMR), differential evolution (DE), firefly (FA), flower pollination (FPA), and the bat (BA) algorithms solving the Ackley function.  It can be seen thet the naked mole rat algorithm found the most opitimal solution in much less iterations than the other algorithms.  The researchers further evaluated the algorithms using five distinct fixed-dimension tests. These tests assess an algorithm’s ability to consistently achieve the same optimal solution, with a lower standard deviation indicating superior performance. Among the fixed-dimension functions tested was the Six Hump Camel function, where the naked mole rat algorithm exhibited the best performance, where it achieved the lowest standard deviation of 0.0201, as shown in Figure 11.  
 Fig. 11  Results of the Six Hump Camel function test of the naked mole rat (NMR), differential evolution (DE), firefly (FA), flower pollination (FPA), and bat (BA) algorithms.  Here, the lowest standard deviation represents the best performance.   Nevertheless, the naked mole rat algorithm was outperformed in three of the fixed dimension functions while showing comparable results in one.  These results demonstrate that the naked mole rat algorithm may have limitations in finding consistent optimization solutions to the same function (Salgotra and Singh, 2019).   Discussion Multiple determinants of the algorithm’s performance were found using a multitude of tests: these tests included unimodal, multimodal, and fixed dimension functions. Compared to standard algorithms, the naked mole rat algorithm performed very well in the unimodal and multimodal functions but was outperformed in the fixed dimension functions. High performance in unimodal and multimodal functions showed that the algorithm can find optimal solutions while avoiding local optima.  However, its inadequate performance in fixed dimension functions showed that it is limited in its ability to repeatedly find the same optimal solution. In other words, this algorithm does not excel in its exploitation.  These abilities and limitations of the naked mole rat algorithm are consistent with the behavior of the naked mole rat colony.  The algorithm’s ability to consistently identify an optimal solution mirrors the naked mole rat colony’s capacity to select the most suitable breeder for the queen. Its effective avoidance of local optima is reflected by the colony’s dynamic adjustment of hierarchy within the caste system.  Finally, the limitation in finding the same solution is also consistent with the eusocial caste system of the colony. The colony does not seek to find the single fittest breeder; rather, it prioritizes identifying a breeder that is sufficiently fit to breed with the queen in a timely manner.    Conclusion This paper explores the naked mole rat algorithm as a representation for the eusocial behavior of the naked mole rat colonies, specifically in their ability to identify a highly suitable mate for the queen. It mimics the process of workers competing to become breeders and subsequently competing to mate with the queen. By mimicking this process, the algorithm finds the “best suiting male” to find an optimal solution to the problem. The naked mole rat algorithm was shown to be very effective at finding optimal solutions compared to other nature inspired algorithms. Thus, it can be concluded that the eusocial behavior of this   species is a design solution to effectively find a suitable mate for the queen.  These design solutions include the hierarchical shifts of males depending on their fitness, and the queen’s choice for the best possible breeder to mate with.   The naked mole rat algorithm provides a deeper understanding of the behavior and purpose of the naked mole rat’s social hierarchy. Thus, by developing nature-inspired algorithms, we uncover the intricate connections between complex mathematics and biology to showcase how evolutionary pressures drive the pursuit of optimal solutions.

title: From Feathers to Formations: A Mathematical Analysis of Starling Murmurations
authors: Maeve Ding, Matt Levasseur, Nicole Shen, Rachael Zhang
abstract: This paper explores the mathematical properties and relationships at play within bird murmurations. Studying the characteristic formation patterns of murmurations reveals practical methods of predator evasion. The rapid amplification of propagating dynamic signals within the murmurations ensures a quick rate of information transmission and therefore greater odds of survival. Birds’ general awareness of the group’s dynamics and formation patterns within the murmuration informs subsequent movements to improve overall coordination. Furthermore, modelling murmurations as a network of interconnected information-processing nodes reveals a linear behavioral correlation model between birds within the murmuration. Noise within the system, individual behavioral fluctuations, is hypothesized to be an essential component of biological networks. Finally, the geometrical properties of avian physiology reflect the complex mechanisms governing biological development and growth.

From Feathers to Formations: A Mathematical Analysis of Starling Murmurations  Maeve Ding, Matt Levasseur, Nicole Shen, Rachael Zhang Abstract This paper explores the mathematical properties and relationships at play within bird murmurations. Studying the characteristic formation patterns of murmurations reveals practical methods of predator evasion. The rapid amplification of propagating dynamic signals within the murmurations ensures a quick rate of information transmission and therefore greater odds of survival. Birds’ general awareness of the group’s dynamics and formation patterns within the murmuration informs subsequent movements to improve overall coordination. Furthermore, modelling murmurations as a network of interconnected information-processing nodes reveals a linear behavioral correlation model between birds within the murmuration. Noise within the system, individual behavioral fluctuations, is hypothesized to be an essential component of biological networks. Finally, the geometrical properties of avian physiology reflect the complex mechanisms governing biological development and growth. Introduction Birds are renowned for their remarkable diversity of form and behavior. This diversity is remarkably displayed by the formation of murmurations: large assemblies of coordinated birds driven by predator evasion (Fig. 1). Relatedly, their features on an individual level have been refined through  evolution  to serve essential ecological functions: from the intricate patterns in feather  geometry  that enhance  flight  to the structural complexities of nests that provide rigid shelter for offspring. This essay explores the fascinating dimensions of avian biology, examining how features such as egg and  beak  geometry as well as flock dynamics contribute to the adaptability and efficiency of bird species. Using mathematical models, we analyze the wave-like patterns of flocks and their coordinated responses to threats. Scale-free correlations observed in flock movements further reveal the emergent order in bird movements, suggesting that simple individual actions can lead to complex, ordered group dynamics. The common denominator of all adaptations within bird species is the enhancement of survival and the minimizing of costly metabolic processes. This paper explores how collective behaviour is merely another instance of birds’ continuous efforts at behavioral and physiological optimization.    
 Fig. 1. European starling murmuration. (Solkær, 2022)  Scale-Free Correlations  Collective Animal Behaviour  The sharing of information within a network containing a set number of nodes can be accomplished in a variety of ways. A network node consists of a branch in a network which processes data and relays it to neighbouring nodes. The rules which govern the transfer of information in a network are referred to as a topology. Topology hence relates the diverse ways in which nodes are connected.    Several topologies can govern the transfer of information in a network (Cavagna  et al ., 2010). A hierarchical architecture is one in which adjacent nodes are not mutually interconnected but are instead all connected to a single node which governs the behaviour of the group. Contrastingly, distributed and scale-free topologies refer to networks wherein adjacent nodes interact to varying degrees: nodes are solely connected to their direct neighbours in a distributed network, whereas there is a greater variety of connections in the network in a scale-free model. It follows, especially in the study of collective animal behaviour, that groups of coordinated  animals  are analogous in function to networks. Studying the topologies which govern such animal networks is fundamental to understanding the physiological mechanisms underlying collective animal behaviours and gaining insight on the evolutionary advantage of such behaviours.   Starling murmurations are formed because of positive chemical feedback loops and are maintained by each individual starling closely monitoring the spatial and temporal distributions (i.e. position and velocity) of its six or seven closest neighbours (Vallee, 2021). The latter defines the interactions between adjacent nodes in the so-called murmuration network: how does the whole network behave? The collective animal behaviour manifested in starlings stems from a self-organizing process as opposed to a centralized one (Cavagna  et al ., 2010). Local interactions between starlings, namely between neighbours within the murmuration, are reflected throughout the entire network. Thus, the topology of the starling murmuration network is scale-free: there exists a correlation between individuals’ behaviour within the group regardless of the distance separating them.   Additionally, the correlation length is the spatial span of the correlated nodes in the network (i.e. nodes communicating either directly or indirectly). This correlation length can be much greater than the range of interaction between adjacent nodes and is influenced by the level of noise within the system. In any case, noise within the network corresponds to external disruptions or internal failures which corrupt the signal being relayed. In a scale-free network, the correlation length corresponds to defined domains of nodes which observe positive (reinforcing) correlations. As all nodes are interconnected in a scale-free network, domains extending past the correlation length of a particular domain are anticorrelated, carrying out the ‘inverse’ or ‘opposite’ behaviour.   Mathematical Analysis and Study of Scale-Free Correlations  In their study, Cavagna and colleagues monitored starling ( Sturnus sturnidae ) murmurations during a period of two years over a roosting site in Rome, Italy (Cavagna  et al ., 2010). Through numerical  analysis , they extracted the spatial distribution as well as the velocities of starlings within each murmuration to compare their scale-free network model to actual data. Murmuring flocks of as little as 122 individuals and as large as 4,268 individuals were observed.    A flock’s cohesion, namely its degree of order, is represented by the polarizability, which is given by Equation 1.    (1)       denotes the number of starlings and   denotes the velocity of each starling within the murmuration. Equation 1 consists of the sum of all velocity unit vectors divided by the number of starlings within the murmuration and its values range between 0 and 1. Equation 1 will yield zero if the unit vectors all point in different directions and will yield values equal or near 1 if there is a strong correlation between the velocities of individuals within the flock. Similarly, the difference between the starling’s velocity within the murmuration and the net velocity of the starling murmuration (starling’s velocity in the murmuration reference frame) is given by Equation 2.    (2)      Where   denotes the relative velocity vector. By construction,   is zero. Indeed, the net velocity of the starlings in the murmuration’s reference frame must be zero because the net velocity of all starlings in the regular reference frame corresponds to the murmuration’s velocity. From their collected data, Cavagna  et al . found that the average polarizability of the twenty-four observed flocks was 0.96±0.03. Furthermore, they were able to observe the presence of strongly correlated domains through their data within a network of strongly correlated individuals (Fig. 2). This reflects the influence of local interactions on the group’s culminating behaviour.

B) Scaled relative velocity vector map of the starling with respect to the frame of reference of the murmuration, clearly displaying two strongly correlated domains in the far-upper extremities. C) Probability distribution of the norm of the velocity vectors (A) and their fluctuations (B). Norm of the velocity fluctuations is on average one degree of magnitude smaller than that of the velocities (Cavagna  et al ., 2010).  Another parameter used to characterize the degree of cohesion within the flock is the correlation function. This function evaluates the average scalar product between velocity fluctuation vectors of starlings within a confined radius. This is accomplished with the Dirac 𝛿-function, which goes to infinity at zero and has a value of zero everywhere else. The Dirac 𝛿-function ‘selects’ a pair of birds at distance r to compute the scalar product of their velocity fluctuations. The correlation function is expressed as follows:   (3)      Where   normalizes the function to a value of 1 at r = 0, and   is the scalar product in three dimensions. The correlation function will evaluate the span of a correlation domain. It follows from the properties of the scalar product that the correlation function will yield larger values (either negative or positive) when the degree of correlation between velocity fluctuations is very high. Likewise, it will return a value of zero when there is no net correlation within a group. Figure 3A reveals the correlation between starlings’ behaviour within a murmuration. At small distances, and up to the correlation length 𝜉, starlings will mutually reinforce one another’s behaviours: they carry out similar means of correcting their velocities to correspond with the group. Relatedly, starlings at a greater distance than the correlation length correct their behaviours oppositely. The presence of correlation and anticorrelation domains is a trivial consequence of setting the sum of all velocity fluctuations to zero. However, the presence of a single correlation domain and a single anticorrelation domain is not trivial. This reflects an inherent mechanism of coordination within murmurations to maintain cohesion. Indeed, there are multiple ways by which a map of vectors can be arranged to sum to zero. Realistically, however, the presence of two domains merely reflects how murmurations are constantly rotating. Both domains correcting velocity in opposite directions is akin to a force couple: two opposite forces create innate torque which will generate constant rotation in space.  
 
 
 Fig. 3.  On the right, the value of the correlation function with respect to the distance separating starling pairs. 𝜉 is the correlation length. On the left, the value of the correlation length as a function on the size of the flock. The correlation length is linearly correlated to the flock size L (Cavagna  et al ., 2010).    Also obtained from experimental data, Figure 3B plots the correlation length, namely 𝐶(𝑟=𝜉) = 0, as a function of flock size. Directly, one can observe that its magnitude is not fixed to some set number of birds or a particular distance: rather, it is linearly scaled with the size of the flock. Linear scaling of the span of correlation between nodes in a network directly corresponds to a scale-free topology. Relatedly, the actual degree of correlation between starlings can be interpreted conceptually through the following equation:   (4)      Equation 4 expresses the degree of correlation between starlings as a scaled power-law. That is, the correlation is proportional at some given power to the actual distance r as well as the relative distance with respect to the size of the flock. Here, 𝑓(𝑥) is a scaling function which consists of the dimensionless relation between the actual distance and the flock size. Hence, as presented in Figure 3, the correlation function, with respect to the ratio of distance and flock size, is also a linear relation. Its derivative is given by Equation 5 and is also plotted in Figure 4. Furthermore, the value of the correlation function at large distances within the flock, the limit of the distance as it approaches infinity, is given by Equation 6.   (5)       (6)        As inferred from Equation 5, the value of 𝛾 is the determining factor as regard the degree at which starlings separated by some distance will be correlated. The greater its value, the more negative the slope of the correlation function will be at a smaller distance between starlings within the flock, indicating a rapid and complete loss of correlation. Contrastingly, at small values of 𝛾, the derivative of the correlation function approaches a constant value of negative one, and its value asymptotically approaches one at very large distances. Cavagna and colleagues concluded, from Figure 4 and with Equation 5, that the average value of 𝛾 amongst all observed starling murmurations was 𝛾 = 0.19±0.08, which effectively corresponds to no decay of correlation, regardless of the murmuration’s span. It is thus a matter of fact that two birds within a 100 m murmuration and separated by 10 m are as strongly correlated as two birds separated by 100 m in a murmuration spanning 1 km.   
 Fig. 4.  The correlation function with respect to the dimensionless quantity  . Its value decreases at an approximately constant rate, as presented in the sub-plot of slope with respect to correlation length (Cavagna  et al ., 2010).  The mechanisms enabling scale-free correlations in animal systems are well-documented. Computer algorithms, based on a simple set of rules, can mimic the murmuring behaviours of birds through velocity vectors within a vector field; individual vector nodes are instructed to adjust their alignment and speed based on that of neighbouring vector nodes which are initially triggered stochastically. Rather, the perplexing nature of bird murmurations relates to the inevitable presence of noise within any system spanning large distances. Noise in bird murmurations is brought forth by slight alignment errors on an individual basis, which corrupts the communication signal. Naturally, it might be hypothesized that minimizing noise within the network would induce higher order and correlation within the system. However, a certain level of noise within a biological-based network such as this one is critical to amplify signals throughout the system. Decreasing the noise beyond a certain threshold within the murmuration would render individuals more insensitive to adjustments in their neighbours’ velocities, a phenomenon referred to as behavioural inertia (Cavagna  et al ., 2010). Hence, achieving a non-decaying correlation occurs by implementing an optimal noise level within the system to both maximize order and correlation. Bird flocks evidently achieve such a critical noise level as informed by the near-zero value of 𝛾, the power law exponent. However, the evolutionary and physiological means underlying this feat are yet to be elucidated.  Collective Movement  Flock Morphology  Starling murmurations tend to maintain constant proportions regardless of flock density, size or composition during regular flocking events. Flocks are thinner on the vertical axis, and wider on the horizontal plane (Ballerini  et al ., 2008). Relatedly, it was found that the thickness   is linearly correlated to the cubic root of the flock’s volume (Fig. 5). These indicate that flock proportions remain constant regardless of volume change (Ballerini  et al ., 2008).  The unit vector   described as “yaw” was found to be nearly parallel to the 𝐺 unit vector ( gravity ), as the cosine of the angle between yaw and  G  bordered the value 1, indicating that the flock’s horizontal plane is parallel to the ground. Thus, normalizing the flocks’ center of mass velocities and calculating their dot product with gravity yield values nearing zero. This evidently suggests that flock velocity during flight is perpendicular to gravity, leading to level flight on the vertical plane (Fig. 6). There is no correlation between the velocity vector and the unit vectors   and  , suggesting that the elongation of a flock is not correlated with its velocity. There are several hypotheses regarding the thin morphology of murmurations on the horizontal plane. First, gravity renders vertical elongations energetically unfavorable. Instead, lateral stretching of the flock is favored. Second, a vertically elongated flock would experience more drag than a laterally stretched flock, reducing the efficiency of collective flight (Ballerini  et al ., 2008). No satisfactory hypothesis could be formulated to explain why the lateral elongation of the   axis is uncorrelated with the direction of velocity. Regardless, maintaining constant flock proportions despite variation in densities and volumes may help preserve consistent flock properties and cohesion over time.   As depicted in Figure 6, flock morphology remains constant during turning sequences.

Thus, the birds at the front of the flock end up on the right side of the flock after the flock enacts a left turn. The angle between   and  G  increases during the turn,   and the angle between   and  V  decreases, indicating that   tilts toward the direction of the turn (Ballerini  et al ., 2008).     Since the flock’s horizontal plane becomes tilted during a turn, the flock experiences drag, like an aircraft “banking” its turns, contributing to its lift. However, flocks are aggregates of individuals and hence do not experience global lifts. It can thus be hypothesized that flocks execute tilted turns to facilitate neighbor detection, as such maneuvers align individuals along a common visual plane.   Topographical Models  Starling murmurations can form intricate and distinct patterns in the sky, ever-changing and evolving into new formations of various densities. Starlings are well-known for their diverse collective escape maneuvers in the face of danger. The level of perceived threat by its members and the flock’s prior configuration are factors which influence a murmuration’s topographical model of escape (Storms  et al ., 2019). A low-level threat corresponds to the absence of a predator in the flock’s vicinity. A medium threat corresponds to the predicament in which a predator is in proximity or following the flock. Finally, a high-level threat describes the situation in which a raptor attacks. Notable escape maneuvers have been identified through starling observation. Wave events are the most eminent and correspond to the propagation of pulses of dark bands throughout the flock.  Wave Events  Wave events facilitate rapid information transfer within the murmuration. The propagation of a repetitive and continually amplifying movement throughout a group allows for information to be transferred at a faster rate than that resulting from the monitoring of the more disorganized dynamics of individual members. This makes wave events effective at decreasing the probability of success of predator attacks. Indeed, a wave’s speed of propagation was found to be on average 13.4 m/s, which is faster than the flock’s speed (10.6 m/s) and comparable to the predator’s speed (11 to 15 m/s), thus making this maneuver a viable and effective technique for predator evasion (Hemelrijk  et al ., 2015). Wave bands are propagated away from the predator, from one end of the flock to the other, as information is derived from the source. Dynamic waves can serve to confuse predators and have been found to occur before or after attacks of medium speed, as well as upon the detection of medium threats. The exact mechanism which underlies the waves of agitation of starlings is still a mystery. Relatedly, models of wave propagation, such as that developed by Hemelrijk  et al ., must further investigate whether these waves of agitation consist of density waves, formed by the modulation of flock density through birds’ acceleration, or orientation waves, which are formed by the shift in orientation of the birds’ bodies when rotating to the side. Starlings’ dark and uniform plumage prevented the identification of the birds’ orientation in the sky due to lack of differences in color between their dorsal and ventral areas, contrary to certain other species. However, the visible change in a bird’s wing surface area from an observer’s point of view could be sufficient means to indicate whether it has rotated to its side (Fig. 7).  
 Fig. 7.  Projected area of simulated bird model when viewed from the side. The maximum projected area corresponds to a 90° rotation, and the minimum projected area corresponds to level flight (Hemelrijk  et al ., 2015).  By observing comparable avian species, the hypothesized rolling motion of starlings during wave events was categorized as either a “zigzag” wherein the bird rolls from one side to the other or a “zig” where the bird rolls solely to one side (Fig. 8).   
 Fig. 8.  Bird trajectory when performing a “zigzag” (A), and a “zig” consisting of rolling to the left and back (B) (Hemelrijk  et al ., 2015).  Interestingly, Hemelrijk and colleagues’ simulation of a falcon attack from the murmuration’s left-side yielded a variety of results:  
 Fig. 9.  Flock response to raptor attack from the left, depicted by images displayed in chronological order. The empirical data is represented by a), all images below result from the model. No wave is formed in b) where the zig is not repeated, nor c) where the maneuver consists of accelerating forward. A double band is propagated throughout the flock when the zigzag is performed in d), as opposed to a single band when the zig is performed in e), which corresponds to empirical data. No wave is formed if the birds are modelled as spheres while performing the zig f) (Hemelrijk  et al ., 2015).   The appropriate wave only results from the performing of “zigs”, demonstrating that wave events should be generated by orientation waves and not density waves, as the simulation fails to produce waves when the birds solely accelerate forward or when the surface area of the birds are modelled to be constant. It was also demonstrated that wave speed is positively correlated with the number of monitored neighbors an individual startling is responsible for since a greater ability to perceive repeating patterns allows for faster information transfer. As the number progresses from 2 to 7 neighbors, the wave speed increased to around 15 m/s, like empirical data which agrees that starlings monitor their six or seven closest neighbors to ensure the flock’s cohesion and synchronization. Wave speed is also positively correlated with distance between neighbors. Since reaction time remains constant, a larger distance between individuals allows for transfer of information across larger distances within the same timeframe. Conversely, wave speed is not correlated with flock size. Relatedly, there are two possible explanations as to why forward accelerations did not produce wave events. First, due to the avoidance of collisions. Indeed, starlings may not desire to approach one another past a certain distance, rendering the formation of a density wave impossible. In fact, the very basis by which murmurations form is the maintaining of a constant distance and relative velocity with one’s neighbours. Density waves would thus violate one of the fundamental rules ensuring flock cohesion. Second, the act of rolling on one’s side can be performed faster than the act of accelerating forward, potentially too slow for the formation of waves (Hemelrijk  et al ., 2015). Changing velocity requires merely the adjustment of the wing’s distribution in space, whereas changing speed requires the expense of additional energy, which birds cannot afford as a regular occurrence.  Blackening  Other notable formations include blackening, where part of the flock or its totality darkens due to compacting. Blackening occurs before or after predator attacks or during situations of medium threat. A flock’s tendency to blacken is independent of predator speed, angle of attack, and repetitiveness of attack, and is the most observed maneuver (Storms  et al ., 2019).   Flash Expansion  Flash expansions are starlings’ escape maneuver of choice in situations of high threat where the raptor attacks at high speeds, from above rather than the side or below (Fig. 10). It consists of the sudden outwards motion of the birds within the murmuration, leading to the expansion of the flock. This maneuver can be performed four to ten times faster than other tactics, naturally conveying its critical importance in situations of immediate danger.   Risks associated with flash expansion consist of a reduction of flock cohesion, and the splitting of the original flock into smaller sub-flocks, which are more susceptible to predator targeting. Hence, to avoid the greater risk of individual predation, starlings tend to resist splitting after flash expansions: 78.3% of observed flash expansions did not result in splits (Storms  et al ., 2019).   
 Fig. 10.  Attacks followed by flash expansion with respect to the hunting approach (Storms  et al ., 2019).   Additional Maneuvers and Formations    Murmurations will regularly perform four other maneuvers in addition to those described above (Fig. 11).  First, vacuole corresponds to the formation of a hole in the flock. This formation is the least observed, making up only 0.6% of all escape methods. Secondly, splits correspond to the splitting of a flock into sub-flocks. The tendency to split is assumed to be correlated with the size of the flock, with larger flocks exhibiting a greater eagerness to split than smaller flocks, as smaller flocks risk aggressive predation. Thirdly, the merging of two sub-flocks, designated by the formation “merge”, allows for a decrease in targeting risk, aiding in survival success. Finally, a thin string of individuals that connect two parts of a flock is called a “cordon”. This pattern is seldom used, making up only 4.4% of the observed patterns of escape. Flock dilution represents the increase of distance between neighbors, resulting in density dilution. In situations of low threat, murmurations adopt a somewhat diluted configuration. The rate of occurrence of various maneuvers is directly correlated to its associated risk and survival benefit (Fig. 12).   
 Fig. 11.  Various methods of collective escape employed by starlings. A are wave events, b and e, are flash expansions, c and f are vacuoles, d and g display cordons (Storms  et al ., 2019).   
 Fig. 12.  The frequency of escape patterns among starlings. Blackening is the most common, followed by wave events, splits, merge, flash expansion, cordon, and vacuole (Storms  et al ., 2019).   The use of certain escape maneuvers was found to be correlated, and often succeeded by others, with higher frequencies of attack corresponding linearly to higher frequencies of escape among starlings (Fig, 13). Falcons prefer consecutive attacks of five second intervals, rendering the combination of escape strategies and a smooth transition even more important. Flash expansions are strongly correlated to attacks, with 25% of attacks leading to their use. Only 21.7% of flash expansions lead to splits, and 83.3% of flash expansions stem from attacks. Splits are strongly correlated with subsequent merging. 54% of flock dilutions lead to blackening, and 28.3% of blackening lead to wave events (Storms  et al ., 2019).

Numbers preceding an arrow represent the ratio of that event that resulted in that secondary event, and numbers succeeding an arrow represent the portion of the secondary event that stems from the primary event (Storms  et al ., 2019).   Physiological Geometry  Feathers  Studying the geometry of a bird’s  feathers  is critical in the analysis of flight optimization. Thus, as explored in our  physics paper , the structure of a feather consists of a central shaft called the rachis, which serves as a “backbone” (Fig. 14). Extending laterally from the rachis are barbs. The barbs then branch into smaller barbules, which interlock via microscopic hooks called barbicels. In conjunction, the arrangement creates a smooth continuous surface, known as the vane, that simultaneously maintains flexibility and rigidity. The feather tapers at the tip, with a broader base. The specific geometry not only streamlines airflow but allows it to be lightweight yet sturdy (Hall 2014). The aerodynamic properties of feathers are governed by the principles of fluid dynamics, which describe how air interacts with the bird’s body during flight. Lift, a critical flight force, can be expressed in terms of air density, velocity, surface area, and the lift coefficient     (10)      Feathers are shaped and angled to maximize   to generate significant lift even at low speeds. Herein lies the relevance of multiple different feather geometries, which are tailored to serve distinct purposes based on morphological attributes.  The  symmetry  of contour feathers, those that cover the bird’s body are critical for balanced flight. They are primarily responsible for streamlining the bird’s overall body and reducing drag (Hall, 2014).  
 Fig. 14:  Parts of the feather (The Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica, 2024).   It is important to note that flight feathers have an asymmetrical structure. In these feathers, for instance the primaries or the secondaries, the vane on the leading edge (side facing direction of flight) is narrower while the trailing edge is broader. This asymmetric structure is crucial for generating efficient lift and thrust. The broader trailing edge provides a larger surface area to capture air and generate lift.  Beaks  The structure and shape of bird beaks, particularly the upper surface and tomium (cutting edge), are essential for understanding their functional morphology and evolution. The study involved the use of random forest models which are suited for complex and non-linear data to explore different response variables. Three types of response variables related to nest-building were tested: a binary indicator of whether the species used a specific material, the primary material category used by each species, and a reduced data for species that only use one material type. The model was built with 5000 decision trees and used predictor variables like beak morphology and body size. The primary nest material prediction had an accuracy up to 59.8% for species that only use one material type. Adding ecological predictors such as diet and material availability further improved accuracy of material use within a range of 63.8% – 96.8%.  (Sheard  et al ., 2023)  To address potential biases and phylogenetic relationships, the phylogenetic generalized linear models (GLMs) were used to make clear phylogenetic dependencies within binary response data. Unlike random forest models, GLMs assume a linear relationship between predictor and response variables. GLMs allowed researchers to interpret how beak traits correlate with nest material use after accounting for evolutionary history. The results were that traits like body size and high flight ability had moderate correlations with nest material choice. However, phylogenetic simulations indicated 66.4-96.9% of the observed material use could contribute to shared evolutionary history. GLMs combining with the random forest models provides a comprehensive view of factors affecting nest material choice. It highlights how both morphology and evolutionary history jointly shape these ecological behaviours (Sheard  et al ., 2023). Egg Geometry  Starlings typically have eggs in a clutch size of 4 to 5. They average 6.4 g and are about 30×21 mm. These specific dimensions contribute to the incredible balance between the function and strength of a bird’s egg (Fig. 16). Eggs are optimized as architectural domes to distribute forces evenly across the shell, protecting them from external forces. The shape also maximizes internal volume for nutrient storage (Sharp, 2023).

While the former three shapes are mathematically well-defined and are represented by quadric equations, no such mathematical equation initially existed for the latter, namely the pyriform. This restricted researchers’ ability to derive a universal egg equation (Narushin  et al ., 2021).

Hence, y defines the level set curve depicting the shape of the egg in 2 dimensions.         L is the egg length, B is the egg’s maximum breadth, and w is the parameter that indicates the distance between two vertical axes corresponding to the maximum breadth and length of the egg (Fig. 18). Additionally, x is an expression in terms of w, B and L (see Appendix). It is important to note that when 𝐿 = 𝐵, the level set curve assumes the shape of a circle. Furthermore, when 𝑤 = 0, y takes the form of an ellipse. The equation was derived with the intent of encompassing all possible egg shapes, thus solving the egg equation problem.

D L/4  is the egg diameter at point L/4 from the pointed end (Narushin  et al ., 2021).  The egg equation’s derivation, and its ensuing mathematical representation of the pyriform egg geometry, can lead to a better understanding of the specific mechanical strengths and advantages of different types of eggs. For instance, pyriform eggs allow for maximum incubation surface against the mother’s brood patch which provides a selective advantage on account of a more energy efficient  thermoregulation  process. Additionally, compared to symmetrical egg shapes, pyriform eggs are less likely to roll away, which consists in a crucial adaptation for birds like starlings, which occasionally nest closer to the ground.   Conclusion  Birds have optimized their murmuring behaviors by regulating critical noise levels within the murmuration. Sufficient noise, namely a baseline number of individual aberrations within the flock, is essential to amplify external signals. These amplified signals generate large dynamic patterns within the murmuration which serve to resist predation. As a plain manifestation of bird murmurations being more than the sum of their parts, the formation of recurring patterns within the flock during flight reflects a certain collective conscience of the group. Birds must move themselves, but they can only do so successfully when coordinating with the entirety of their flock. This fact is further emphasized upon considering that murmurations exhibit a scale-free behavioral correlation. Thus, collective awareness results in the adoption of various efficient murmuration patterns for the survival of the flock. Directly, the minimization of the murmuration’s height in the vertical axis and the maximization of its width in the horizontal axis results in less drag being exerted on the birds and therefore a more efficient means of locomotion.   Mathematical models and geometric analyses deepen our understanding of avian biology, particularly in the context of starling murmurations. Indeed, the mechanisms underlying information transmission within murmurations are highly optimized and in many ways reflect the protocols which humans have implemented in computer systems to facilitate computationally intensive tasks. Networks composed of interconnected nodes receive and process information to conduct binary operations in deep learning: in the case of murmuring starlings, these binary operations consist of staying put or modulating their velocities with respect to those of their neighbors. While manifestations of biomimetics in technology are prevalent, they in many ways fail to compare to those of biological systems which have been fine-tuned and improved over the course of millions of years. Studying the mutual interactions between organisms, whether it be the emerging properties of a collective or a mutualism, can only serve to deepen our own prowess in engineering and technology.  Appendix The following expression in terms of w, L and B is a key relation in the universal egg equation.
